teile.einleitung: The second law of thermodynamics is one of the most important laws of nature in physics. Put simply, it says that disorder, called entropy, increases over time in an isolated system. It explains why hot tea cools down and why a bedroom does not tidy itself.
wichtigste: The second law says that entropy increases over time in an isolated system.
Put simply, entropy is a measure of disorder.
Heat flows by itself only from a warmer to a colder body.
It was formulated mainly by Rudolf Clausius, who taught in Zurich for a long time.
It shows that a perpetual motion machine is impossible.
It explains why many processes only run in one direction.

abschnitte.text: **Thermodynamics**, the science of heat, is a part of physics. It studies heat, energy and how they change from one form into another. The first law says that energy is never lost, but only changes its form. The second law says in which **direction** such changes happen by themselves.

**Entropy** is a physical quantity that is described simply as a measure of disorder. More precisely, it tells you in how many ways the particles of a system can be arranged. In an isolated system, which exchanges neither energy nor matter, it cannot decrease. That is why everything tends by itself towards an evenly spread state.

A hot cup of tea cools down in a room, but never gets hot again by itself. An ice cube in a glass of juice melts until everything has the same temperature. A drop of ink spreads out in water, but never gathers back into a drop on its own. And a child’s bedroom tends to get untidy, whereas tidying up costs **energy**.

In 1850 the German physicist **Rudolf Clausius** stated that heat cannot pass by itself from a colder to a warmer body. From 1855 to 1867 he taught at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today’s ETH. During his time in Zurich, in 1865, he introduced the term **entropy**. Earlier, in 1824, the Frenchman Sadi Carnot had laid important foundations on the efficiency of steam engines.

The second law shows that no machine can turn heat completely into work. Some is always lost to the surroundings as waste heat, for example in a car engine. A machine that runs for ever and does work at the same time, a **perpetual motion machine**, is therefore impossible. A fridge can make it colder inside, but it needs electricity to do so and gives off heat at the back.

The Austrian **Ludwig Boltzmann** explained entropy through the movement of countless particles and probability. Disordered states are simply far more likely than ordered ones. Because entropy increases, many processes only run in one direction; this is called the **arrow of time**. That is why you notice straight away when a film of a glass breaking is played backwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how disordered or evenly spread out a system is.
An area that exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings.
An imaginary machine that would run for ever without any supply of energy.
The part of physics that deals with heat and energy.

gewusst: Living things build up order, but only because they take in energy and in doing so make their surroundings all the more disordered.
Ludwig Boltzmann’s famous formula for entropy is written on his gravestone in Vienna.
Some researchers think that the universe might end in a state of maximum entropy in the distant future.

teile.einleitung: The cell wall is a firm covering that surrounds the cell in plants, fungi and bacteria. It gives the cell its shape and strength, rather like a framework or a box. Animal cells, and so our own cells too, have no cell wall.
wichtigste: The cell wall gives the cell its shape and strength.
In plants it consists mainly of cellulose.
Fungi have cell walls made of chitin, bacteria of murein.
Animal cells have no cell wall.
Lignin is laid down in cell walls and makes wood hard.
In 1665 Robert Hooke saw chambers in cork and coined the word “cell”.
Plasmodesmata connect neighbouring plant cells through the cell wall.

abschnitte.text: The **cell wall** lies outside the cell membrane, the thin skin that encloses every cell. It is firm but lets through water and many dissolved substances. Plants, fungi, algae and most bacteria have a cell wall. Animal cells, on the other hand, have none, which is why they are softer and can change their shape more easily.

In plants the cell wall consists mainly of **cellulose**, long chains of sugar building blocks. Cellulose is the most common natural substance on Earth, and paper and cotton are made of it. In wood, **lignin** is also laid down, which makes the walls hard and stable. Fungi have cell walls made of **chitin**, the same substance that insects' shells are made of. The most important building material of the bacterial cell wall is called murein.

In plant cells, water presses against the cell wall from the inside; this is called **turgor**. The cell wall withstands this pressure, which is why a plant cell does not burst in pure water. The pressure inside keeps leaves and stems firm. If there is not enough water, the pressure drops and the plant's leaves droop.

Neighbouring plant cells are connected to each other despite their walls. Through fine channels, the **plasmodesmata**, water, nutrients and signals can pass from cell to cell. In this way the cells of a plant work together like one big team. A single cell wall can contain thousands of these channels.

In 1665 the English researcher **Robert Hooke** examined a thin slice of cork under his microscope. He saw many small chambers that reminded him of monks' cells in a monastery. So he called them “cells”. What Hooke saw were actually the empty cell walls of dead cork cells.

Cell walls are very useful to us: wood, paper, cotton and linen are made of them. In our food they are important **dietary fibre**, which helps digestion. The cell wall also plays a part in medicine. The antibiotic penicillin disrupts the building of the bacterial cell wall so that the bacteria die, while our cells, which have no cell wall, are spared.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm substance made of sugar chains, of which plant cell walls are made.
A hard building material in fungal cell walls and insect shells.
The water pressure inside a plant cell.
A substance that turns cell walls woody and hard.

gewusst: A cotton thread consists almost entirely of cellulose.
Cows can only digest grass because microbes in their stomach break down the cellulose of the cell walls.
The slice of cork that Robert Hooke examined came from the bark of the cork oak.

teile.einleitung: Active noise cancelling is a technique that cancels out disturbing noise with anti-noise. Headphones with this feature produce a sound that is exactly the opposite of the noise. Together the two sound waves add up to almost silence.
wichtigste: Active noise cancelling is based on destructive interference.
A microphone picks up the disturbing noise.
The anti-noise is shifted in phase by 180 degrees so that the waves cancel each other out.
The technique works best with low, steady noises.
High sounds are blocked mainly by the passive insulation of the ear cushions.
There is a feedforward method and a feedback method.
Active noise cancelling is also used in aeroplane cabins and cars.

abschnitte.text: Noise is a sound wave that makes the air vibrate back and forth. In **active noise cancelling** a device deliberately produces a second sound wave. It is calculated so that it cancels out the noise. The technique is known as Active Noise Cancelling, or **ANC** for short.

When two waves meet, they overlap; this is called **interference**. If a wave crest meets a wave trough exactly, they cancel each other out. For this, the anti-noise must be **shifted in phase by 180 degrees** compared with the noise. This cancelling out is called **destructive interference**. You can imagine it like two children pulling on a rope equally hard in opposite directions.

A **microphone** in the headphones picks up the disturbing noise. A small chip calculates the matching anti-noise in fractions of a second, and the speaker plays it. In the **feedforward method** the microphone sits on the outside and measures the noise before it reaches the ear. In the **feedback method** it sits inside the ear cup near the speaker and checks what actually arrives. Good headphones combine both methods.

The technique works best with low, steady noises such as the hum of aircraft engines or trains. Such waves are long and easy to predict. High and sudden sounds, such as voices or clinking, are harder to cancel out. Here it is mainly the passive insulation of the ear cushions that does the blocking. That is why you can often still hear quiet conversations with such headphones.

The idea is old: the German physicist **Paul Lueg** applied for a patent for it in the 1930s. The technique only became usable, however, with fast electronics. Pilots were the first to use it, to protect their hearing in the noisy cockpit. Today it is found in many headphones and is also used in aeroplane cabins and cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: The overlapping of two or more waves.
Tells you at which point in its vibration a wave is at a given moment.
A sound wave that copies a noise exactly in mirror image.
Protection from noise by material, for example thick ear cushions.

gewusst: Two loud noises can add up to almost silence.
Some headphones have a transparency mode that deliberately lets outside sounds back in.
The idea of anti-noise was patented long before there were portable headphones.

teile.einleitung: Alpha decay is a kind of radioactive decay in which a heavy atomic nucleus ejects an alpha particle. In the process the nucleus turns into a different element. The process can only be explained with quantum physics and the astonishing tunnel effect.
wichtigste: In alpha decay a nucleus gives off a helium nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons.
Alpha decay occurs mainly in heavy nuclei.
Alpha decay turns radium-226 into radon-222.
The alpha particle leaves the nucleus thanks to the quantum mechanical tunnel effect.
Alpha particles typically have an energy of a few MeV.
The energy spectrum of a nuclide consists of sharp, discrete lines.
The Geiger-Nuttall rule says: the greater the energy of the alpha particles, the shorter the half-life.

abschnitte.text: In alpha decay an unstable nucleus ejects an **alpha particle**, that is two protons and two neutrons. As a result the atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number by 4. In this way, for example, **radium-226** becomes the noble gas **radon-222**. Alpha decay occurs mainly in heavy nuclei such as uranium, thorium, radium and polonium.

Inside the nucleus the strong nuclear force holds the particles together. Seen from outside, the nucleus is surrounded by an electrical repulsion, the **Coulomb barrier**. Strictly speaking the alpha particle has too little energy to get over this wall. According to quantum physics, however, it can slip through with a small probability, as if it were taking a tunnel through a mountain. George Gamow found this explanation through the **tunnel effect** in 1928.

Alpha particles from natural decays usually have an energy of a few **MeV**, that is millions of electronvolts. For a particular nuclide they always have precisely fixed energies. Their spectrum therefore consists of sharp, discrete lines. Because the alpha particle is much lighter than the remaining nucleus, it gets most of the kinetic energy. In the decay of radium-226 it is around 98 per cent; the rest goes to the new nucleus as **recoil**.

The **half-life** is the time after which half of the nuclei have decayed. It varies greatly among alpha emitters: uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, radium-226 of around 1600 years. In 1911 Hans Geiger and John Nuttall discovered a connection, the **Geiger-Nuttall rule**. The greater the energy of the alpha particles, the shorter the half-life.

Often the new nucleus is itself radioactive again and decays further. This produces whole **decay chains**, in which alpha and beta decays alternate. Thorium-232 decays through such a chain to stable lead-208. This chain contains exactly 6 alpha decays. Geologists also use such chains to work out the age of rocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particular kind of atomic nucleus with a fixed number of protons and neutrons.
A quantum effect by which particles get through a barrier even though their energy is really not enough to do so.
The time in which half of the radioactive nuclei decay.
Megaelectronvolt, a unit of energy for very small particles.

gewusst: The radon found in some cellars is produced by the alpha decay of radium in the ground.
Some alpha emitters decay in fractions of a second, others take billions of years.
Alpha decay was one of the first processes that could be explained with quantum physics.

teile.einleitung: The stopping distance is the whole distance a vehicle travels from the moment a danger is spotted until it comes to a standstill. It is made up of the reaction distance and the braking distance. If you understand it, you understand why speed and attention are so important in traffic.
wichtigste: The stopping distance is made up of the reaction distance and the braking distance.
The reaction distance is the distance you travel before you even brake.
The reaction distance does not depend on the brakes or the state of the road.
The braking distance increases with the square of the speed.
Twice the speed means roughly four times the braking distance.
On wet or icy roads the braking distance becomes much longer.
Distraction, for example by a mobile phone, makes the reaction distance longer.

abschnitte.text: When a driver sees a danger, first the **reaction time** passes, usually about one second. During this time the car carries on without braking; this is the **reaction distance**. Only after that does the **braking distance** begin, until the car stands still. Both together give the stopping distance. If the reaction distance is 14 m and the braking distance 12 m, the stopping distance is 26 m.

You calculate the reaction distance as speed times reaction time. For the braking distance the formula is v² divided by twice the **deceleration**. A car at 72 km/h travels 20 m per second. With a reaction time of 1 s and a deceleration of 10 m/s², that gives 20 m plus 20 m, so a stopping distance of 40 m. At 120 km/h and 8 m/s² it is already around 103 m, as long as a football pitch.

How strongly a car can brake depends on the tyres, the brakes and the road. On dry tarmac a car manages about 8 to 10 m/s². On a wet road it is often only 4 m/s², and on snow and ice much less still. At 20 m/s and a reaction time of 1 s, the stopping distance on a wet road increases to 70 m. That is why you should drive more slowly in the rain and keep a bigger gap.

If a child jumps onto the road 15 m in front of a car, every kilometre per hour counts. With a reaction time of 1 s and a deceleration of 8 m/s², a car at 30 km/h just manages to stop in time. At 50 km/h the car is still heading towards that spot almost without braking during that time. That is why many Swiss residential areas have **30 km/h zones** and shared zones.

If you look at your phone, you react much later. If the reaction time at 36 km/h goes up from 1 s to 2 s, the stopping distance becomes 10 m longer. Tiredness and alcohol also make the reaction time much longer. For children this means: cars cannot stop immediately, even if they seem to be going slowly. At a **zebra crossing** you should therefore wait until the vehicles have really stopped.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time between spotting a danger and pressing the brake.
The distance you still travel during the reaction time.
The distance from starting to brake until coming to a standstill.
How strongly a vehicle slows down when braking, measured in m/s².

gewusst: At 50 km/h a car travels almost 14 m in one second of reaction time.
With the same braking force, a car at 50 km/h has a braking distance almost three times as long as one at 30 km/h.
Driving schools teach a rule of thumb: the braking distance in metres is roughly the speed divided by 10, multiplied by itself.

teile.einleitung: Laundry detergents are cleaning products that loosen dirt and stains from clothes. A washing powder or liquid detergent contains a whole mixture of substances, each with its own task. They work together like a little team against fat, protein, starch and coloured stains.
wichtigste: Surfactants loosen fat and dirt from the fibres.
Enzymes called proteases remove protein stains such as blood or egg.
Amylases break down starch stains such as sauce or porridge.
Bleaches remove coloured stains such as tea or red wine.
Optical brighteners make white washing look brighter.
With hard water you need more detergent, because limescale interferes with the surfactants.
In Switzerland, phosphates in laundry detergents were banned because they over-fertilised the lakes.
Washing at 30 instead of 60 degrees saves energy, because the water has to be heated less.

abschnitte.text: Detergents come as **powder**, as liquid or as ready-made portions in small pouches. They are used together with water in the washing machine or when washing by hand. Thousands of years ago, people were already washing with **soap**, which was made from fat and ash. Modern detergents have existed since the early 20th century.

The most important substances in detergent are the **surfactants**. A surfactant particle has one end that likes water and one end that likes fat. The fat-loving end grabs the dirt, and the water-loving end holds on in the water. In this way the dirt is loosened from the fibre and washed away with the water.

**Enzymes** are tiny helpers that break certain substances down into small pieces. **Proteases** break down protein, for example in stains of blood, egg or grass. **Amylases** break down starch, for example from sauce, porridge or potatoes. Because enzymes already work at low temperatures, you can often wash at 30 or 40 degrees today.

**Bleaches** remove coloured stains such as tea, coffee, red wine or fruit juice. They are found mainly in detergents for white washing. **Optical brighteners** turn invisible ultraviolet light into bluish light. This makes white things look brighter, even though they are not cleaner.

In many areas of Switzerland the tap water is **hard**, which means it contains a lot of lime. Lime interferes with the surfactants, so more detergent is needed there. In the past, **phosphates** were used as water softeners. Because they over-fertilised the lakes and led to strong algae growth, Switzerland banned phosphates in laundry detergents in 1986.

The right amount is printed on the packet and depends on the water hardness and the dirt. Too much detergent does not make the washing cleaner but only pollutes the waste water. If you wash at 30 instead of 60 degrees, you save a lot of **energy**. Detergents should also be kept tightly closed and out of reach of small children, because they are not for eating.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that links fat and water and so loosens dirt.
A protein substance that breaks down certain other substances.
Shows how much lime is dissolved in the water.
A substance that works like fertiliser and used to be contained in detergents.
A substance that makes white washing look brighter through a bluish glow.

gewusst: The enzymes in detergents work in a similar way to the digestive substances in our stomach.
Optical brighteners glow under black light, which is why white T-shirts shine so brightly at the disco.
After the phosphate ban, many Swiss lakes became much cleaner again.

teile.einleitung: A meadow is an area where mainly grasses and herbs grow and which is mown regularly. A colourful flower meadow is a paradise for bees, butterflies, grasshoppers and many other animals. In Switzerland, meadows shape the landscape from the Central Plateau right up into the Alps.
wichtigste: Mainly grasses grow in a meadow.
A meadow is mown, while on a pasture the animals eat the grass directly.
Flower meadows are only mown late in summer so that the flowers can form seeds.
On flower meadows, bees find nectar and carry pollen from flower to flower.
A meadow that is fertilised little has more different flowers.
In summer, crickets and grasshoppers chirp in the meadow.
The skylark breeds on the ground in meadows and fields.

abschnitte.text: A meadow is an area of grass created by people that is **mown** regularly. Without mowing, bushes and trees would grow over time, and forest would develop. The cut grass is fed to cows, sheep and horses as fresh fodder or dried as **hay**. On a **pasture**, on the other hand, the animals eat the grass directly where it grows.

Most of what grows in a meadow is **grasses**, for example cocksfoot, meadow foxtail or false oat-grass. In between, herbs bloom, such as dandelion, oxeye daisy, meadow clary, clover and bellflowers. Which plants grow depends on the soil, the climate and the way the meadow is managed. A species-rich meadow can contain many dozens of different plant species.

A heavily fertilised **rich meadow** grows quickly and provides a lot of fodder, but it is often green and monotonous. A meadow that is fertilised little, a **nutrient-poor meadow**, grows more slowly but has many more different flowers. Especially valuable are **dry meadows** on sunny slopes, where rare orchids and butterflies are found. Switzerland protects its most valuable dry meadows and pastures in a national inventory.

Bees, bumblebees and butterflies collect **nectar** from the flowers. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower and so pollinate the plants. In summer, **crickets** and grasshoppers chirp in the grass. The skylark breeds on the ground, and brown hares, mice and earthworms also live in the meadow.

Flower meadows are only mown late in summer, so that the flowers can form **seeds**. That way they can spread again the next year. If a meadow is mown too early and too often, many flowers and animals disappear. Farmers in Switzerland receive payments if they mow species-rich meadows late.

In Switzerland there are meadows from the Central Plateau high up into the mountains. In mountain areas, hay is often still harvested on steep slopes, sometimes even by hand. Today many municipalities and private individuals create **flower meadows** in gardens and parks. Even a small patch of meadow that is not mown all the time helps insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dried grass that is used as winter fodder for animals.
An area of grass on which animals eat the grass directly.
A meadow that is fertilised little and has many different flowers.
Pollen gets from one flower to another so that seeds can form.
Sweet juice in flowers that bees and butterflies drink.

gewusst: Without regular mowing, most meadows in Switzerland would turn into forest over time.
Grasshoppers hear with ears that are on their legs or on their body.
Dozens of plant species can grow on a single square metre of nutrient-poor meadow.

teile.einleitung: Etiolation is the pale, long and thin growth of plants that stand in the dark. The plant puts all its energy into growing longer in order to reach the light as quickly as possible. You can easily observe this yourself with cress in a cupboard.
wichtigste: Etiolation is the pale, long growth of plants in the dark.
Seedlings in the dark grow long and thin.
Cress from a dark cupboard is yellowish and pale.
If you put pale seedlings in the light, they gradually turn green.
Under a paddling pool, the lawn turns yellow and pale after a few days.
White asparagus is deliberately grown without light so that it stays white.
A green plant that gets no light at all for a very long time dies.

abschnitte.text: When plants grow without light, they look quite different from normal. Their stems become very long and thin, the leaves stay small and the colour is **yellowish and pale**. This is called **etiolation**; in German it is called “Vergeilung”. The German word comes from an old meaning of “geil”, which used to mean something like “growing rampantly”.

Plants need light to make food with the green pigment **chlorophyll**; this is called photosynthesis. Without light the plant hardly makes any chlorophyll, which is why the green colour is missing. It then lives on the stores in the seed, the tuber or the bulb. It puts almost all of these stores into growing longer, so that it may still reach the light, like a seedling working its way up through the soil.

Sow cress in two bowls and put one of them in a dark cupboard for a week. The cress in the cupboard becomes **long, thin and pale**, while the other stays short, strong and green. If you then put the pale cress in the light, it gradually turns green, because it now makes chlorophyll. Potatoes that lie in a dark cellar for a long time also grow long, pale shoots.

Sometimes gardeners deliberately let vegetables grow in the dark. **White asparagus** grows under heaped-up ridges of earth and is cut before it reaches the light, so it stays white and tender. **Chicory** is also forced in the dark so that its leaves stay pale and less bitter. Celery is also protected from light so that the stalks become more tender.

If a paddling pool, a tent or a board stands on the lawn for a few days, the grass underneath is **yellow and pale** afterwards. It usually recovers if it gets light again quickly. But if a green plant gets no light at all for a very long time, it uses up all its stores and **dies**. Houseplants in places that are too dark often show slight etiolation, with long gaps between the leaves.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical term for pale, long growth in the dark; in German “Vergeilung” or “Etiolement”.
The green plant pigment that captures light.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.
A young plant that is just growing out of the seed.

gewusst: In the dark, an etiolated plant can grow much longer in a short time than a plant of the same age in the light.
Greenish asparagus forms when the asparagus tips come into daylight and make chlorophyll.
The bean sprouts that you buy in the shop have also grown etiolated.

teile.einleitung: The centimetre is a unit for measuring length and is abbreviated cm. One centimetre is a hundredth of a metre. Centimetres are used to measure things that are neither too big nor too small, such as a pencil, a book or a person's height.
wichtigste: Centimetre is abbreviated cm.
One centimetre has 10 millimetres.
100 centimetres make one metre.
The nail on your little finger is about 1 centimetre wide.
A new pencil is about 18 centimetres long.
A child aged 7 is about 120 centimetres tall.
The centimetre is the best unit for the length of a rubber.

abschnitte.text: The **centimetre** is a unit of length in the **metric system**. The prefix “centi” comes from the Latin word “centum” for a hundred. That is because a centimetre is one hundredth of a **metre**. A centimetre in turn is made up of 10 millimetres. That is why on a ruler the centimetres are marked with long lines and the millimetres with short lines.

The nail on your little finger is about 1 centimetre wide, which is a handy measure for estimating. A new pencil measures about 18 centimetres, and an A4 exercise book is just under 30 centimetres tall. **Height** is also usually given in centimetres; a 7-year-old child is about 120 centimetres tall. Clothes sizes and bike sizes are also often measured in centimetres. To measure, you use a **ruler**, a folding rule or a tape measure.

You calculate with centimetres just as with other numbers. 5 centimetres and 7 centimetres add up to 12 centimetres. If you cut 10 centimetres off a 30-centimetre ribbon, 20 centimetres are left. When **converting**, this rule helps: 1 m = 100 cm and 1 cm = 10 mm. So 1.5 metres are exactly 150 centimetres.

Units for areas and spaces are also made from the centimetre. A **square centimetre** (cm²) is a square with sides 1 centimetre long, about as big as a fingertip. A **cubic centimetre** (cm³) is a cube with edges 1 centimetre long. It holds exactly one millilitre of water. So one litre equals 1000 cubic centimetres.

The metric system with the metre and centimetre was invented in **France** at the end of the 18th century. Before that there were different measures everywhere, such as the ell, the foot or the inch, which made trade difficult. In Switzerland the metric system has applied since 1877. Today it is used in almost every country in the world. In the USA, however, people still often measure in **inches** in everyday life; one inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres long.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed amount used to measure something, for example the metre or the kilogram.
A tenth of a centimetre.
A straight measuring tool with a printed scale.
A system of measurement in which units are converted in steps of ten.

gewusst: In the morning you are about 1 to 2 centimetres taller than in the evening, because the discs in your back get squeezed a little during the day.
Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, so about one centimetre in three months.
The screen sizes of televisions and mobile phones are often given in inches, not in centimetres.

teile.einleitung: An ammeter is a measuring instrument used to measure electric current. It shows how many amperes are flowing through a circuit. For it to measure correctly, it has to be connected into the circuit in a particular way.
wichtigste: An ammeter is used to measure electric current.
The reading is given in amperes or milliamperes.
An ammeter is connected in series in the circuit.
It has a very small internal resistance so that it hardly obstructs the current.
Today the ammeter is usually part of a multimeter.
With a clamp meter you can measure current without opening the circuit.
Connected wrongly, an ammeter can cause a short circuit.

abschnitte.text: An **ammeter** shows how strong the electric current in a circuit is. The name is made up of ampere and the Greek word for measuring. There are instruments with a needle and scale and instruments with a digital display. It shows small currents in milliamperes and large ones in amperes. There are often several **measuring ranges** that you can switch between.

An ammeter must be connected in **series**. This means you break the circuit and put the instrument in the gap, so that all the current flows through it. So that it does not distort the measurement, it has a very small **internal resistance**. A voltmeter for voltage, on the other hand, is connected in parallel. Anyone who accidentally connects an ammeter in parallel across a battery causes a short circuit.

Older instruments often work with a **moving-coil movement**. In it the current flows through a small coil of wire between the poles of a magnet. The current turns the coil itself into a magnet, so that it turns and moves the needle. The stronger the current, the further the needle swings. Digital instruments, on the other hand, measure the voltage across a very small resistor and calculate the current from it.

Today people usually use a **multimeter**, which can measure current, voltage and resistance. You choose what is to be measured with a rotary switch. Electricians often use a **clamp meter**. It is simply placed round a cable and measures the magnetic field produced by the current. That way you do not have to break the circuit.

At school you build simple circuits with a battery, a small bulb and an ammeter. This shows you, for example, that the same current flows everywhere in a series circuit. In a parallel circuit, on the other hand, the current divides. It is important to start with the largest measuring range so that the instrument is not overloaded. Work on mains sockets is off limits for pupils.

begriffe.erklaerung: A circuit in which all the components lie one after another in the same current path.
The resistance of a measuring instrument itself.
A measuring instrument for current, voltage and resistance.
A direct connection between two terminals, through which a very large current flows.

gewusst: The first instruments for measuring current used a compass needle that was deflected by the current in the wire.
A clamp meter measures the current without touching the cable.
Many multimeters have their own small fuse built in for measuring current.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, the Web or WWW for short, is a huge network of linked web pages that you can look at with a browser. It was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN near Geneva, so very close to Switzerland. Today billions of people use it every day.
wichtigste: The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN.
In 1989 he submitted his proposal for a new information system.
Originally it was meant to help researchers share information.
Since the very beginning, web pages have been written in the language HTML.
The world's first website had the address info.cern.ch.
On 30 April 1993, CERN made the Web free for everyone.
The Web is not the same as the internet but a service that runs on it.

abschnitte.text: The **World Wide Web** consists of billions of web pages that are connected to each other by **links**. With one click you jump from one page to the next. To look at web pages you need a program called a **browser**. The Web is not the same as the internet: the internet is the worldwide network of computers, and the Web is one of the services that run on it, like email.

The British physicist and computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** worked at the research centre **CERN** on the border near Geneva. Thousands of researchers from all over the world worked there with different computers. In March 1989 he submitted a proposal for a new information system that would let them share knowledge easily. His boss is said to have written on it “vague but exciting”. The Belgian computer scientist Robert Cailliau helped him to build it.

Berners-Lee invented three things that still form the basis today. **HTML** is the language in which web pages are written. HTTP is the transfer protocol, that is, the rule for how pages get from the server to the browser. The URL is the address of a page, for example info.cern.ch. The world's first website ran at this address, on a NeXT computer at CERN.

On 30 April 1993, CERN announced that the Web could be used by everyone freely and at no cost. Nobody had to pay licence fees. In the same year the browser Mosaic appeared, which could also show pictures next to the text. After that the Web grew explosively. In 1994 Berners-Lee founded the **W3C**, which still sets the standards for the Web today.

Today about 5.5 billion people worldwide use the internet and therefore almost always the Web too (as of 2024). People read the news, watch videos, learn, play and shop. Learning websites like this one also run on the Web. To keep the Web safe for everyone, most sites now encrypt their data, which you can recognise by **HTTPS** in the address.

Not everything on the Web is true. You should check who is behind a site and whether the information is backed up. Only enter personal data such as your address or passwords on trustworthy sites. If you are unsure, it helps to ask your parents or teachers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program for looking at web pages, for example Firefox or Chrome.
The markup language used to build web pages.
A clickable reference that leads to another page.
The address of a web page.
The European Organization for Nuclear Research near Geneva.

gewusst: The world's first website can be seen again today at its old address info.cern.ch.
The computer on which the Web ran had a note on it warning people not to switch it off.
Tim Berners-Lee was knighted by the British Queen for his invention.

teile.einleitung: The cell membrane is a wafer-thin covering that surrounds every cell. It separates the inside of the cell from its surroundings and decides which substances may get in and out. Without the cell membrane there would be no life, because all cells have one.
wichtigste: All cells, from bacteria to human cells, have a cell membrane.
The cell membrane is selectively permeable; it lets only certain substances through.
It consists mainly of a double layer of fat molecules, the lipids.
In the fluid mosaic model, proteins float freely in the lipid layer.
The passage of water through a semi-permeable membrane is called osmosis.
Diffusion is the spreading of particles by themselves from high to low concentration.
Ions such as sodium or potassium get through the membrane via special channel and transport proteins.

abschnitte.text: The **cell membrane** is the outer boundary of every cell. It is only about seven to ten millionths of a millimetre thick and can therefore only be seen with an electron microscope. Even so, it holds the contents of the cell together and protects them. Plant cells also have a firm cell wall on the outside, with the cell membrane lying directly beneath it.

The membrane consists mainly of a **lipid bilayer**. Each lipid molecule has a water-loving head and two water-repelling tails. The heads point outwards towards the water and the tails point inwards towards each other, rather like a sandwich. Many **proteins** are built into this layer, and according to the **fluid mosaic model** from 1972 they float in it freely like islands.

The cell membrane is **selectively permeable**, which means it lets only certain substances through. Small particles such as oxygen or carbon dioxide can simply pass through it. Larger or electrically charged particles such as sugar or ions need **channel and transport proteins** to do so. Some of these proteins work like pumps and use energy in the process, for example the sodium-potassium pump in nerve cells.

Particles spread out by themselves from places of high to places of low concentration; this is called **diffusion**. In this way a drop of ink in a glass of water slowly spreads through the whole glass. When water passes through a semi-permeable membrane, this is called **osmosis**. If you put a red blood cell in distilled water, so much water flows in that it bursts.

On its surface the cell membrane carries identification marks by which cells recognise each other. In this way the immune system can tell the body's own cells from foreign ones. The membrane also contains **receptors**, which receive messenger substances such as hormones and pass signals on to the inside of the cell. Many organelles inside the cell are also surrounded by similar membranes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two layers of fat molecules that form the basic structure of the membrane.
Letting through only certain substances and not others.
The spreading of particles by themselves from high to low concentration.
The movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane.
A protein that recognises signals such as messenger substances and passes them on.

gewusst: It would take about 10,000 cell membranes stacked on top of each other to be as thick as a sheet of paper.
Soap bubbles are also made of a double layer of molecules with a water-loving and a water-repelling part.
The cell membrane is not rigid but about as runny as olive oil.

teile.einleitung: A brace is a device that slowly moves crooked teeth or a badly positioned jaw into the right position. Many children and teenagers in Switzerland wear a brace for a while. They are treated by an orthodontist.
wichtigste: You wear a brace so that your teeth become straight and your bite is right.
Orthodontists are the specialists in charge.
A brace that you can take out yourself is called a removable brace.
With a fixed brace, small plates called brackets are stuck onto the teeth.
With a fixed brace, thorough tooth brushing is especially important.
Many children get a brace between the ages of 9 and 14.
With a fixed brace you have to be careful with sticky and hard foods.

abschnitte.text: Some teeth grow crooked, are too crowded or have gaps that are too big. The upper and lower jaws do not always fit together well either. A **brace** applies gentle, constant pressure and so moves the teeth very slowly. Straight teeth are easier to clean and give a good **bite** for chewing.

The specialist field is called **orthodontics**, and the specialists are orthodontists. Often the school dentist or the family dentist sends a child for an assessment. There, X-rays and impressions or scans of the teeth are taken. Then a plan is made for how long and with which brace the treatment will be.

A **removable brace** is made of plastic and wires and can be taken out for eating and brushing. It only works if you really wear it for as many hours as prescribed. With a **fixed brace**, small plates called **brackets** are stuck onto the teeth and connected with an archwire. There are also almost invisible plastic aligners, which are changed regularly.

Many children get a brace between the ages of 9 and 14, because the jaws and teeth are still growing then. A treatment often lasts one to three years. Every few weeks the orthodontist checks the progress and adjusts the brace. After the brace is removed, you usually wear a **retainer** so that the teeth do not move back.

With a fixed brace, bits of food easily get stuck, so thorough **tooth brushing** after every meal is especially important. Special small brushes help you clean between the wire and the teeth too. Sticky foods such as chewing gum or caramel and hard things such as nuts or ice cubes can loosen the brackets. After an adjustment it often feels tight for a few days; that is normal and passes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The branch of dentistry that corrects crooked teeth and jaws.
A small plate that is stuck onto a tooth with a fixed brace.
A thin wire or a plastic splint that holds the teeth in position after treatment.
The way the upper and lower teeth meet.

gewusst: Teeth can only move because the bone around the tooth root slowly rebuilds itself.
Brackets are made not only of metal but also of see-through ceramic.
Adults can still wear a brace too, but the treatment then often takes longer.

teile.einleitung: The state of matter describes the form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas. With water you can easily observe all three states, as ice, as liquid water and as water vapour. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or a gas depends mainly on the temperature.
wichtigste: The three most important states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Water exists as ice, as liquid water and as water vapour.
Whether a substance is solid, liquid or a gas depends on temperature and pressure.
Water melts at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
The changes are called, for example, melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
The particle model explains the states well.
A fourth state is plasma, found for example in lightning and in the sun.

abschnitte.text: A **solid** substance such as ice or stone has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. A **liquid** such as water or milk has a fixed volume, but takes the shape of its container. A **gas** such as air or water vapour has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and spreads out through the whole space. Depending on the temperature, the same substance can exist in all three states.

All substances are made of tiny particles. In a solid the particles sit close together in an orderly way and only wobble in their places. In a liquid they are also close together, but can slide past each other. In a gas the particles fly quickly through the space, far apart from each other. The warmer a substance is, the more strongly its particles move.

When ice is warmed, it **melts** into water; when water cools, it **freezes** into ice. When water is heated, it **evaporates**, and on a cold window pane the vapour condenses back into drops. Some substances change directly from solid to gas; this is called sublimation. The opposite change is called deposition, and that is how hoar frost forms on cold winter days. Washing also dries in frosty weather, because the ice in it sublimates.

Water only boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there at a lower temperature. On the Jungfraujoch at around 3450 metres it already boils at below 90 degrees. That is why pasta takes longer to cook there. A **pressure cooker**, on the other hand, raises the pressure, so that water gets hotter than 100 degrees and food cooks faster.

Most substances shrink as they cool. Water is an exception: it is densest at 4 degrees Celsius and expands when it freezes. That is why **ice** floats on water and lakes freeze from the top. In this way fish can survive the winter at the bottom of the lake. This property is called the **anomaly of water**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The change from gas to liquid, for example on steamed-up windows.
The direct change from solid to gas.
The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil.
A very hot gas that conducts electricity, often called the fourth state of matter.

gewusst: Dry ice, made of frozen carbon dioxide, never becomes liquid but turns directly into gas.
Because water expands when it freezes, full glass bottles can burst in the freezer.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

teile.einleitung: Sugar is a sweet-tasting substance that we know mainly as white crystals from the kitchen. Chemically it belongs to the carbohydrates, which living things use as a source of energy. It is also fascinating how sugar dissolves in water and turns into caramel when heated.
wichtigste: The chemical name for table sugar is sucrose, and it is obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane.
Sugar dissolves well in water, but not in cooking oil.
A liquid in which sugar is completely dissolved is called a solution.
Stirring and warm water help sugar to dissolve faster.
Fine icing sugar dissolves faster than coarse sugar grains.
If you keep adding more sugar to water, at some point some is left lying on the bottom.
If you heat sugar strongly in a pan, caramel forms.

abschnitte.text: In everyday life **sugar** usually means table sugar, chemically called **sucrose**. It is made of two smaller sugar building blocks, glucose and fructose. In chemistry all these substances count as **carbohydrates**. Plants make sugar during photosynthesis with the help of sunlight.

Worldwide, sugar is mainly obtained from **sugar cane**, a tall grass from warm countries. In Europe, on the other hand, people use **sugar beet**. In Switzerland sugar beet is processed in the factories in Aarberg in the canton of Bern and in Frauenfeld in Thurgau. There the beet is sliced, the sweet juice is extracted, thickened and dried into crystals.

If you put sugar in water, the crystals slowly disappear, but the sugar is still there, because the water tastes sweet. The sugar particles spread out between the water particles and a **solution** forms. **Stirring**, warm water and fine sugar such as icing sugar speed up dissolving. In cooking oil, however, sugar does not dissolve; the grains simply stay where they are.

Water can only take up a certain amount of sugar, even though this amount is surprisingly large. At room temperature around two kilograms of sugar dissolve in one litre of water. Once this limit is reached, it is called a **saturated solution**, and any more sugar stays on the bottom. Even more sugar dissolves in hot water, which is used when making syrup.

If you heat sugar strongly in a pan, it first melts into a clear liquid. With more heat it turns golden yellow to brown and **caramel** forms with its typical smell. In the process the sugar molecules change chemically. If the sugar gets too hot, it burns and tastes bitter, so care is needed when caramelising, because hot sugar causes bad burns.

Sugar gives the body energy quickly; the brain and muscles especially need it. Too much sugar, however, can lead to being overweight and to tooth decay. The World Health Organization recommends eating only a little added sugar. A lot of sugar is hidden in fizzy drinks, ketchup or breakfast cereals, so it is worth looking at the list of ingredients.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name for table sugar.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that give the body energy.
A liquid in which another substance is completely dissolved.
A solution in which no more of a substance can dissolve.
A brown, aromatic substance that forms when sugar is heated strongly.

gewusst: At room temperature you can dissolve about twice as much sugar in a litre of water as the water itself weighs.
A sugar beet contains only about one sixth of its weight in sugar.
If you let a saturated sugar solution evaporate slowly, large sugar crystals grow, known as rock sugar.

teile.einleitung: Most substances shrink as they cool and become denser. Water is an exception: it is densest at about 4 °C and even expands when it freezes. This anomaly of water makes ice float and lets fish survive the winter.
wichtigste: Water is densest at about 4 °C.
If you cool water from 4 °C to 1 °C, its volume increases.
When water freezes, its volume increases by about 9 per cent.
Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³ and therefore floats on water.
A lake freezes from the surface downwards.
At the bottom of a deep frozen lake the water is about 4 °C.
Water freezing in rock cracks splits the rock apart; this is called frost shattering.

abschnitte.text: **Anomaly** means a departure from the rule. Almost all substances become denser as they cool and denser still as a solid. Water, on the other hand, only becomes denser down to about 4 °C. If it cools further, it expands again. When it freezes, it suddenly gets about 9 per cent bigger, and at 0.92 g/cm³ ice is lighter than liquid water.

The reason lies in **hydrogen bonds**. These are weak bonds between water molecules. In ice these bonds arrange the molecules in a regular **crystal lattice** with many empty spaces. That is why ice takes up more room than liquid water. Even shortly before freezing, small groups like this form, which is why water already expands below 4 °C.

In winter a lake cools from the top. Water at 4 °C, being the heaviest water, sinks to the bottom. Colder water stays at the top and finally freezes into a layer of ice. The ice acts like an **insulating layer** and protects the water below from cooling further. In this way fish and other animals survive the winter, even in mountain lakes such as Lake Sils in the Engadine, which freezes over every winter.

When water gets into cracks in rocks and freezes, it expands and presses with great force. Over time this breaks the rock apart; this is called **frost shattering**. In the Alps this creates slopes of scree below rock faces. Roads also get potholes in winter when water gets into cracks and freezes. Water pipes and glass bottles can burst in frosty weather.

Because ice is slightly lighter than water, only about a tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the sea. Most of it lies invisible below the surface, which is where the saying “the tip of the iceberg” comes from. Only a few other substances behave like water. One example is the metal **gallium**, whose solid form floats on its melt. Bismuth and silicon also expand when they solidify.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example grams per cubic centimetre.
A departure from normal behaviour.
A weak attraction between water molecules.
The breaking of rock by water freezing in cracks.

gewusst: Without the anomaly, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and many animals would die in winter.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst because the water needs more room when it freezes.
The metal gallium melts at only around 30 °C and can turn liquid in a warm hand.

teile.einleitung: Forgetting means that we can no longer remember something that we once knew. This happens to everyone every day, and it is even useful. But with a few tricks you can make sure that important things stay in your memory.
wichtigste: You forget most of something newly learned soon after learning it.
Repetition helps most against forgetting.
Forgetting is useful, because it allows the brain to get rid of unimportant things.
People who sleep too little forget more.
When a word almost comes to you, you say: it is on the tip of my tongue.
A shopping list helps you not to forget anything when shopping.
If you always put your house key in the same place, you forget less often where it is.

abschnitte.text: Our **memory** constantly stores impressions, but by no means everything stays. New things first land in the **short-term memory**, which holds only a few things for a short time. Only what is important or repeated gets into the **long-term memory**. Forgetting means that a memory has faded or that you cannot call it up at the moment.

In 1885 the German researcher **Hermann Ebbinghaus** was one of the first to study how quickly we forget. To do so, he learned meaningless syllables by heart and later tested how much he still knew. He found out that you forget most things **soon after learning**, and after that forgetting slows down. This pattern is called the **forgetting curve**.

What helps most is to **repeat** what you have learned, at ever greater intervals: after a day, after three days, after a week. A flashcard box uses exactly this principle. **Sleep** is also important, because during sleep the brain consolidates what you have learned during the day. People who sleep too little forget more.

For shopping you write a **shopping list**, and for appointments you use a diary. In the past, people tied a knot in their handkerchief to remind them of something. You are least likely to forget your house key if you always put it in the same place. Mnemonics, that is, little memory rhymes or sayings, help when learning sequences and rules.

If we remembered everything, our heads would be full of unimportant things such as every number plate we have ever seen. Through forgetting, the brain gets rid of **unimportant things** and can concentrate on what matters. Sometimes a memory is only blocked for a short time: the word is **on the tip of your tongue** but will not come. Often it pops up again later all by itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The brain's ability to store what has been experienced and learned.
A store for a few things over a short time.
A store for knowledge and memories over a long time.
A graph of how quickly what has been learned is lost over time.
A memory aid, for example a saying or rhyme.

gewusst: The short-term memory can only remember about seven things at the same time.
Very few people have such an exceptional memory that they can remember almost every day of their life.
A smell can suddenly bring back a long-forgotten memory.

teile.einleitung: Wild bees are all species of bee except the honeybee, which people keep as a domestic animal. In Switzerland alone there are about 600 different species, from tiny ones to the large carpenter bee. They are hard-working pollinators and essential for many flowers and fruit trees.
wichtigste: Wild bees are all species of bee except the honeybee.
About 600 species of wild bee live in Switzerland, and bumblebees are among them.
Most wild bees live alone and not in large colonies.
Many wild bees build their nest in the ground.
Wild bees pollinate flowers and are therefore very important for plants.
Wild bees do not make honey for people.
Most wild bees are very peaceful and hardly ever sting.

abschnitte.text: **Wild bees** are all the bees that are not kept by people, that is, all species except the honeybee. More than 20,000 species are known worldwide, and about 600 in Switzerland. The furry **bumblebees** are also wild bees. Some species are only a few millimetres long, whereas the violet **carpenter bee** is almost as big as a bumblebee.

abschnitte.titel: Nests in the ground and in wood
abschnitte.text: Most wild bees live as **solitary bees**, that is, alone, without a colony or a queen. Many species dig their nests in the ground, for example mining bees in sandy, open places. The **mason bee** uses hollow plant stems or holes in walls and seals its nesting tube with mud. The carpenter bee gnaws its tunnels into rotten wood, and the **leafcutter bee** lines its nest with round pieces that it cuts out of leaves.

Wild bees collect pollen and nectar and store a supply of it in each nest chamber. Their larvae later feed on it. Many species specialise in very particular plants and, for example, collect only from bellflowers or willows. If this plant is missing, the bee species cannot survive there.

When wild bees fly from flower to flower, they carry pollen with them and so **pollinate** the plants. Only pollinated flowers form fruit and seeds. With cherries, apples or strawberries, wild bees often make for a better harvest. Bumblebees even fly in cool weather, when honeybees are still staying in the hive.

In Switzerland, a large proportion of wild bee species are considered endangered. There is a lack of flowering meadows, open patches of ground and old wooden structures, and pesticides also harm them. If you want to help, you can plant native wild flowers in your garden or on your balcony and hang up a **bee hotel**. A patch of unmown meadow or a small heap of sand also provides a habitat for many species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bee that lives alone and does not form a colony.
Transferring pollen from one flower to another.
Fine flower dust that bees collect as protein-rich food.
A little house with tubes built by people, in which wild bees can nest.

gewusst: The violet carpenter bee is the largest wild bee in Switzerland and buzzes loudly, but it is very peaceful.
Some wild bees build their nests in empty snail shells.
Many wild bees fly for only a few weeks a year.

teile.einleitung: Ethology, also called behavioural biology or behavioural research, studies how and why animals behave. It asks, for example, why birds sing, how bees communicate or why goslings follow their mother. To find out, researchers patiently observe animals in the wild and in the laboratory.
wichtigste: Behavioural research studies the behaviour of animals.
Konrad Lorenz became famous because young geese followed him like a mother.
When goslings follow the first creature they see, it is called imprinting.
Animals that are active mainly at night are called nocturnal.
When watching wild animals, you have to be quiet and keep your distance.
For each observation, researchers note the date, time and place.
With binoculars or from a raised hide, you can watch animals from a distance.

abschnitte.text: **Behavioural biology** is a branch of biology that deals with the behaviour of animals and also of humans. It asks what an animal does, how it learns it and what it is useful for. Another name for it is **ethology**. It studies, for example, the search for food, communication, living together in groups and raising the young.

The Austrian **Konrad Lorenz** raised greylag geese, and the goslings ran after him as if he were their mother. The Dutchman Niko Tinbergen studied gulls and sticklebacks, among others, and the Austrian Karl von Frisch decoded the **waggle dance** of honeybees. All three received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine together in 1973. From 1960 the Briton Jane Goodall observed wild chimpanzees and discovered that they use tools.

Some behaviour is **innate**, for example a newborn mammal searching for milk. Other behaviour is learned, such as how a young bird sings its song. A special case is called **imprinting**: goslings follow the first moving creature they see shortly after hatching. Normally this is their mother; with Lorenz it was Lorenz himself.

Many animals have a fixed daily rhythm. **Nocturnal** animals such as owls, bats, hedgehogs and badgers search for food mainly in the dark. Diurnal animals such as most songbirds and squirrels are out and about during the day. Some animals, such as roe deer, are especially active at dusk and dawn.

If you want to watch wild animals, above all you have to **be quiet and keep your distance**, so that the animals are not disturbed. With **binoculars** you can see them well from a distance; hunters and researchers also use a **raised hide** at the edge of the forest. For each observation you write down the date, time and place, as well as exactly what the animal is doing. In Switzerland, for example, the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach studies the behaviour of birds, such as their migration to the south.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for behavioural research.
Rapid learning in a short period after birth that lasts a long time.
Awake and active mainly at night.
Innate behaviour that an animal does not have to learn.
A dance with which honeybees show other bees the way to food.

gewusst: With the waggle dance, bees even show the direction and distance of a source of food.
Crows and ravens can solve puzzles and use tools.
Today some animals carry small transmitters so that researchers can follow their routes precisely.

teile.einleitung: Probability says how good the chances are that something will happen. Some things are certain, some impossible, and many lie somewhere in between. With simple fractions you can even work out how big the chance is when rolling a dice or drawing a ball.
wichtigste: An event can be certain, possible or impossible.
Impossible means that it can never happen, for example a 7 with a normal dice.
It is certain, for example, that the sun will rise again tomorrow morning.
The probability of a 6 when rolling a dice is 1/6.
When tossing a coin, heads and tails are equally likely, 1/2 each.
You calculate: favourable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes.
Probabilities always lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

abschnitte.text: An event is **certain** if it happens in any case, for example drawing a red ball from a bag containing only red balls. It is **impossible** if it can never happen, such as rolling a 7 with a normal dice. In between there are likely and unlikely events. That it will snow in the city of Zurich in July, for example, is very unlikely.

If all outcomes are equally likely, you divide the number of **favourable outcomes** by the number of all possible outcomes. A dice has 6 sides, one of which is the 6, so the probability is 1/6. There are three even numbers (2, 4 and 6), so the chance of an even number is 3/6, that is, 1/2. If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, you draw a red one without looking with a probability of 3/10.

If there are 9 red balls and 1 blue ball in a bag, you will probably draw a red one. With 3 green and 3 yellow balls, both colours are equally likely. A **spinner** with 3 red and 1 blue section of the same size is more likely to stop on red, with a probability of 3/4. The larger the share of a colour, the greater its chance.

If you toss two coins, there are four equally likely outcomes: heads-heads, heads-tails, tails-heads and tails-tails. Only one of them is heads twice, so the probability is 1/4. You can also calculate: 1/2 times 1/2 makes 1/4. It is important to know that a coin has no memory: even after five heads in a row, the chance of heads on the next toss is again exactly 1/2.

In 1654 the mathematicians **Blaise Pascal** and Pierre de Fermat wrote letters to each other about games of chance and in this way laid the foundation of probability theory. In his book “Ars Conjectandi”, which came out in 1713, the Basel mathematician Jakob Bernoulli demonstrated the **law of large numbers**. It says that with very many trials, the results come closer to the calculated probability. So if you roll a dice thousands of times, the 6 comes up roughly every sixth roll.

The weather forecast often gives a probability of rain, for example 70 per cent. Insurance companies calculate how likely accidents or damage are. Games such as the Swiss board game Eile mit Weile or the lottery are also based on chance and probability. If you understand probabilities, you can judge risks better and are less easily fooled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A possible outcome of a trial, for example “rolling a 6”.
Something that cannot be predicted exactly; in German “Zufall”.
The outcomes that you hope for or that you count.
A share of a hundred; 50 per cent is the same as 1/2.

gewusst: In the Swiss lottery, the chance of winning the jackpot is only about 1 in 31 million.
Even in a class of 23 children, it is more likely than not that two have their birthday on the same day.
The term “law of large numbers” goes back to a mathematician from Basel, Jakob Bernoulli, even though he did not yet use the name himself.

teile.einleitung: The prototype metre was a metal bar that used to define exactly how long a metre is. The idea of the metre arose in France at the time of the Revolution and was based on the size of the Earth. Today the metre is no longer tied to a bar but to the speed of light.
wichtigste: The metre was introduced in France during the French Revolution.
It was based on the distance from the North Pole to the equator; a metre was one ten-millionth of it.
The international prototype metre of 1889 was made of platinum and iridium.
Its X-shaped cross-section meant that it hardly bent.
Its length applied exactly at 0 °C.
Since 1983 the metre has been defined using the speed of light.
The word “metre” comes from Greek and means “measure”.
The metric system has been compulsory throughout Switzerland since 1877.

abschnitte.text: In the past, almost every town had its own measures of length, such as the ell, the foot or the fathom, and they were of different lengths everywhere. This made trade very difficult. During the **French Revolution**, people wanted to create a single measure for everyone that was based on nature. This is how the **metre** came about; its name comes from the Greek word for measure.

A metre was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the **North Pole to the equator**. To determine this distance, the researchers Delambre and Méchain spent years from 1792 measuring the arc of the meridian between Dunkirk and Barcelona. From their measurements, a platinum bar was made in 1799, called the Mètre des Archives. Today we know that because of small measuring errors this bar turned out about 0.2 millimetres too short.

In 1875, 17 states, including Switzerland, signed the **Metre Convention**, an agreement on common measures. After that, a new international **prototype metre** was made of 90 per cent platinum and 10 per cent iridium and declared the standard in 1889. The bar had an **X-shaped cross-section** so that it hardly bent. Its length applied exactly at 0 °C, because metal expands when warm.

A metal bar can be damaged and changes with temperature. That is why in 1960 the metre was defined using the wavelength of light from krypton atoms. Since 1983 the metre has been the distance that **light** travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This fixes the **speed of light**, and every well-equipped laboratory in the world can determine the metre itself.

Until the 19th century, Switzerland had many cantonal measures, such as the Swiss foot of 30 centimetres. Since **1877** the **metric system** has been compulsory throughout Switzerland. Today the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for precise length measurements. Kilometres, centimetres and millimetres are all derived from the metre.

begriffe.erklaerung: A standard that used to define the exact length of a metre; in German “Urmeter”.
An imaginary line on the Earth that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole.
An international agreement of 1875 on common units of measurement.
A system of measurement based on the metre and steps of ten.
How fast light moves, about 300,000 kilometres per second.

gewusst: The prototype metre of 1889 is still kept in Sèvres near Paris today.
Today almost all countries in the world use the metre; only the USA still mainly uses feet and miles in everyday life.
Because the metre was derived from the Earth, a meridian circle of the Earth is almost exactly 40,000 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Inches and feet are old units of length that were originally based on parts of the body. Today they are used mainly in the USA, but we come across them here too, for example with screens or bike wheel rims. An inch measures exactly 2.54 centimetres, a foot exactly 30.48 centimetres.
wichtigste: A foot has 12 inches, and three feet make a yard.
The inch is called “Zoll” in German and measures exactly 2.54 cm.
A foot measures exactly 0.3048 m.
Screen diagonals and bike wheel rims are often given in inches.
In aviation, altitude is usually given in feet.
In everyday life, it is mainly the USA that still uses inches, feet and miles.
In the 19th century the Swiss foot measured exactly 30 cm.

abschnitte.text: In the past, people measured lengths with their own bodies. The **inch** was about the width of a thumb, the **foot** the length of a foot. Because people are different sizes, almost every town and every country had its own measure. A Basel foot was therefore not the same length as a Zurich foot. This made trade and building complicated.

A foot has 12 inches, and 3 feet make a **yard**. Since 1959 the units have been fixed exactly at international level: an inch measures 2.54 cm, a foot 0.3048 m and a yard 0.9144 m. The symbol for inches is often ″, for feet ′. So 10,000 feet are exactly 3048 metres, which is higher than most of the mountains in Switzerland.

In the 19th century many cantons agreed on a common measure. The **Swiss foot** was fixed at exactly 30 cm, so that it fitted in with the metric system. From 1877 the **metre** became the official unit of length throughout Switzerland. Since then, feet and inches have no longer been official measures here.

Even so, we come across the inch all the time. The size of televisions, computer screens and mobile phones is usually given in inches, measured diagonally across the **screen diagonal**. So a 55-inch television has a diagonal of 139.7 cm. Bike wheel rims, car tyres, pipes and screws are also often measured in inches, for example a 26-inch bike.

In aviation, **altitude** is given in feet almost everywhere in the world. A passenger aircraft often flies at about 35,000 feet, which is about 10.7 kilometres. Air traffic controllers speak of flight levels; FL 350 stands for 35,000 feet. The common unit makes sure that pilots from all over the world understand each other.

In everyday life it is mainly the **USA** that still uses inches, feet and miles. In Britain, miles are usual on road signs, but otherwise metric units are mostly used. The different systems can lead to expensive mistakes. In 1999 the space probe Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because two teams had used different units of measurement.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of length of 2.54 cm, “Zoll” in German.
A unit of length of 12 inches or 30.48 cm.
A unit of length of 3 feet or 91.44 cm.
The system of measurement with the metre, litre and kilogram, which is based on steps of ten.

gewusst: In German a foot is “Fuss”, and in English the plural of foot is feet.
Some rules still describe a football pitch in yards; for example, the penalty spot is 12 yards from the goal.
In the USA, the heights of mountains are given in feet on maps.

teile.einleitung: An active ingredient is the part of a medicine that actually produces the effect in the body. A tablet usually contains only a small amount of active ingredient; the rest are excipients. The doctor Paracelsus already realised that the right amount is always what matters.
wichtigste: The active ingredient produces the healing effect; excipients take care of shape, shelf life and easy intake.
An antagonist binds to a receptor and blocks it without activating it.
The doctor Paracelsus, born in Einsiedeln, taught in essence that the dose alone makes the poison.
A prodrug is an inactive precursor that only becomes the active ingredient in the body.
The therapeutic range describes the gap between an effective and a toxic dose.
Biologics are medicines whose active ingredients are made in living cells.
In 1897 Felix Hoffmann of the company Bayer produced acetylsalicylic acid in pure form.
The abbreviation INN stands for the international non-proprietary name of an active ingredient.

abschnitte.text: An **active ingredient** is a substance that has a particular effect in the body, for example relieving pain or bringing down a fever. In a tablet it is mixed with **excipients** such as starch, sugar or colourings. The excipients give the tablet its shape, make it keep longer and make it easier to swallow. Active ingredients come from plants, animals, fungi or bacteria, or are made in the laboratory.

abschnitte.titel: How does an active ingredient work?
abschnitte.text: Many active ingredients dock onto **receptors**, which are docking sites on the body's cells. You can imagine it like a key that fits a lock. An active ingredient that switches the receptor on is called an agonist. An **antagonist** only occupies the lock and blocks it without activating it.

The doctor **Paracelsus**, who was born in Einsiedeln around 1493, taught in essence: the dose alone determines that a thing is not a poison. Every active ingredient can do harm in too large an amount. The **therapeutic range** shows how big the gap is between the effective and the toxic dose. If the therapeutic range is small, the dose must be especially accurate.

A **prodrug** is a precursor that is inactive at first and is only converted into the active ingredient in the body, for example in the liver. **Biologics** are medicines whose active ingredients are made in living cells, such as antibodies. They are often used against serious illnesses such as rheumatism or cancer. Making them is very complicated.

Every active ingredient has a chemical name, an international non-proprietary name and often several brand names. The non-proprietary name is called the **INN** and is set by the World Health Organization. That is why the active ingredient ibuprofen has the same name all over the world, even if medicines containing it carry different brand names. A well-known example is acetylsalicylic acid, which **Felix Hoffmann** at Bayer produced in pure form in 1897 and which became known as aspirin.

The **Basel** region is an important centre of the pharmaceutical industry, with large companies such as Roche and Novartis. New active ingredients are researched and produced there. Before a medicine may be sold in Switzerland, it must be tested and approved by the authority **Swissmedic**. You should only ever take medicines as instructed by professionals or according to the package leaflet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in a medicine that has no healing effect but ensures its shape and shelf life.
A docking site on a cell to which a substance can bind.
The amount of an active ingredient that you take.
An active ingredient that blocks a receptor without switching it on.
The Swiss authority that tests and approves medicines.

gewusst: Acetylsalicylic acid is related to a substance in willow bark, which was used against pain long ago.
In some tablets the active ingredient makes up only a tiny part of the weight.
Paracelsus's real name was Theophrastus Bombast von Hohenheim.

teile.einleitung: Scientific misconduct means that researchers work dishonestly, for example by inventing data, faking results or copying texts. This is a serious offence, because science depends on people being able to rely on results. Fortunately, many such cases are discovered and exposed.
wichtigste: The three main forms are abbreviated FFP: fabrication, falsification, plagiarism.
Fabrication means inventing data; falsification means changing real data.
Plagiarism is copying someone else's work without naming the source.
A retracted scientific paper is officially considered no longer valid.
Well-known cases are Jan Hendrik Schön, Diederik Stapel and Andrew Wakefield.
The platform Retraction Watch collects retracted scientific papers.
Honorary authorship and salami slicing are also considered questionable practices.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **scientific misconduct** when researchers deliberately or through gross negligence break the rules of good science. The three most serious forms are abbreviated **FFP**, after the words fabrication, falsification and plagiarism. Fabrication means simply making data up. Falsification means changing real data so that it fits better. **Plagiarism** is copying other people's ideas or texts without naming the source.

Besides FFP there are smaller offences. With **honorary authorship**, someone is listed as an author of a paper without having made a significant contribution. With **salami slicing**, the results of one study are spread over as many small papers as possible, so that the list of publications gets longer. Leaving out measurements that do not fit can also be a problem. Practices like these distort the picture of research.

The German physicist **Jan Hendrik Schön** worked at Bell Labs in the USA. He published many sensational papers about new kinds of components in electronics. In 2002 it was discovered that he had faked measurement data; among other things, identical curves turned up in different experiments. Many of his papers were retracted, and his doctorate was later taken away from him.

In 1998 the British doctor **Andrew Wakefield** claimed in the journal “The Lancet” that there was a link between the measles vaccination and autism. Later investigations showed serious flaws and dishonesty, and in 2010 the study was retracted. Many large studies have since shown that there is no such link. The Dutch social psychologist **Diederik Stapel** had invented data for studies for years and was exposed in 2011.

Fakes are often noticed when other researchers cannot repeat an experiment. Attentive colleagues, students or experts who check pictures and numbers carefully also uncover a great deal. If a mistake or fraud is confirmed, the paper is **retracted**; this is called a retraction. The online platform **Retraction Watch** has been collecting and commenting on such cases since 2010.

In Switzerland, the Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences have published a **Code of Conduct for Scientific Integrity**. It sets out what good scientific practice is, such as handling data honestly and citing correctly. Universities have offices that people can turn to if they suspect misconduct. Pupils, too, learn to name their sources and not to copy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Passing off other people's texts or ideas as your own without naming the source.
A report on a piece of research in a scientific journal.
The official withdrawal of a scientific paper.
Honesty and reliability in your own work.

gewusst: Before he was exposed, Jan Hendrik Schön was considered a possible candidate for a Nobel Prize.
In 2010 Andrew Wakefield lost his licence to practise as a doctor in Britain.
There are now computer programs that track down faked or copied pictures in scientific papers.

teile.einleitung: In science, repetition means carrying out an experiment or a measurement again in exactly the same way. Only if a result comes out several times can you really trust it. A single experiment can easily give a result that happened by chance.
wichtigste: Researchers repeat experiments to check whether the result is right.
A repetition must take place in exactly the same way as the first experiment.
A single experiment can easily show a chance result.
So that others can copy an experiment, a precise description is needed.
