When other researchers copy an experiment too, you see whether the result is really right.
The same values in several measurements show that a measurement is reliable.
When results fluctuate, you measure more often and compare.

abschnitte.text: In an **experiment**, you ask nature a question and test it with a trial. If you repeat the trial under the same conditions, roughly the same thing should come out. If that is the case, the result is **reliable**. If something different comes out each time, you have to look more closely.

A single experiment can be influenced by **chance**. A gust of wind, a small measuring error or a special day can distort the result. That is why, for example, you count birds in the garden on several days, because every day can be different. Only many repetitions show what is typical.

A paper aeroplane flies 3 metres once, 5 metres once and 4 metres once. With so few throws you do not yet know exactly how far it usually flies. It is best to throw it more often and compare the distances. From all the values you can then calculate the **mean**, which here would be 4 metres.

abschnitte.titel: Repeating in exactly the same way
abschnitte.text: A repetition only makes sense if it takes place in **exactly the same way** as the first experiment. You use the same materials, the same measuring instruments and the same method. If Tom measures the length of a leaf three times and gets 6 centimetres each time, his measurement is reliable. If the values vary a lot, perhaps the measuring was inaccurate.

In science it is important that **other researchers** can also copy an experiment. This requires a precise description of the materials, procedure and measurements, the **lab report**. If other teams come to the same result, it is regarded as confirmed. This ability to be checked is called **reproducibility**.

Repetitions protect against wrong conclusions and errors. Before a new medicine is approved, for example, its effect is tested in many studies with many people. In the classroom, too, it is worth taking measurements several times. In this way you learn to trust results only once they have been confirmed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned trial with which you test a question.
The average of several measurements.
A precise description of how an experiment took place and what came out of it.
A result can be confirmed by others with the same experiment.

gewusst: Some famous discoveries turned out to be wrong because other researchers could not repeat them.
The more often you measure, the less individual outliers count.
Repetition also helps with learning, because knowledge stays in the memory better.

teile.einleitung: In additive colour mixing, new colours are made by laying coloured light on top of each other. Almost all colours can be mixed from red, green and blue, and together they make white. This is exactly how every screen conjures up its colourful pictures.
wichtigste: The three primary colours of additive colour mixing are red, green and blue.
If you mix all three equally bright, you get white.
If none of the three lamps is on, you see black.
Green and blue light together make cyan.
The mixing is called additive because light is added and the mixture gets brighter.
In 1853 Hermann Grassmann described the laws of additive colour mixing.
Screens use additive colour mixing; there, orange is made from a lot of red, some green and no blue.

abschnitte.text: In additive colour mixing, lights of different colours are mixed together. The three **primary colours** are red, green and blue, abbreviated **RGB**. Each extra light makes the mixture brighter. That is why it is called additive, from the Latin word for adding. If no light shines at all, it stays black.

Red and green together make yellow. Green and blue make **cyan**, a bright turquoise blue. Red and blue make **magenta**, a strong pink. All three together make white. If you change the brightness of the three lights, millions of other shades are created.

In our retina there are three kinds of **cones**, sense cells for colour. One kind reacts mainly to red light, one to green and one to blue. The brain compares the signals and creates the impression of colour from them. That is why mixing just these three colours is enough to fake almost any colour.

Mobile phones, televisions and computer screens are made up of millions of tiny dots, the **pixels**. Each pixel has a red, a green and a blue part, each of which can shine brighter or darker. From a distance they merge in the eye into one colour. For orange, for example, there is a lot of red, some green and no blue. Stage spotlights and coloured LED lamps also mix their colours in this way.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton already showed that white light is made up of all colours. In 1853 the German mathematician **Hermann Grassmann** described the laws of additive colour mixing. In 1861 the Scottish physicist **James Clerk Maxwell** showed one of the first colour pictures. To do so, he projected red, green and blue partial images of a tartan ribbon on top of each other.

With coloured pencils and watercolours mixing works differently. There each colour swallows part of the light, so the mixture gets darker. This is called **subtractive colour mixing**. Printers work this way with cyan, magenta, yellow and black.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for red, green and blue, the primary colours of light.
A tiny dot of an image on a screen.
Sense cells in the eye with which we see colours.
Mixing of dyes or paints in which the mixture gets darker.

gewusst: Yellow on a screen contains no yellow light at all, only red and green.
With a magnifying glass you can make out the little red, green and blue dots of light on many screens.
White light on a mobile phone screen is made when all three colour dots shine at full strength.

teile.einleitung: The Vostok ice core is a column of ice more than three kilometres long that was drilled out of the ice at the Vostok research station in Antarctica. The ice is like an archive: it stores how warm it was and what the air was made of. In this way the core shows the climate of roughly the last 400,000 years.
wichtigste: Vostok station lies on the East Antarctic Ice Sheet.
In 1983 a temperature of minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was recorded there, the lowest air temperature ever measured at a weather station.
Russia, France and the USA analysed the ice core together.
The ice core covers about four ice-age cycles.
Air bubbles in the ice are samples of the atmosphere from the time when the ice formed.
Past temperatures can be read from the ratio of heavy to light isotopes in the water.
Temperature, CO2 and methane largely moved in parallel.

abschnitte.text: **Vostok** station was founded by the Soviet Union in 1957 and lies in the middle of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It is at about 3500 metres above sea level because the ice there is so thick. On 21 July 1983, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was measured here, the cold record at a weather station. Hidden beneath the ice lies the huge **Lake Vostok**, a lake of liquid water under almost four kilometres of ice. Today the station is run by Russia.

An **ice core** is a long, round column of ice that is brought up piece by piece from the ice with a hollow drill. At Vostok, drilling went on for many years until, in 1998, a depth of over 3600 metres was reached. The ice formed from snow that fell year after year and was pressed together. The deeper you drill, the older the ice. The lowest layers that can be analysed are about 400,000 years old.

Real air from the past is trapped in tiny **air bubbles**. From it, you can measure how much carbon dioxide and methane there used to be in the atmosphere. The temperature at the time can be read from the **isotopes** of the water: in cold periods the snow contains fewer heavy water molecules. Dust and volcanic ash in the ice also tell us something about the past climate. In this way every layer of ice becomes a page in a climate diary.

The analysis by researchers from Russia, France and the USA was published in 1999. It showed about four **ice-age cycles**, that is, an alternation of long cold periods and shorter warm periods. The CO2 level varied between about 180 ppm in ice ages and about 300 ppm in warm periods. Temperature, CO2 and methane rose and fell largely together. Today the CO2 level of the air, at over 420 ppm (as of about 2025), is clearly higher than at any time in these 400,000 years.

The Vostok ice core was a milestone in **climate research**. It showed impressively how closely greenhouse gases and temperature are linked. Later the European ice core **EPICA Dome C** went back as far as about 800,000 years. The University of Bern, one of the leading centres for ice core analysis, played a major part in this research. Today researchers are looking for even older ice that is more than a million years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long column of ice drilled out of a glacier or ice sheet.
Forms of the same chemical element that have different weights.
Parts per million, a measure of how much of a substance is in the air.
The alternation between a long cold period and a shorter warm period.

gewusst: The drilling was deliberately stopped above Lake Vostok so that the lake water would not be polluted.
The ice at great depth is under such high pressure that it can crack and shatter after being brought up.
At Vostok the air is so thin and cold that even walking is hard work.

teile.einleitung: Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist who invented the world’s first battery around 1800. His voltaic pile was the first to supply a steady electric current. The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after him.
wichtigste: Alessandro Volta came from Italy and was born in Como in 1745.
Around 1800 he invented the voltaic pile, the first usable battery.
He was inspired by Luigi Galvani’s experiments with frogs’ legs.
In 1801 he demonstrated his invention to Napoleon.
He discovered the gas methane in a marsh.
The unit volt is named after him and gives the electrical voltage.
A normal socket in Switzerland has 230 volts.

abschnitte.text: Alessandro Volta was born in 1745 in **Como** on Lake Como, not far from the Swiss border at Chiasso. Even as a young man he was fascinated by electricity. Later he became professor of physics at the University of **Pavia**. He died in 1827 in his home town of Como.

In 1775 Volta improved the **electrophorus**, a device with which you can produce and store electric charge. In 1776 he studied gas bubbles rising from the mud of a marsh on Lake Maggiore. In doing so he discovered the flammable gas **methane**. He even built a kind of pistol in which an electric spark set the gas alight.

The doctor Luigi Galvani from Bologna had observed that frogs’ legs twitch when touched with two different metals. Galvani believed that the electricity came from the animal itself. Volta disagreed and suspected that the current was produced by the contact between the two metals. To prove this, he carried on researching and in doing so invented the battery.

Around 1800 Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper alternately on top of each other. Between them he put pieces of cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water. This tower, the **voltaic pile**, supplied a lasting electric current for the first time. In 1801 Volta demonstrated his invention to **Napoleon** in Paris, who later made him a count.

The voltaic pile was the starting point for the study of electric current. Shortly afterwards researchers used it to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. In Volta’s honour the unit of electrical voltage is called the **volt**. The number of volts on a battery gives its voltage; a socket in Switzerland has 230 volts. In Como the Tempio Voltiano museum commemorates the famous scientist.

begriffe.erklaerung: The push that makes electric current flow, measured in volts.
The first battery, a stack of metal discs and soaked cardboard.
An old device for producing electric charge.
A flammable gas that forms, for example, in marshes.

gewusst: Volta’s portrait used to be on the Italian 10,000 lire note.
Volta’s name is on every device that has a voltage given in volts.
You can even build a simple battery with a lemon, a copper coin and a galvanised nail.

teile.einleitung: Xavier Mertz was a Swiss polar explorer from Basel who took part in one of the most dramatic expeditions to Antarctica. With the Australian Douglas Mawson and the Briton Belgrave Ninnis, he explored unknown land. Only Mawson survived this journey; Mertz died on the ice in January 1913.
wichtigste: Xavier Mertz was born in Basel in 1882.
He travelled to Antarctica with Douglas Mawson's expedition.
As a skier and mountaineer he was well prepared for the ice.
On the expedition he was in charge of the sledge dogs.
In December 1912 his companion Belgrave Ninnis fell into a crevasse.
Mertz died in 1913, according to today's assumption from poisoning by vitamin A.
The Mertz Glacier in Antarctica is named after him.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Basel on the ice
abschnitte.text: **Xavier Mertz** was born in Basel on 6 October 1882. He studied law and natural sciences and earned two doctorates, including at the universities of Bern and Lausanne. In his free time he was an enthusiastic **mountaineer** and climbed Mont Blanc, among other peaks. As a **skier** he was very successful and became Swiss ski jumping champion in 1908.

From 1911 the Australian geologist **Douglas Mawson** led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition. He took on Mertz as a ski expert, which was unusual at the time, because he had actually wanted to take mainly Britons and Australians. The group travelled to Antarctica on the ship Aurora and built its camp on the coast at **Cape Denison**. It is one of the windiest places on Earth. Mertz and Belgrave Ninnis were in charge of the **sledge dogs**.

In November 1912 Mawson, Mertz and Ninnis set off to explore unknown land to the east. Mertz went ahead on skis and found the way for the dog sledges. On 14 December 1912 Ninnis fell into a deep **crevasse** with the biggest sledge and the strongest dogs. With him went the tent and most of the food. Mawson and Mertz were about 500 kilometres from the camp.

On their desperate journey back, the two men had to kill and eat their remaining dogs. They also ate the dogs' **liver**, which contains a great deal of vitamin A. Mertz grew weaker and weaker and died on 8 January 1913. According to today's assumption he died of **vitamin A poisoning**, but this is not certain. Mawson struggled on alone.

About a month later Mawson reached the camp at Cape Denison. The expedition ship Aurora had left only a few hours before. However, some men had stayed behind to search for the missing explorers. Mawson therefore had to spend another whole winter in Antarctica before he was picked up at the end of 1913.

Mawson named the **Mertz Glacier** in East Antarctica after his Swiss companion. It was the first glacier the three had crossed on their journey. At the camp at Cape Denison, a wooden cross commemorates Mertz and Ninnis. Mawson later wrote that Mertz had been a brave and cheerful companion.

begriffe.erklaerung: A research journey into an unknown or hard-to-reach area.
A deep crack in glacier ice, often hidden by snow.
A vital substance that can be poisonous in very large amounts.
The ice-covered area around the South Pole.

gewusst: The story of Mawson's survival is considered one of the great heroic tales of polar exploration.
Douglas Mawson was later pictured on the Australian 100-dollar note.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne is a large museum about transport and mobility. There you can see trains, ships, aircraft, cars and even space travel up close. Since it opened in 1959 it has been one of the most visited museums in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Swiss Museum of Transport is in Lucerne on Lake Lucerne.
It was opened in 1959.
Its subject is transport and mobility.
You can look at trains, ships and aircraft.
The planetarium shows the starry sky.
It is one of the most visited museums in Switzerland.
You can try out many of the exhibits yourself.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Museum of Transport**, in German “Verkehrshaus der Schweiz”, is in the Lido district of **Lucerne**, right on the shore of Lake Lucerne. It was opened on 1 July **1959** and has been extended again and again since then. It is run by an association, not by the state. It is one of the **most visited museums** in Switzerland.

In the rail transport hall there are numerous real **locomotives** and carriages from more than 150 years of railway history. They include the famous brown Gotthard locomotive with the nickname “Crocodile”. Visitors can feel like a **train driver** in the simulator. In the road transport exhibition there are bikes, carriages, PostBuses and cars from different periods.

In the aviation section, real aircraft are on display, for example a passenger plane of the former Swissair of the type Convair Coronado. Shipping on Swiss lakes is also a topic, with boats, model ships and bridge controls. A separate area tells the story of **space travel** and of how people fly into space. In this way the museum shows how people and goods travel by land, by water and in the air.

In the **planetarium**, the starry sky is projected onto a round dome, so that you feel as if you were under the night sky. There you learn how stars, planets and galaxies are structured. In the large film theatre, documentaries are shown on a huge screen. In the Swiss Chocolate Adventure you experience on a ride how chocolate is made and transported.

The Museum of Transport is a museum for **touching and trying things out**. At many stations, children can press buttons themselves, explore vehicles and try out technology. In the outdoor area there are playgrounds and vehicles to discover. The Hans Erni Museum, which shows works by the Lucerne artist Hans Erni, is also part of the Museum of Transport.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to move from place to place.
A room with a dome in which the starry sky is shown artificially.
A person who drives a locomotive.
A device that imitates a real situation, for example a train journey.

gewusst: The Gotthard locomotive “Crocodile” got its nickname because of its long, narrow front sections, which look like a crocodile.
The Museum of Transport owns a collection of many thousands of objects, of which only some are on display.
On a large aerial photo that you can walk on, you can stroll across the whole of Switzerland in the Museum of Transport.

teile.einleitung: Cell theory is one of the most important basic ideas of biology. It states that all living things are made of cells and that every cell comes from another cell. It was developed in the 19th century by German researchers.
wichtigste: Cell theory says that all living things are made of cells.
In 1838 the botanist Matthias Jacob Schleiden declared that all plants are made up of cells.
In 1839 Theodor Schwann applied cell theory to animals.
Schleiden and Schwann wrongly believed that cells formed from a shapeless mass.
Around 1852 Robert Remak was one of the first to show that cells form by division.
As early as 1831, Robert Brown had described the nucleus as a regular part of plant cells.
The covering cells around nerve fibres are named after Theodor Schwann.

abschnitte.text: **Cell theory** sums up three principles. First, all living things consist of one or more cells. Second, the cell is the smallest unit of life. Third, every cell arises only from a cell that already exists, through **cell division**. Today these ideas are regarded as the foundation of the whole of biology and medicine.

As early as 1665, Robert Hooke had seen small chambers in cork and called them cells. A little later Antoni van Leeuwenhoek discovered living single-celled organisms with his powerful lenses. For a long time, however, people did not know that cells occur in all living things. Better **microscopes** in the 19th century made more accurate observations possible. In 1831 Robert Brown described the **nucleus** as a regular part of plant cells.

In 1838 the German botanist **Matthias Jacob Schleiden** declared that all plants are made up of cells. He considered the cells to be the actual building blocks from which a plant is put together. Schleiden discussed his observations with the physiologist Theodor Schwann. In doing so they noticed that animal tissues also show similar structures. This gave rise to the idea that plants and animals are built on the same principle.

**Theodor Schwann** worked in Berlin for the famous physiologist **Johannes Müller**. In 1839 he showed in a book that animals are made of cells too. Back in 1836 he had discovered the digestive enzyme **pepsin** in the stomach. Schwann cells, which wrap around nerve fibres like insulation, are named after him. With this, cell theory was extended to all living things.

Schleiden and Schwann still believed that new cells formed from a **shapeless mass**, rather like crystals in a liquid. Around 1852 the researcher **Robert Remak** was one of the first to show that cells form by division. The doctor **Rudolf Virchow** made this finding famous with the Latin sentence “Omnis cellula e cellula”. It means: every cell comes from a cell. Virchow also realised that many diseases can be traced back to changed cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: The teaching that all living things are made of cells and that cells come from cells.
The process in which one cell becomes two new cells.
A researcher who studies plants.
A researcher who studies how bodies and organs work.
A protein that speeds up processes in the body, such as digestion.

gewusst: Schleiden was originally a lawyer before he devoted himself entirely to plants.
For a long time Robert Remak received little recognition, because many people regarded the better-known Virchow as the discoverer of cell division.
Cell theory later helped people to understand how wounds heal and how diseases such as cancer develop.

teile.einleitung: Evaporation is the process in which liquid water slowly turns into invisible water vapour and escapes into the air. This happens without the water having to boil. That is why puddles, washing and wet hair dry all by themselves.
wichtigste: In evaporation, water passes into the air as an invisible gas.
Water as an invisible gas is called water vapour.
A bowl of water on the windowsill gets emptier and emptier over time.
Water evaporates faster in the sun, in warmth and in wind.
Water evaporates faster in a wide, shallow bowl than in a narrow glass.
If salt water evaporates completely, the salt is left behind.
Evaporation cools, which is why people sweat in the heat.

abschnitte.text: Water consists of tiny particles that are constantly moving. At the surface, individual fast particles can leave the liquid and fly into the air. This process is called **evaporation**. The water turns into **water vapour**, an invisible gas. Unlike boiling, this happens even at normal temperatures, and even when it is cold.

Heat is the most important driving force, which is why water evaporates faster in the sun than in the shade. **Wind** also helps, because it blows away the damp air above the water. A large **surface** is also important, which is why water dries faster in a wide, shallow bowl. If the air is already very damp, on the other hand, only a little evaporates.

Wet washing dries fastest outside in sun and wind. Puddles after rain also disappear by themselves after a while. When we sweat, the sweat evaporates on the skin and takes heat with it. You can also feel this **evaporative cooling** when you come out of the swimming pool wet and the wind is blowing.

Substances dissolved in water, such as salt, do not evaporate with it. If you let salt water evaporate completely, the salt is left behind as white crystals. In warm countries, sea salt is obtained in this way in shallow basins, the **salt pans**. In Switzerland, salt is obtained from salt solutions that are pumped out of the ground and then evaporated, for example in Schweizerhalle, Riburg and Bex.

Every day huge amounts of water evaporate from seas, lakes, soils and plants. The water vapour rises, cools high up and forms clouds. From these, rain or snow later falls again. So without evaporation there would be no **water cycle** and hardly any precipitation on land.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in the form of an invisible gas.
The cooling that occurs when water evaporates and takes heat with it.
The constant journey of water from sea and land into the air and back as rain.
The amount of water vapour contained in the air.

gewusst: Snow and ice can also turn directly into water vapour without melting first.
On a hot summer's day, a large tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water through its leaves.
The visible white “steam” above a cup of tea is actually already tiny water droplets again.

teile.einleitung: Antimatter is the mirror image of ordinary matter. For every particle there is an antiparticle with the same mass but the opposite charge. When matter and antimatter meet, they disappear and turn into pure energy.
wichtigste: With his equation for the electron, Paul Dirac predicted the positron.
Carl D. Anderson detected the positron in cosmic rays in 1932.
When an electron and a positron meet, they usually annihilate into gamma photons.
An antiproton has a negative elementary charge.
In 1995 antihydrogen atoms were made for the first time at CERN.
Positron emission tomography (PET) in hospitals uses positrons.
Why there is almost only matter in the universe is an unsolved mystery.

abschnitte.text: Every particle has an **antiparticle**. The antiparticle of the electron is called the **positron** and is positively charged. The antiproton, on the other hand, is negatively charged. An antihydrogen atom can be built from an antiproton and a positron. Antimatter has the same mass as normal matter.

In 1928 the British physicist **Paul Dirac** set up an equation for fast electrons. It followed from it that there had to be a positively charged counterpart. In 1932 the American **Carl D. Anderson** actually found this positron in cosmic rays. Both received a Nobel Prize for this. In 1955 the antiproton was also discovered in California.

When matter and antimatter meet, they destroy each other. This **annihilation** turns all their mass into energy, usually into gamma radiation. According to Einstein’s formula E = m · c², 1 g of antimatter and 1 g of matter give around 1.8 · 10^14 joules. That is about as much electricity as a large nuclear power station such as Gösgen supplies in about two days. Unfortunately, making antimatter costs far more energy than you get back.

**CERN** near Geneva is the most important centre for antimatter research. In 1995 a few antihydrogen atoms were made there for the first time. Today the Antiproton Decelerator slows antiprotons down so that researchers can catch them in **magnetic traps**. In 2023 the ALPHA-g experiment showed that antihydrogen falls downwards in a gravitational field just like normal matter. Altogether only tiny amounts have been made so far, much less than a millionth of a gram.

In hospitals antimatter is used in **positron emission tomography**, PET for short. Patients are injected with a weakly radioactive substance that gives off positrons. The positrons immediately annihilate with electrons in the body. The resulting gamma rays are measured and show, for example, where tumours are.

In the Big Bang equal numbers of particles and antiparticles should really have been created. Today, however, the universe consists almost entirely of matter. Where the antimatter has gone is one of the biggest open questions in physics. Researchers at CERN are looking for tiny differences between matter and antimatter that could explain this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle with the same mass as a normal particle but the opposite charge.
The antiparticle of the electron, positively charged.
The mutual destruction of a particle and an antiparticle, which produces energy.
A large European research centre for particle physics near Geneva.

gewusst: Bananas contain radioactive potassium and therefore now and then give off tiny amounts of positrons.
Antihydrogen cannot be kept in a normal bottle, because it would immediately annihilate with the walls.
Positrons are sometimes produced in thunderstorms too, as satellites have measured.

teile.einleitung: The woolly mammoth was a large, hairy relative of today's elephants. It lived during the last ice age on the cold steppes of Europe, Asia and North America, including Switzerland. Because whole mammoths have even been found in frozen ground, we know a great deal about these animals today.
wichtigste: The woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) was an ice-age proboscidean, an animal with a trunk.
Its closest living relative today is the Asian elephant.
A thick coat and small ears protected it from the cold.
It fed mainly on grasses and herbs.
Well-preserved mammoths with skin and hair have been found in the permafrost of Siberia.
The last mammoths lived until about 4000 years ago on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean.
In Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich, a museum recalls important mammoth finds.

abschnitte.text: The **woolly mammoth** was about as big as an African elephant today and could weigh several tonnes. Typical features were its long, strongly curved **tusks**, which could grow over three metres long in old males. Its body was covered with a dense, long coat and a thick layer of fat. Its small ears and short tail lost only a little heat.

During the last **ice age**, woolly mammoths lived on what is called the mammoth steppe. This cold, dry grassland stretched from Western Europe across Siberia to North America. Mammoths mainly ate grasses and herbs, which they ground up with their large, ridged molars. In winter they cleared away the snow with their trunks and tusks to get at food.

In the permanently frozen ground of Siberia, the **permafrost**, several mammoths have been found with skin, hair and even stomach contents. Especially famous is **Lyuba**, a baby mammoth discovered on the Yamal Peninsula in 2007. She is about 42,000 years old and almost completely preserved. From finds like these, researchers have even been able to study the mammoth's genetic material and so prove its close relationship with the **Asian elephant**.

Mammoths also roamed the area of today's Switzerland when large parts of the country were covered by glaciers. Their bones and teeth have been found in many places, often during gravel extraction. Particularly well known is **Niederweningen** in the canton of Zurich, where important mammoth remains were discovered in 1890 and 2003. A small museum in the village shows the finds and the life of the ice-age animals.

Stone Age people hunted mammoths and used their meat, fur, bones and ivory. In some areas they even built huts from mammoth bones. In caves in France there are paintings and engravings of mammoths, and people carved small figures from their ivory.

At the end of the ice age, about 10,000 years ago, it became warmer and the mammoth steppe disappeared. At the same time the animals were hunted by people; both together probably led to their **extinction**. On remote **Wrangel Island** in the Arctic Ocean, a small group survived until about 4000 years ago. By then the pyramids were already being built in Egypt.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very long, extended incisor tooth in elephants and mammoths.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
A long period when it was much colder on Earth and glaciers covered large areas.
The cold, dry grassland of the ice age in which mammoths lived.
The material of the tusks of elephants and mammoths.

gewusst: When the Egyptian pyramids were being built, mammoths were still living on Wrangel Island.
Because so many mammoth tusks lie in the ground in Siberia, mammoth ivory is still dug up there today.
The baby mammoth Lyuba is so well preserved that remains of her mother's milk were still found in her stomach.

teile.einleitung: Unit prefixes are small word parts such as “kilo”, “milli” or “mega” that are put in front of a unit. They show by which power of ten the unit has to be multiplied. So instead of 1000 metres you simply write 1 kilometre.
wichtigste: Prefixes come in front of a unit and make it bigger or smaller.
Kilo means 1000, mega a million, tera a trillion.
Milli means a thousandth, centi a hundredth, deci a tenth.
Nano stands for a billionth.
Hecto means a hundred times, as in hectolitre.
In 2022 quetta was introduced as the largest prefix, for 10 to the power of 30.
The prefixes belong to the International System of Units, SI.

abschnitte.text: A **prefix** is a word part that is put in front of a unit of measurement, for example “kilo” in kilogram. It says how many times the unit is taken. Each prefix stands for a **power of ten**, that is, 10, 100, 1000 and so on. There is also a symbol for each: k for kilo, m for milli, M for mega.

Hecto (h) means 100, as in hectolitre or hectare. Kilo (k) means 1000, mega (M) a million and giga (G) a billion. Tera (T) stands for a trillion, that is, 10 to the power of 12. Even bigger are peta, exa, zetta, yotta, ronna and, at the very top, **quetta** for 10 to the power of 30.

Deci (d) means a tenth, as in decilitre, which is often used in Switzerland for cooking. Centi (c) is a hundredth, milli (m) a thousandth. Micro (µ) stands for a millionth and **nano** (n) for a billionth. Bacteria are measured in micrometres, and viruses and parts of computer chips in nanometres.

The first prefixes came about with the **metric system** in France after the Revolution, at the end of the 18th century. The names for large values mostly come from Greek, for example “kilo” from chilioi for a thousand. For small values, Latin words were used, for example “milli” from mille. In 1960 the **International System of Units**, SI, was established. In November 2022 the prefixes ronna, quetta, ronto and quecto were added.

We come across prefixes all the time in everyday life: kilometres, millilitres, megawatts or gigabytes. With computers there is something special, because memory is often measured in powers of two. For this there are separate **binary prefixes** such as kibi for 1024 and mebi. Because this confuses many people, memory cards usually still just say GB.

With the symbols, capital and small letters matter. A small m means milli, a capital M means mega. So 1 mW is a milliwatt, whereas 1 MW is a megawatt, which is a billion times more. That is why you have to be precise when writing **units**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number such as 10, 100 or 1000, that is, 10 multiplied by itself several times.
A fixed measure such as the metre, gram or second.
The International System of Units, which applies almost everywhere in the world.
A letter such as k or m that abbreviates a prefix.

gewusst: The mass of the Earth is about 6 ronnagrams, a number with 27 zeros in grams.
The kilogram is the only base unit in the SI that already has a prefix in its name.
A hair is about 50,000 to 100,000 nanometres thick.

teile.einleitung: A dowsing rod is a forked stick with which some people try to find water or minerals underground. Someone who searches with it is called a dowser. Scientific tests show, however, that the rod finds no more than chance does.
wichtigste: People use a dowsing rod to try to find water or minerals.
A classic dowsing rod is a Y-shaped forked branch.
People who search with a dowsing rod are called dowsers.
The rod moves because of tiny, unconscious muscle movements.
In many areas you hit groundwater almost everywhere, which is why dowsers often seem successful.
Whether someone really finds anything can only be checked with a fair blind test.
Nobody has ever won the prize of one million dollars for proving supernatural abilities.

abschnitte.text: A classic dowsing rod is a **Y-shaped forked branch**, often made of hazel wood. The dowser holds the two ends in their hands and puts the rod under slight tension. Then they walk slowly across an area. If the tip suddenly swings up or down, they believe they have found something. Today some people also use two bent metal wires or a **pendulum**.

The dowsing rod has been known for centuries. In 16th-century mining, miners used it to look for ores such as silver. In 1556 the scholar Georgius Agricola showed men with dowsing rods in his famous book on mining, but he himself was sceptical. Later it was used mainly to search for **water** for wells. Even today there are dowsers who look for so-called water veins or “earth rays”.

The rod does not move by itself but because of **unconscious muscle movements** of the hands. These tiny movements happen without you noticing or wanting them. This is called the **ideomotor effect**. Just expecting that there might be water here is enough to make the tensed fork move. This effect is also behind pendulum swinging and moving a glass on a spirit board.

In Switzerland and many other areas there is **groundwater** in the soil almost everywhere at some depth. So anyone who drills deep enough often finds water, no matter where the rod swung. Groundwater also usually does not flow in narrow “veins” but fills the pores and cracks of rock layers such as gravel and sand over large areas. Groundwater experts, the **hydrogeologists**, therefore use geological maps and measurements instead of dowsing rods. Dowsers' successes can be explained by chance and experience.

You can test fairly whether dowsing rods work: with a **blind test**. For example, water is passed through hidden pipes, and neither the dowser nor the observers know which pipe is carrying water at the moment. In such tests, dowsers did not hit the right pipe more often than by mere guessing. For a long time the James Randi Educational Foundation offered one million dollars for proof of supernatural abilities. Nobody won this prize, not even a dowser.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who searches for water or minerals with a dowsing rod.
Water that collects in the ground in the spaces between rock, sand and gravel.
An experiment in which the person being tested does not know where the right answer is.
Small movements of the body that you make unconsciously because you are thinking of something.

gewusst: Dowsers are often honestly convinced, because they really do not feel their own muscle movements.
In blind tests, even experienced dowsers often came to completely different results at the same spot.
The German name “Wünschelrute” comes from the word “wünschen”, to wish, because people believed it showed what they wished for.

teile.einleitung: The amplitude is the greatest displacement of an oscillation or wave from its rest position. It tells you how strongly something is vibrating. With sound, the amplitude determines how loud a note is.
wichtigste: The amplitude is the greatest displacement from the rest position.
The rest position is the position in which a vibrating body would be at rest.
The greater the amplitude of a sound wave, the louder the sound.
The pitch of a note does not depend on the amplitude, but on the frequency.
If the amplitude gets smaller over time, it is called a damped oscillation.
On an oscilloscope you can see the amplitude from the height of the curve.
The further you are from the sound source, the smaller the amplitude and the quieter the sound.

abschnitte.text: Everything that swings back and forth has a **rest position**, the position in which it would stand still. The **amplitude** is the greatest distance from this rest position. If a pendulum swings 10 cm to the left and 10 cm to the right, the amplitude is 10 cm. So you only measure from the middle to the outermost point, not from the far left to the far right.

Sound is a vibration of the air. The greater the amplitude of this vibration, the **louder** we hear the sound. The pitch, on the other hand, depends on the **frequency**, that is how often per second something vibrates. If you pluck a guitar string harder, the note gets louder but not higher. Loudness is measured in **decibels**.

A pendulum or a swing does not keep swinging for ever. Because of friction and air resistance, the amplitude gets a little smaller with every swing. This is called a **damped oscillation**. A gong that has been struck also slowly gets quieter, because its amplitude decreases. Shock absorbers in a car deliberately make vibrations stop quickly.

With an **oscilloscope** you can show vibrations as a curve on a screen. The height of the curve shows the amplitude, and the distance between the wave crests shows the frequency. Music programs on a computer also show sounds as a waveform. You can recognise loud parts by high peaks and quiet parts by flat ones.

Water waves also have an amplitude: it is roughly the height of a wave crest above the calm water level. During earthquakes **seismographs** record the amplitude of the ground vibrations. From this, experts calculate the strength of the earthquake. In Switzerland this is done by the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich.

begriffe.erklaerung: The position in which a vibrating body stands still when nothing pushes it.
How many vibrations take place per second, measured in hertz.
The gradual shrinking of an oscillation.
A measuring instrument that shows vibrations as a curve on a screen.

gewusst: A whisper and a scream can have exactly the same pitch; they differ only in amplitude.
If you move twice as far from a sound source, the amplitude roughly halves in open space.
Radio used to have amplitude modulation, AM for short, in which the music was carried in the amplitude of the radio wave.

teile.einleitung: A washing machine washes dirty clothes almost by itself. It mixes water and detergent, moves the washing in a rotating drum and spins the water out at the end. In the past, washing clothes was hard manual work that often took a whole day.
wichtigste: In a washing machine the washing turns in a drum.
Detergent loosens the dirt from the clothes.
During spinning, the drum turns fast and pushes the water out.
In the past, washing was done by hand with a washboard.
Many Swiss blocks of flats have a shared laundry room.
You sort the washing so that no colour runs onto light-coloured clothes.
The tumble dryer dries the washing with warm air.
The care label shows, with a number in a washtub, how hot an item of clothing may be washed.

abschnitte.text: A washing machine is an electric household appliance for washing clothes, bed linen and towels. Its most important part is the **drum**, a stainless steel cylinder with many small holes. In Switzerland, **front loaders** are especially common, which you fill through a round door at the front. There are also top loaders, which you fill from above.

First the machine lets water in and heats it with a heating element. Then the drum turns alternately left and right, so that the washing moves and the **detergent** loosens the dirt. After that, the dirty water is pumped out and the washing is rinsed with fresh water. Finally comes **spinning**: the drum turns very fast, and the water is pushed outwards through the holes.

In the past, **wash day** was hard work. The washing was boiled in large cauldrons, scrubbed on a **washboard** and rinsed at the fountain or in the river. Then it was wrung out and hung up. In the 20th century, electric washing machines spread and made housework enormously easier.

In many Swiss blocks of flats, the residents share a **laundry room** in the basement. A laundry rota sets out who may do their washing on which day. Anyone who misses their wash day or does not clean the machine sometimes causes arguments between neighbours. In newer flats, on the other hand, there is often a machine of your own.

Before washing, you sort the washing by colour so that a red T-shirt does not dye the white socks pink. The **care label** in an item of clothing shows with symbols how it may be washed. A number in a washtub gives the highest temperature, for example 30 or 60 degrees. If you wash at a lower temperature and fill the drum well, you save electricity and water.

After washing, you hang the washing up or put it in the **tumble dryer**, which in Switzerland is called a “Tumbler”. It dries the clothes with warm air in a rotating drum. Modern appliances with a heat pump use much less electricity than older models. But the most economical way is still drying in the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rotating container in the washing machine in which the washing lies.
Turning the drum very fast so that the water flies out of the washing.
The Swiss word for a tumble dryer.
A small label in clothing with symbols showing how to wash and care for it.

gewusst: During spinning, the drum in many machines turns more than 1000 times a minute.
The laundry rota in the laundry room is a typically Swiss part of everyday life.
Washboards are sometimes still played as a musical instrument today.

teile.einleitung: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is a United Nations body that brings together the world's knowledge about climate change. For this, thousands of experts read research papers and summarise them in large reports. Governments all over the world rely on these reports when they make decisions about climate protection.
wichtigste: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is known in English as the IPCC.
It was founded in 1988 by the UN organisations WMO and UNEP.
Its secretariat is in Geneva.
It does no research of its own but assesses published studies.
It works in three working groups with different topics.
In 2007 it received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.
Since 2023 the Briton Jim Skea has been its chair (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: In German the panel is often called the “Weltklimarat” (world climate council); its official English name is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, **IPCC** for short. It was founded in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization **WMO** and the United Nations Environment Programme **UNEP**. Almost all the countries in the world are members, including Switzerland. Its secretariat is in Geneva.

The IPCC does not do research itself. Instead, hundreds of experts from all over the world read thousands of published studies and summarise the state of knowledge. The drafts are checked and commented on by many more experts and by governments. At the end, each report gets a short **Summary for Policymakers**, which all the member states approve together.

**Working Group I** studies the scientific basis, that is, how and why the climate is changing. Working Group II deals with the effects on people and nature and with adapting to them. **Working Group III** deals with mitigating climate change, that is, with how emissions of greenhouse gases can be reduced. There is also a group that develops methods for counting greenhouse gases.

Since 1990 the IPCC has published six large **assessment reports**; the latest was completed in 2023. They state that humans have clearly warmed the climate. The **special report** of 2018 on global warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius is also well known. It shows how much less damage there is if warming is limited to 1.5 rather than 2 degrees. The seventh large report is currently in preparation.

In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with the former US Vice-President **Al Gore**. They were honoured for their work in spreading knowledge about human-made climate change. The IPCC reports are an important basis for international agreements such as the **Paris Agreement** of 2015. In it, the states committed themselves to keeping warming well below 2 degrees.

Many Swiss researchers work on the IPCC. The Bern climate researcher **Thomas Stocker**, for example, led Working Group I for the fifth assessment report, which came out in 2013. For Switzerland the results are particularly important, because the Alpine region is warming faster than the global average. This can be seen, among other things, in the retreat of the glaciers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English abbreviation for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that holds heat in the atmosphere.
A large report that summarises current knowledge on a topic.
A long-term change in the climate, today above all warming caused by humans.

gewusst: Several hundred authors from dozens of countries often work on a single assessment report, without being paid for it.
Every sentence of the Summary for Policymakers is approved word for word by the representatives of all the member states together.
The IPCC has its secretariat in the building of the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Mass-energy equivalence says that mass and energy can be turned into each other. In 1905 Albert Einstein summed this up in the famous formula E = mc². Even a tiny amount of mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein’s formula E = mc² describes how mass and energy can be turned into each other.
E stands for energy, m for mass and c for the speed of light.
The speed of light is around 300,000 kilometres per second.
Einstein published the idea in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern.
Because c² is huge, a small amount of mass contains a great deal of energy.
The sun shines because it turns mass into energy through nuclear fusion.
Nuclear power stations also use this relationship.

abschnitte.text: In the formula **E = mc²**, E stands for energy, m for mass and c for the **speed of light**. The small sign ² means that c is multiplied by itself. The speed of light is about 300,000 kilometres per second, and squared that is an enormous number. That is why just one gram of mass corresponds to around 25 million kilowatt hours of energy. That is enough to supply several thousand Swiss households with electricity for a whole year.

**Albert Einstein** was born in Ulm in 1879 and later went to school in Aarau. He studied at ETH Zurich and from 1902 worked at the Federal Patent Office in Bern. There, in 1905, he published several ground-breaking papers, which is why it is called his miracle year. They included the **special theory of relativity** and, shortly afterwards, the derivation of E = mc². His former flat on the Kramgasse in Bern is now the Einstein House.

In the **sun**, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei; this is called **nuclear fusion**. The helium produced is slightly lighter than the hydrogen was before. The missing mass is released as energy and reaches us as light and heat. In this way the sun loses more than 4 million tonnes of mass every second. Even so, it is so big that it will go on shining for billions of years.

In **nuclear fission**, too, a small part of the mass is turned into energy. Heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium are split into smaller pieces. In nuclear power stations this energy heats water, and the steam drives turbines. In Switzerland such power stations are located, for example, in Gösgen, Leibstadt and Beznau. Sadly, the same physics was also used for atomic bombs.

The formula really always applies, even when we do not notice it. A charged battery, for example, is minimally heavier than a flat one. The difference, however, is so tiny that no scales can measure it. The other way round, mass can also be created from energy; this happens in large **particle accelerators** such as at CERN near Geneva. There, collisions create new particles from kinetic energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The speed of light, around 300,000 kilometres per second.
The joining of light atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
The splitting of heavy atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
Einstein’s theory about space, time, mass and energy.

gewusst: Einstein did not receive the Nobel Prize in 1921 for E = mc², but for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
In his first paper on the subject, Einstein did not yet write the formula E = mc² in the form that is famous today.
At CERN near Geneva, scientists observe every day how new particles with mass are created from energy.

teile.einleitung: Scientists are people who study and research something very carefully; they are also called researchers. They ask questions about the world and look for answers using methods that can be checked. Their work has given us medicines, computers and a better understanding of the universe.
wichtigste: Researchers study and investigate things very carefully.
They work with observations, experiments and measurements.
Their results are published and checked by others.
There are natural sciences, humanities, social sciences and engineering.
Many work at universities, in companies or at research centres such as CERN.
Mistakes and errors are part of science too.

abschnitte.text: **Researchers** want to find out how the world works. They observe carefully, measure, calculate, read a lot and exchange ideas with others. Some study tiny particles, others distant galaxies, animals, diseases or the history of humankind. What always matters is that others can check their results.

It starts with a question, for example: why do leaves turn colourful in autumn? Then you suggest a possible answer, a **hypothesis**. With an **experiment** or observations you test whether the guess is right. If it is not, it is rejected or improved, and so knowledge grows step by step.

In the **natural sciences** such as physics, chemistry and biology, people study nature. The humanities deal with things like language, history and art. The social sciences study how people live together. Engineers use this knowledge to build bridges, machines or computers.

Researchers write up their results in **scientific papers**. Before these are published, other experts check the work critically; this is called peer review. Other teams repeat the experiments to see whether they find the same thing. In this way mistakes are discovered and reliable knowledge is built.

Switzerland is one of the countries with a particularly large amount of research. Well-known universities include **ETH Zurich** and EPFL in Lausanne, along with ten cantonal universities. At CERN near Geneva, thousands of people from all over the world research the smallest particles. The Swiss National Science Foundation supports many research projects with money.

In 1905 Albert Einstein developed important parts of his theory of relativity in Bern, while he was working at the patent office there. **Marie Curie** researched radioactivity and is still the only person to have received Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences. Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees in Africa for decades. Young people can do research too, for example in the competition run by **Swiss Youth in Science** (“Schweizer Jugend forscht”).

begriffe.erklaerung: A reasoned guess that you test with experiments.
A planned test used to investigate a question.
The checking of a piece of research by other experts before it is published.
A well-tested explanation that brings many observations together.

gewusst: The German word “Wissenschaft” comes from “Wissen”, knowledge, just as the English word science comes from the Latin for knowledge.
Many important discoveries happened by chance, for example penicillin in 1928.
Today most researchers work in teams, and some scientific papers from CERN have more than a thousand authors.

teile.einleitung: The Vienna Circle was a group of philosophers, mathematicians and scientists who met in Vienna from the 1920s. They wanted to make philosophy as clear and precise as the natural sciences. Their ideas still influence thinking about science today.
wichtigste: The Vienna Circle was led by Moritz Schlick.
It stood for logical empiricism.
Its members included Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath and Hans Hahn.
The young logician Kurt Gödel attended meetings.
In 1929 the manifesto “The Scientific Conception of the World: The Vienna Circle” was published.
Only sentences that can be checked through experience were regarded as meaningful.
In 1936 Moritz Schlick was shot dead at the University of Vienna.

abschnitte.text: The leader of the circle was the philosopher and physicist **Moritz Schlick**, who taught at the University of Vienna from 1922. From 1924 a group met regularly on Thursdays for discussions. It included the philosopher **Rudolf Carnap**, the social scientist Otto Neurath and the mathematician Hans Hahn. The young logician Kurt Gödel also attended meetings as a student. The philosopher Karl Popper was close to the circle, but he was a critic and not a member.

The Vienna Circle stood for **logical empiricism**. Knowledge was to be based either on experience and observation or on logic and mathematics. A sentence was only regarded as meaningful if it could be checked through experience; this is called **verifiability**. That is why they regarded many questions of the old philosophy, for example about a being behind all things, as meaningless.

In 1929 the manifesto “The Scientific Conception of the World: The Vienna Circle” was published. From 1930, together with colleagues in Berlin, the circle published the journal “Erkenntnis” (Knowledge). The work “**Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus**” by Ludwig Wittgenstein, which had come out in 1921, was discussed intensively. Carnap wrote important books about the logical structure of science.

Otto Neurath found a famous image for science. We are like sailors who have to rebuild their ship on the open sea, without ever being able to take it apart in a dock. This means that knowledge can never be built up from a completely firm foundation. You improve it bit by bit while you are using it. This image is known today as **Neurath's boat**.

On 22 June 1936, Moritz Schlick was shot dead at the University of Vienna by a former student. Even before that, the political climate in Austria had become hostile towards the circle. Many members were of Jewish origin or politically on the left and had to flee, at the latest after the **Anschluss**, the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in 1938. Most went to the USA or to England.

Through emigration, the ideas of the Vienna Circle spread all over the world. The **philosophy of science**, that is, thinking about how science works, was strongly shaped by it. Many of its theses are now regarded as too strict, for example the criterion of verifiability. But its demand for clear language and verifiable statements is still important today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The view that knowledge comes from experience and observation.
The possibility of confirming a statement as true through observation.
The study of correct reasoning.
The field that studies how science arrives at knowledge.

gewusst: A few years after his visits to the circle, Kurt Gödel proved that in mathematics there are true statements that cannot be proved.
Otto Neurath also invented picture symbols that influenced later pictograms at stations and airports.
To explain its ideas to a wide audience, the circle founded the Ernst Mach Society in 1928.

teile.einleitung: Magnification tells you how much bigger or smaller an image is compared with the real object. You calculate it by dividing the image size by the object size. It plays an important role in photography, microscopy and projection.
wichtigste: Magnification is the image size divided by the object size.
It is also equal to the image distance divided by the object distance.
If it is greater than 1, the image is bigger than the object.
If it is less than 1, the image is reduced, as in a camera.
By the usual sign convention, a negative magnification means that the image is upside down.
A slide 24 mm high is projected to a height of 1.2 m with a magnification of 50.
With a magnification of 1 : 1 the image is exactly the same size as the object.

abschnitte.text: **Magnification** is often abbreviated with the Greek letter beta. It gives the ratio of the **image size** B to the **object size** G. The formula is: magnification equals B divided by G. A value of 2 means that the image is twice as big as the object. A value of 0.5 means that the image is half as big.

With a lens you can also calculate the magnification from the distances. It is equal to the **image distance** b, the distance from the image to the lens, divided by the **object distance** g. If an object is 30 cm in front of a lens and the image forms 15 cm behind it, the magnification is 15 divided by 30, that is 0.5. Together with the lens equation, you can then predict the size of the image. For example, an object 2 cm high placed 12 cm in front of a converging lens with a focal length of 8 cm gives an image 4 cm high.

In a **camera** large things are reduced onto a small sensor, so the magnification is much less than 1. If a house front 3 m high is to fill a sensor exactly 24 mm high, you need a scale of 1 : 125. A camera with a 50 mm focal length shows a person 1.8 m tall standing 10 m away only about 9 mm high. In **macro photography** you photograph small things such as insects at a scale of 1 : 1 or even larger. Then a fly is as big on the sensor as in real life.

With a **projector** it is the other way round: a small image is thrown onto a screen greatly enlarged. A slide 24 mm high is enlarged to a height of 1.2 m with a magnification of 50. The images in a **microscope** and a magnifying glass are also enlarged. For a microscope the magnification is usually given as, for example, 40 times or 400 times. The closer the object moves to the focal point of a converging lens, the bigger the image becomes.

A converging lens produces an **inverted image** on a screen, which is upside down. By the usual sign convention the magnification is then negative. A positive value means an upright image, like the one you see with a magnifying glass. In our eye, too, the image on the retina is upside down, and the brain turns it round. Often, though, people simply calculate with the absolute value, that is without the sign.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the lens and the image.
The distance between the object and the lens.
The distance between the lens and the point at which parallel light rays meet.
Photographing very small things at life size or larger.

gewusst: If an object is exactly twice the focal length in front of a converging lens, the image is exactly the same size as the object.
The scale on a map, such as 1 : 25,000, follows the same idea as magnification.
In a pinhole camera the magnification depends only on the distances, without any lens at all.

teile.einleitung: Materials testing examines how strong, hard, tough or flawless a material or component is. For this, engineers pull, press, strike or scan samples. In this way it is made sure that bridges, aircraft, cable cars and bikes are safe.
wichtigste: Materials testing determines the properties of materials and finds defects in components.
A distinction is made between destructive and non-destructive testing methods.
In a tensile test, a sample is pulled until it breaks, and in this way the strength is determined.
The Charpy impact test checks toughness under sudden loading.
The Wöhler diagram shows how many load cycles a component can withstand before it breaks through fatigue.
Ultrasonic testing is part of non-destructive materials testing.
In Switzerland, Empa in Dübendorf is a well-known research institute for materials testing.

abschnitte.text: In **materials testing**, you measure how a material behaves under load. You want to know how much force it can withstand, how hard it is and whether it breaks in a brittle way or deforms first. You also look for hidden defects such as cracks or air bubbles. The results are important for the safety of buildings, vehicles and machines.

In a **tensile test**, a bar is clamped into a machine and slowly pulled apart. The **stress** is the force divided by the cross-sectional area: 10 kilonewtons on 100 square millimetres gives 100 megapascals. In the elastic range, stress equals the modulus of elasticity times strain. So with steel, which has a modulus of elasticity of 210 gigapascals, a strain of 0.1 per cent gives 210 megapascals.

In **hardness testing**, a small ball or point is pressed into the material and the dent is measured. In the **Charpy impact test**, a pendulum hammer strikes through a notched sample, which tests the toughness under sudden loading. Components that are loaded again and again can break after many load cycles; this is called **fatigue**. The German engineer August Wöhler studied this in the 19th century on railway axles, which is where the Wöhler diagram comes from.

In **non-destructive testing**, the component stays whole and can still be used. In **ultrasonic testing**, sound waves are sent into the material and are reflected back by cracks, similar to an ultrasound scan at the doctor's. X-rays can be used to look inside welds. **Eddy current testing** only works on components that conduct electricity, such as metals.

Some materials slowly deform when they are under constant load for a long time and are hot. This process is called **creep**. It is important, for example, for turbine blades in aircraft engines and power stations. That is why such materials are often tested for many weeks or months at high temperatures.

**Empa**, the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, was founded in 1880 and has its headquarters in Dübendorf. It tests and researches materials for construction, transport, energy and medicine. Cable car ropes, bridge parts and train components are also tested regularly in Switzerland. In this way damage can be discovered before anything happens.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force acting on a particular area of a material.
A number that shows how stiff a material is; in German “E-Modul”.
The ability of a material to absorb energy without breaking straight away.
The failure of a component after many repeated loads.
Slow deformation under constant load, especially at high temperatures.

gewusst: One megapascal is exactly one newton per square millimetre.
A component can break through fatigue even though each individual load is far below its strength.
Ultrasonic testing and ultrasound at the doctor's are based on the same principle, the echo of sound waves.

teile.einleitung: Alpha radiation is a form of radioactive radiation in which an atomic nucleus flings out small particles. These alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons. In air they only travel a few centimetres, but inside the body they can do great damage.
wichtigste: An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons, so it is a helium nucleus.
Alpha particles have a double positive charge.
In alpha decay the atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number by 4.
In air alpha radiation only travels a few centimetres.
Even a sheet of paper or the skin stops alpha radiation.
Breathed in or swallowed, alpha emitters are especially dangerous.
In a cloud chamber alpha particles show up as short, thick trails of mist.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and break down by themselves; they are called **radioactive**. In alpha decay such a nucleus flings out an **alpha particle**. It consists of two protons and two neutrons and is therefore a helium nucleus. Because it contains two protons, it has a double positive charge. Alpha particles leave the nucleus at a few per cent of the speed of light.

When a nucleus gives off an alpha particle, it loses two protons and two neutrons. Its **atomic number** therefore falls by 2, and it becomes a different element. The **mass number** falls by 4. Uranium-238, for example, turns into thorium with the mass number 234.

Alpha particles are large and heavy and keep colliding with air particles. That is why they only travel a few centimetres in air. Even a sheet of paper or the outermost layer of skin stops them. From outside, alpha radiation is therefore hardly dangerous. It is quite different if an **alpha emitter** is breathed in or swallowed: then it releases all its energy into body cells in a tiny space and can badly damage them.

In 1899 the physicist **Ernest Rutherford** distinguished two kinds of radiation and named them after the Greek letters alpha and beta. Later he fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil and in this way discovered the tiny atomic nucleus in 1911. Alpha particles can be made visible in a **cloud chamber**. There they leave short, thick trails of mist, rather like the vapour trails of aeroplanes.

The artificial element **americium** is an alpha emitter and was often used in smoke detectors. There it makes the air in a small chamber conduct electricity; smoke disturbs this current and sets off the alarm. A natural alpha emitter is the noble gas **radon**, which can get into houses from the ground. In Switzerland radon occurs mainly in the Alps and the Jura, so the Federal Office of Public Health gives tips on airing rooms and sealing buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A helium nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons.
The property of some atomic nuclei to break down by themselves and give off radiation.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the chemical element.
A device in which the paths of radiation particles become visible as trails of mist.

gewusst: A large part of the helium on Earth comes from alpha particles produced in rocks.
Alpha radiation is stopped by a single sheet of paper.
Space probes such as Voyager get their electricity from the heat of an alpha emitter, plutonium.

teile.einleitung: The sunset glow is the red, orange or pink light in the sky when the sun goes down. It happens because in the evening sunlight travels a particularly long way through the air. In the Alps even the mountain peaks turn red; this is called alpenglow.
wichtigste: The sunset glow happens because at sunset sunlight has a long way to travel through the air.
Blue light is scattered more strongly by the air than red light.
You see the sunset glow in the west, where the sun sets.
The setting sun often looks orange-red.
At midday the sun is not red, because its light has only a short way to go through the air.
Dust in the air can make a sunset glow especially strong.
The red glow of mountain peaks at sunset is called alpenglow.

abschnitte.text: The **sunset glow** is the reddish colouring of the sky and clouds during and shortly after sunset. Because the sun sets in the west, you see the sunset glow mainly in that direction. The matching glow in the east in the morning is called the **dawn glow**. Both are among the most beautiful light displays in the sky.

Sunlight looks white, but it is made of all the colours of the rainbow. When it passes through the air, blue light is bent off in all directions by the tiny air particles much more strongly than red light; this is called **Rayleigh scattering**. That is why the sky is blue during the day. In the evening the sun is low, and its light has to travel a very long way through the atmosphere before it reaches us.

On this long journey the blue light is almost completely scattered to the side. What is left are mainly the yellow, orange and **red parts** of the light. That is why the sun looks orange-red as it sets and colours the clouds to match. At midday the sun is high, its light has only a short way to go through the air, and so it looks yellowish white.

Dust, smoke and tiny droplets in the air can strengthen the sunset glow. After big **volcanic eruptions** such as that of Krakatoa in 1883, there were strikingly colourful sunsets all over the world for months. Saharan dust, which is sometimes blown as far as Switzerland, also produces intense colours. When clouds are lit from below, they often glow a particularly lovely pink or purple.

In the Alps the snow-covered peaks often glow red at sunset while the valleys already lie in shadow. This **alpenglow** is a popular subject for photos, for example on the Matterhorn, the Jungfrau or the Säntis. An old German weather saying goes: “Red sky in the evening brings fine weather.” It is often true, because a sunset glow shows that the sky is clear in the west, and in central Europe the weather usually comes from the west.

On Mars it is exactly the other way round: there the sky is reddish during the day, and at sunset a bluish glow appears around the sun. This is because of the fine dust in the thin Martian air, which scatters light differently from the Earth’s air. Photos of this have been taken, for example, by the Mars rover Curiosity. So a sunset on Mars is **bluish**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of light in different directions by tiny particles.
The scattering of light by air particles, which affects blue light much more strongly than red.
The red glow of mountain peaks shortly after sunset.
The reddish colouring of the sky at sunrise.

gewusst: You can sometimes still see a sunset glow after the sun has already set for you, because clouds high up are still lit.
On Mars sunsets are blue; on Earth they are red.
After the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 the evening sky over New York glowed so red that the fire brigade turned out because of a supposed fire.

t1ie9ito.t: Derivative of position with respect to time

teile.einleitung: How fast is a bike going at exactly this moment? The answer is given by the derivative of position with respect to time. It links the physics of motion with mathematics and is one of the most important tools of mechanics.
wichtigste: The derivative of position with respect to time gives the instantaneous velocity.
The second derivative of position with respect to time is the acceleration.
The derivative of acceleration with respect to time is called jerk.
In a position-time graph the instantaneous velocity is the gradient of the tangent.
The gradient of the secant between two points gives the average velocity.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed differential calculus in the 17th century.
If the derivative is zero, the body is standing still at that moment.

abschnitte.text: A moving body is at a particular position x at every time t. This relationship is written as a function **x(t)** and drawn in a **position-time graph**. A straight line means steady motion. A curved line shows that the body is getting faster or slower.

If you join two points on the graph with a straight line, you get a **secant**. Its gradient is the average velocity between the two moments. If you move the two points closer and closer together, the secant becomes a **tangent**. Its gradient is the instantaneous velocity at exactly that moment. This is precisely what the derivative calculates; it is written v(t) = x'(t).

If a body moves according to x(t) = 3t² + 2t, its velocity is v(t) = 6t + 2. After 2 seconds it is therefore 14 m/s. For x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² you get v(t) = 6t² − 6t, so 36 m/s after 3 seconds. A ball with x(t) = −2t² + 8t has v(t) = −4t + 8; it stands still for a moment after 2 seconds. Oscillations can also be calculated this way: from x(t) = 4·sin(2t) it follows that v(t) = 8·cos(2t), so 8 m/s at time zero.

If you differentiate the velocity once more, you get the **acceleration**. It is therefore the second derivative of position. For x(t) = 5t³ you get a(t) = 30t, so 30 m/s² after one second. The next derivative is called **jerk**. A large jerk is unpleasant, so engineers design roller coasters, lifts and railway curves so that the jerk stays small.

The mathematics of derivatives is called **differential calculus**. Isaac Newton in England and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Germany developed it independently of each other in the late 17th century. Newton needed it to describe the motion of the planets. The notation dx/dt comes from Leibniz and is still used today. The Bernoulli family of mathematicians from Basel and Leonhard Euler also greatly extended the method.

begriffe.erklaerung: The velocity at exactly one particular moment, as shown on a speedometer.
A mathematical tool that tells you how fast a quantity is changing at that moment.
A straight line that just touches a curve at one point.
A straight line that cuts a curve at two points.
How fast the acceleration changes.

gewusst: A car’s speedometer is really showing the derivative of position with respect to time all the time.
The derivatives after jerk even have joking English names: snap, crackle and pop.
Leonhard Euler from Basel wrote one of the first great textbooks of differential calculus.

teile.einleitung: A conspiracy theory claims that a secret group is behind important events and is secretly controlling the world. Such stories offer seemingly simple explanations for complicated or frightening things. If you know how they work, you can recognise and check them better.
wichtigste: A typical idea is that a group's secret plan explains everything.
Conspiracy narratives assume that nothing happens by chance.
Counter-evidence is often interpreted as part of the conspiracy.
Simple explanations are attractive especially in uncertain times.
Real conspiracies such as the Watergate affair were proved with evidence.
Huge secret plans with thousands of people in the know are very unlikely.

abschnitte.text: A **conspiracy theory** explains events through the secret plan of a powerful group. Three basic assumptions are typical: nothing happens by chance, nothing is as it seems, and everything is connected. Because in science the word “theory” stands for well-tested explanations, experts prefer to speak of **conspiracy narratives**. Often a person or group is made a **scapegoat** without any evidence.

abschnitte.titel: Why they are hard to disprove
abschnitte.text: Followers often interpret counter-evidence as part of the conspiracy. Anyone who disagrees is then seen as being in on it or as having been fooled. As a result, a conspiracy narrative cannot be disproved by any evidence. That is exactly what distinguishes it from scientific statements, which can be measured against evidence.

Some people claim that the **Moon landing** of 1969 was only filmed in a studio. Against this is the fact, among others, that astronauts left laser reflectors on the Moon, which researchers still aim at from Earth today. Others believe that the white trails behind aircraft are poison. In fact, these **contrails** consist mainly of ice crystals that form from the water vapour in the exhaust.

There are also real conspiracies, but they are uncovered with evidence. A famous example is the **Watergate affair** in the USA from 1972. At that time there was a break-in at the office of the opposing party, and journalists revealed that people close to President Richard Nixon were behind it. Nixon resigned in 1974. The difference: here there were documents, witnesses and court cases.

Conspiracy narratives offer **simple explanations** for difficult events such as illnesses or crises. They give people the feeling of knowing more than others. Especially in uncertain times, many look for something to hold on to and for someone to blame. On top of this, such stories spread quickly on social media.

Ask yourself who is making a claim and what **evidence** there is. With huge conspiracies involving thousands of people, it is very likely that someone would give something away. Trustworthy sources name their facts and can be checked. It also helps to talk calmly and kindly with people who believe such stories.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person or group who is blamed for a misfortune without evidence.
Proof or a verifiable fact that supports a statement.
A white cloud trail of ice crystals behind aircraft flying at high altitude.
