A political scandal in the USA that led to the resignation of President Nixon.

gewusst: The laser reflectors of the Apollo missions on the Moon have been used by observatories on Earth for more than 50 years.
The name Watergate comes from a building complex in Washington where the break-in took place.
Many conspiracy narratives are very old and keep reappearing in new versions.

teile.einleitung: The run-up is the fast running or riding before a jump or throw. During it the athlete builds up speed, that is kinetic energy. This energy is used at take-off or release to get further or higher.
wichtigste: During the run-up you build up speed and therefore kinetic energy.
In the long jump: the faster the run-up, the longer the jump.
Long jumpers measure out their run-up so that they hit the take-off exactly.
In the pole vault you run up with a long pole, in the javelin with the javelin in your hand.
In the modern high jump you run up in a curve.
Ski jumpers get their speed by going down the in-run.
Shot putters do not take a long run-up, because they have to stay in the circle.

abschnitte.text: A **run-up** is a stretch on which you build up momentum before a movement. In terms of physics, you build up **kinetic energy**. At take-off or release this energy is turned into height or distance. That is why you get much further with a run-up than from standing. You can easily try this out by jumping once from standing and once with a run-up.

In the **long jump**: the faster the run-up, the longer the jump. The best long jumpers are almost as fast as sprinters at take-off. So that they hit the **take-off board** exactly, they measure out their run-up in steps and put down a marker. If you step over the board, the jump does not count. In the triple jump, too, a fast, accurate run-up is decisive.

In the modern **high jump** you run up in a curve and jump over the bar backwards. This technique is called the Fosbury flop, after the American Dick Fosbury, who became Olympic champion with it in 1968. In the **pole vault** you run up with a long, flexible pole. The pole stores the energy of the run-up, bends and catapults the vaulter upwards.

In the **javelin** you run up with the javelin in your hand and then throw it from behind a line. The run-up gives the javelin extra momentum. Shot putters, on the other hand, do not take a long run-up, because they have to stay in the throwing circle. They build up their momentum with a spin or a glide inside the circle.

Ski jumpers get their speed by going down the **in-run**. On big hills they reach almost 100 km/h this way. The Swiss ski jumper Simon Ammann won Olympic gold in ski jumping four times. In gymnastics you take a run-up to the **vaulting table**, jump onto a springboard and push off with your hands. Here, too, a fast, controlled run-up decides the height of the vault.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that a body has because of its speed.
The board in the long jump from which you have to take off.
A high jump technique in which you jump over the bar backwards.
The steep track down which ski jumpers travel to the take-off.

gewusst: From standing, even good athletes only jump a little over three metres; with a run-up, over eight metres.
Many ski jumps today have an in-run made of ice so that the skis glide quickly and evenly.
Thanks to the run-up and the pole, pole vaulters get over six metres high.

teile.einleitung: The race to the South Pole was an exciting contest between the Norwegian Roald Amundsen and the Briton Robert Falcon Scott. Both wanted to be the first to reach the southernmost point on Earth. Amundsen won on 14 December 1911, while Scott's expedition ended tragically.
wichtigste: Roald Amundsen and Robert Falcon Scott both wanted to be the first to reach the South Pole.
Amundsen's group reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911.
Amundsen's polar party consisted of five men.
Sledge dogs were the most important factor in Amundsen's success.
His base camp, Framheim, was on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf.
Scott's group arrived about 5 weeks later and found a tent with a letter and a Norwegian flag.
Scott and his companions died on the way back.
Today the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station commemorates both rivals.

abschnitte.text: **Roald Amundsen** was an experienced Norwegian polar explorer who had already sailed through the Northwest Passage. **Robert Falcon Scott** was an officer in the British Navy and had already explored Antarctica on an earlier expedition. Both set off with their ships in 1910, Amundsen on the **Fram** and Scott on the Terra Nova. Only one of them could be the first at the pole.

Amundsen had announced publicly that he was going to the **North Pole**. When it was reported in 1909 that the North Pole had already been reached, he secretly changed his goal. Only during the voyage did he tell his crew and Scott that he wanted to go to the South Pole. That was how the race began.

Amundsen built his base camp, **Framheim**, on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf. He relied entirely on **sledge dogs** and on skis, which his men were very good at using. Scott relied on motor sledges, ponies and on his men pulling the sledges themselves. The motor sledges soon broke down, and the ponies suffered badly from the cold.

On **14 December 1911**, Amundsen and four companions reached the South Pole. They put up a tent, raised the Norwegian flag and left a letter. About five weeks later, on 17 January 1912, Scott arrived with four men. Their disappointment was huge when they saw the Norwegians' tent.

On the long way back, Scott and his companions were caught in icy storms and had too little food and fuel. All five men lost their lives, the last of them only a few days' march from a supply depot. Search parties found their tent with the **diaries** a few months later. Amundsen's team, on the other hand, returned to Framheim in good health.

The race is regarded as one of the great adventures of **polar exploration**. It shows how important good planning, suitable equipment and experience are in extreme cold. The American **Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station** at the pole bears the names of both explorers. Today scientists from many countries do research there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The region around the South Pole, almost completely covered with ice.
A huge sheet of ice that extends from the land out over the sea and floats.
A research journey into a little-known area.
A person who explores the regions around the North or South Pole.

gewusst: Amundsen's ship, the Fram, is now in a museum in Oslo.
At the South Pole it is so cold that in winter the temperature can fall below minus 60 degrees.
At the South Pole, every direction points north.

teile.einleitung: Ocean acidification means that seawater is slowly becoming more acidic because of carbon dioxide from the air. The main cause is the exhaust gases from coal, oil and natural gas. For corals, mussels and snails with chalky shells, this is a big problem.
wichtigste: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in seawater.
So far the oceans have absorbed about a quarter of the CO2 released by humans.
Since the beginning of industrialisation, the pH of surface water has fallen by about 0.1.
Today it is about 8.1.
If the pH falls by 0.1, the concentration of hydrogen ions rises by about 26 per cent.
Carbonate ions become scarcer, so that shell-builders find it harder to build their shells.
Corals and sea butterflies form aragonite, which dissolves more easily than calcite.
Sea butterflies are regarded as an early warning sign of ocean acidification.

abschnitte.text: Since **industrialisation**, humans have been burning large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas, which produces **carbon dioxide**, CO2 for short. Some of it stays in the air and strengthens the greenhouse effect. So far the oceans have absorbed about a quarter of the CO2 released by humans. This slows down warming, but it changes the chemistry of seawater.

When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, **carbonic acid** forms, similar to sparkling mineral water. This increases the amount of hydrogen ions, and the **pH** falls. The surface water of the oceans today has a pH of about 8.1, so it is actually still slightly alkaline. But since the beginning of industrialisation the value has fallen by about 0.1, and because the pH scale is logarithmic, this corresponds to about 26 per cent more hydrogen ions.

Many sea animals build shells and skeletons from **lime**, that is, from calcium carbonate. For this they need **carbonate ions** from the water, but it is precisely these that become scarcer with acidification. Corals and sea butterflies form a crystal form called **aragonite**, which dissolves more easily than the form calcite. That is why they are particularly sensitive.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences for life in the sea
abschnitte.text: The tiny, free-swimming **sea butterflies** have a thin aragonite shell and are regarded as an early warning sign of ocean acidification. They are an important food for fish such as salmon and for whales. Oysters, mussels, sea urchins and **coral reefs** also suffer when they have to use more energy to build their lime. Because many animals depend on one another, the whole food web in the sea can be affected.

The most important measure against ocean acidification is to release less CO2. This includes renewable energy, using energy sparingly and burning less fossil fuel. Researchers measure the pH of the oceans at many stations and with measuring buoys to follow the development. Switzerland is a landlocked country, but with its CO2 emissions it too contributes to ocean acidification.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a liquid is.
A weak acid that forms when CO2 dissolves in water.
A crystal form of lime, of which corals, for example, are made.
Living things that build shells or skeletons from lime.
The period from about 1800 when factories and machines spread.

gewusst: Ocean acidification is sometimes called the “evil twin” of climate change.
A fall in pH of only 0.1 sounds small, but it means about a quarter more acid particles.
Cold water can absorb more CO2 than warm water, which is why the polar seas are acidifying especially quickly.

teile.einleitung: A roller coaster is a ride in a theme park on which cars race over steep hills, through bends and sometimes through loops. The exciting thing about it is pure physics: after the first hill the train usually carries on without any motor at all. The energy it needs is stored in the height.
wichtigste: On a classic roller coaster a chain lift pulls the train up the first hill.
The first hill is usually the highest, because no more energy is added after that.
Going downhill, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.
The roller coaster is fastest at the lowest point.
Without friction the mass of the passengers has no effect on the speed.
Launched roller coasters are strongly accelerated by motors at the start.
Many modern roller coasters brake with eddy current brakes without touching the rails.

abschnitte.text: A roller coaster consists of rails on which a train of several cars runs. The German name means “figure-of-eight ride” and comes from early rides whose track ran in the shape of an eight. There are **wooden roller coasters** and **steel roller coasters**, with steel allowing tight bends and loops. Ice slides, which people rode down in Russia as early as the 17th century, are regarded as their forerunners. That is why in some languages roller coasters are still called “Russian mountains” today.

First a **chain lift** slowly pulls the train up to the highest point. There the train has a lot of **potential energy**. As it rolls down, this energy is turned into **kinetic energy**, and it gets faster and faster. When it climbs again, it slows down, because the kinetic energy turns back into potential energy. Because some energy is lost through friction, every further hill must be lower than the first.

Without friction you can calculate the speed at the bottom with the formula v equals the square root of 2 times g times h. With a drop of 45 metres and g equal to 10 m/s², this gives 30 m/s, that is 108 km/h. Mass does not appear in this formula, so a full train is as fast as an empty one. This is because a heavy train has more potential energy, but also has more mass to accelerate. In reality the air and rolling friction slow it down a little.

On a **launched roller coaster** motors accelerate the train to a high speed within a few seconds at the start. This is often done with linear motors that work with magnetic fields. In a **loop** the centrifugal force presses the passengers into their seats, so that they do not fall out even upside down. Modern loops are not perfectly round but tighter at the top, so that the forces stay more comfortable for the body.

At the end of the ride the train must stop safely. Many modern rides use **eddy current brakes**. Metal fins on the train pass between strong magnets, and the magnetic fields brake without any contact. These brakes hardly wear out and even work without electricity. In addition, lap bars and belts hold the passengers securely in their seats.

Many Swiss families visit Europa-Park in Rust in Germany, which is not far from Basel. There are many big roller coasters there. In Switzerland, too, there are smaller theme parks with roller coasters. Roller coasters are also put up at fairs such as the Basel Autumn Fair.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that a body has because it is high up.
Energy that a body has because it is moving.
A moving chain that pulls the train up the first hill.
A brake that slows things down with magnets without touching the rails.

gewusst: On some roller coasters passengers feel several times their body weight when they go through a bend at the bottom.
At the top of a hill you can feel almost weightless for a moment; this is called airtime.
Without friction a fully loaded train is just as fast as an empty one.

teile.einleitung: A viral vector vaccine is a vaccine in which a harmless carrier virus brings the instructions for an antigen into the body's cells. The cells then make this antigen themselves, and the immune system learns to recognise it. Vector vaccines became well known above all during the Covid-19 pandemic and in the fight against Ebola.
wichtigste: In a vector vaccine, a harmless carrier virus brings the gene for an antigen into body cells.
In several Covid-19 vector vaccines, adenoviruses served as carriers.
In the Covid-19 vector vaccines, the instructions for the spike protein were delivered.
The Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV was approved in 2019 and is a vector vaccine that can replicate.
A non-replicating vector cannot multiply in the body.
The DNA of an adenovirus vector stays outside the chromosomes and is broken down again.
Antibodies against the vector itself can weaken the effect when it is given repeatedly.
Very rare thromboses with a lack of platelets led to restrictions in 2021.

abschnitte.text: A vaccination trains the **immune system** to recognise a pathogen before you meet it. This requires an **antigen**, that is, a typical feature of the pathogen, for example a protein on its surface. With a **vector vaccine**, it is not the antigen itself that is injected but a harmless carrier virus, the vector. It brings the gene, that is, the instructions for the antigen, into body cells.

The carrier virus has been changed in the laboratory so that it cannot cause disease. It enters cells and delivers the instructions there. Following these instructions, the cell makes the antigen and shows it to the immune system. In response, the body makes **antibodies** and defence cells, which protect it more quickly in the event of a real infection.

In several vaccines against Covid-19, **adenoviruses** served as carriers, that is, viruses that otherwise cause, for example, mild colds. They brought the instructions for the **spike protein** of the coronavirus into the cells; the virus uses this protein to dock onto cells. Examples are the vaccines from AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson. Against Ebola, the vaccine **rVSV-ZEBOV** was approved in 2019; in it, a different virus that can replicate serves as the carrier.

A **non-replicating vector** can get into the cell but cannot multiply there. A replicating vector, on the other hand, can multiply in the body for a while, which can strengthen the immune response. The DNA of a non-integrating adenovirus vector does not get into the chromosomes but stays outside them and is broken down after a while. That is why it does not change human genetic material.

One disadvantage is that the body can also make antibodies against the vector itself. If the same vector is given several times, this can weaken the effect. In 2021, very rare **thromboses** with a lack of platelets occurred after adenoviral Covid-19 vaccines, that is, blood clots together with few blood platelets. That is why their use was restricted in several countries; in Switzerland mainly mRNA vaccines were used.

begriffe.erklaerung: A carrier that brings something to a particular place, here a harmless virus.
A feature of a pathogen by which the immune system recognises it.
A family of viruses that can normally cause mild colds.
Proteins of the immune system that recognise and mark pathogens.
A blood clot that blocks a blood vessel.

gewusst: For the AstraZeneca vaccine, an adenovirus from chimpanzees was used, against which humans have hardly any defences.
The Russian vaccine Sputnik V used two different adenoviruses for the first and second doses to get around the vector problem.
The word vector comes from the Latin vehere and means carrier or driver.

teile.einleitung: Birds are the best fliers among the vertebrates: they glide, soar, hover and dive down at breathtaking speed. Their body is completely geared towards flying, from their hollow bones to their feathers. For centuries people have watched birds fly in order to learn to fly themselves.
wichtigste: Many bird bones are hollow inside and therefore especially light.
A bird's wing is curved on top, similar to an aircraft wing.
When a bird floats through the air without beating its wings, it is called gliding.
Migratory birds such as geese often fly in a V formation, because this saves energy.
Owls fly almost silently and were the model for quiet fans.
More than 500 years ago, Leonardo da Vinci drew flying machines modelled on birds.
Otto Lilienthal watched the stork especially closely.
Many aircraft have upturned wingtips modelled on birds.

abschnitte.text: Birds have many special features that allow them to fly. Many of their bones are **hollow inside** and filled with air, so that they are light and yet stable. Powerful **breast muscles** move the wings, and the feathers form a smooth, light wing surface. Instead of heavy teeth, birds have a light beak.

A bird's wing is **curved on top** and flatter underneath, similar to an aircraft wing. When air flows over it, **lift** is created, which pushes the bird upwards. By beating its wings, the bird also creates thrust, that is, forward momentum. When **gliding**, it holds its wings still and slowly sinks; birds of prey and storks also let themselves be carried upwards by warm, rising air, called **thermals**.

Hummingbirds can stand still in the air with very fast wingbeats; this is called **hovering flight**. Kestrels stay in one spot above a meadow when they hover. In a dive, the **peregrine falcon** reaches well over 300 kilometres per hour, making it the fastest animal in the world. Outside the breeding season, the common swift stays in the air without a break for months.

Migratory birds such as geese and cranes often fly in a **V formation**. Each bird uses the upwash created at the wingtips of the bird in front and so saves energy. The tiring position at the front changes again and again. **Owls**, on the other hand, fly almost silently, because their feathers are finely serrated and soft at the edges, so mice cannot hear them coming.

More than 500 years ago, **Leonardo da Vinci** was already drawing flying machines modelled on birds. The German aviation pioneer **Otto Lilienthal** watched the stork especially closely and published a book on bird flight in 1889. From 1891 he was one of the first people to make repeated gliding flights. Today many aircraft have upturned wingtips, so-called winglets, and quiet fans imitate the wings of owls; this is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that pushes a wing upwards in the air.
Flying without beating the wings, during which the bird slowly sinks.
Rising warm air that carries birds upwards.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.
An upturned wingtip on aircraft.

gewusst: A common swift can stay in the air for up to about ten months without landing.
A bird's skeleton often weighs less than its feathers.
Depending on the species, hummingbirds beat their wings dozens of times per second.

teile.einleitung: Albert Einstein was one of the most famous physicists of all time. With his theory of relativity he completely changed our picture of space, time and energy. He had his most important ideas in Switzerland, while he was working at the patent office in Bern.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein was born in 1879 in Ulm in Germany and died in 1955 in Princeton in the USA.
He studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today’s ETH.
In 1901 he became a Swiss citizen.
From 1902 he worked at the Federal Patent Office in Bern.
In his miracle year of 1905 he published several ground-breaking papers, including the formula E = mc².
He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1921.
In 1933 he moved to the USA, where he lived until his death.

abschnitte.text: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in **Ulm** and grew up in Munich. As a teenager he attended the cantonal school in **Aarau** and passed his school-leaving exam there. After that, from 1896 to 1900, he studied physics and mathematics at the **Polytechnic in Zurich**. In 1901 he became a Swiss citizen.

Because he could not find a job at a university, Einstein worked from 1902 at the **Federal Patent Office** in Bern. There he examined inventions and thought about physics in his spare time. For a while he lived at **Kramgasse 49** in Bern’s old town. He met friends for discussions and jokingly called the group the “Olympia Academy”.

In 1905 Einstein published several papers that changed physics. He explained that light consists of small packets of energy, and so provided the explanation for the **photoelectric effect**. He set out the **special theory of relativity**, according to which time and space are not the same for everyone. From this came the famous formula **E = mc²**: mass and energy can be turned into each other. In the same year he wrote his doctoral thesis at the University of Zurich.

In 1915, in Berlin, Einstein completed the **general theory of relativity**. It describes gravity as the curving of space and time by large masses. You can imagine it like a heavy ball on a stretched sheet, which makes a dip. In 1919 measurements during a solar eclipse confirmed that light is bent by the sun.

Einstein was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for the year 1921, for his explanation of the photoelectric effect. When the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, he was persecuted as a Jew. He moved to the USA and did research in **Princeton** until his death on 18 April 1955. All his life he campaigned for peace.

Without Einstein’s theories the **GPS** in your phone would calculate inaccurately, because clocks in satellites run differently from those on Earth. Lasers and solar cells are also based on his ideas about light. In Bern you can visit the **Einstein House** on the Kramgasse. The Bern Historical Museum also has a large exhibition about his life.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein’s theory that explains how space, time and gravity are connected.
A formula that says mass contains a huge amount of energy; c is the speed of light.
An authority that examines and protects new inventions.
Light can knock electrons out of a metal.

gewusst: The chemical element einsteinium is named after Albert Einstein.
Einstein was a citizen of Switzerland and kept his Swiss citizenship until the end of his life.
His most famous formula came about while he was still working during the day as an examiner at the patent office.

teile.einleitung: Attraction is a force that pulls things towards each other. You probably know it best from magnets that hold paper clips or nails. But not everything is attracted by a magnet, and that is exactly what makes experiments so exciting.
wichtigste: The force with which a magnet pulls iron towards it is called attraction.
Things that a magnet can attract are called magnetic.
Magnets mainly attract iron, nickel and cobalt.
Wood, gold, aluminium, glass and plastic are not attracted.
Both poles of a magnet attract an iron nail.
A magnet can attract from a short distance without touching.
The magnetic force also works through cardboard, paper and water.

abschnitte.text: In **attraction** two things move towards each other. A magnet attracts an iron nail even before it touches it. The closer the nail gets, the stronger the force becomes. Both poles of the magnet, the **north pole** and the **south pole**, attract iron. Between two magnets only unlike poles attract each other; like poles repel each other.

Objects that a magnet attracts are called **magnetic**. These include above all things made of iron and steel, but also of nickel and cobalt. A wooden ball, a ring of real gold or a drinks can made of aluminium are not attracted. The Swiss 5-centime coin also stays where it is, because it is made of a copper alloy. A tin can made of tinplate, which is thin steel, on the other hand, is attracted.

Put a **paper clip** on a thin piece of cardboard and move a magnet underneath it. The paper clip moves along with it, because the attraction works through the cardboard. This also works through a glass of water or through your hand. If you hang several paper clips one below the other on a magnet, they briefly become small magnets themselves. In this way you can make a whole chain.

It is not only magnets that attract. The Earth pulls all objects towards it; that is **gravity**. That is why an apple falls from a tree. Electric charges also attract each other when one is positive and one is negative. That is why a rubbed balloon attracts small scraps of paper or your hair.

Magnets hold drawings on the fridge and close bags and cupboard doors. At recycling centres large magnets separate iron and steel from other waste. The needle of a **compass** is a small magnet that the Earth’s magnetic field points to the north. More than 2000 years ago people in Greece and China already knew stones that attract iron. These stones made of magnetite gave the magnet its name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Attracted by a magnet, for example iron.
The places at the ends of a magnet where the force is strongest.
The invisible area round a magnet in which its force acts.
The attraction with which the Earth pulls all things towards it.

gewusst: Not every coin is magnetic, but some euro coins with a steel core are attracted by magnets.
The name magnet probably comes from the region of Magnesia in Greece, where magnetic stones were found.
The Earth itself is also a giant magnet; otherwise no compass would work.

teile.einleitung: Aerodynamics is the science of how air flows around moving bodies. It explains why aeroplanes fly, why racing cars have wings and why golf balls have dimples. In sport, good aerodynamics can decide between victory and defeat.
wichtigste: Aerodynamics studies how air flows around moving bodies.
Air resistance slows down everything that moves through the air.
In wind tunnels engineers and sports teams measure how strongly the air slows things down.
Aeroplane wings produce lift, while Formula One wings press the car down onto the road.
The dimples on a golf ball reduce air resistance.
Tight, smooth racing suits and pointed time-trial helmets let the air flow away better.
In places high up, the thinner air slows things down less.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: “aer” means air and “dynamis” means force. **Aerodynamics** is a branch of fluid dynamics. It studies the forces that arise when air flows past a body. The most important are the braking **air resistance**, also called drag, and **lift**, which acts at right angles to the flow.

An aeroplane wing is shaped and tilted slightly so that it deflects the air downwards. The air flows faster over the top, and the pressure above the wing is lower than below it. This pushes the wing upwards; that is lift. The German Otto Lilienthal studied this in the 1890s with his own gliding flights. In 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered flight.

With cars the main aim is low air resistance, so that they use less energy. How streamlined a car is, is described by the **drag coefficient**, or Cd value for short. Formula One cars have large wings at the front and back that work like upside-down aeroplane wings. They press the car onto the road so that it does not skid in bends. This force is called **downforce**.

Cycling and ski teams measure the air resistance of their athletes in a **wind tunnel**. In time trials, cyclists wear helmets with a long, pointed shape so that the air flows away better. On the track a closed disc wheel is often used at the back to avoid air swirls from the spokes. Speed skaters and skiers wear very tight, smooth suits. And because the air is thinner at altitude, sprint and cycling records are often easier to achieve in places high up.

A golf ball has several hundred small dimples. They make a thin, swirling layer of air form right on the surface. As a result, the airflow only separates from the ball further back, and the **wake** of swirling air behind the ball becomes smaller. This lowers the air resistance, and the ball flies much further than a smooth ball.

Many ideas in aerodynamics come from nature. Birds have curved wings and spread their feathers at the wing tips to reduce swirls. Many aeroplanes today have similar upturned wing tips, known as **winglets**. The shape of dolphins and penguins also shows how to glide through a medium with little resistance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving body.
The force that pushes a wing upwards.
A facility in which air is blown in a controlled way past models or people.
A number that shows how streamlined a shape is.

gewusst: A golf ball without dimples would only fly about half as far.
At high speed a cyclist has to use most of their effort against air resistance.
The Swiss Formula One team Sauber in Hinwil has its own wind tunnel.

teile.einleitung: The white stork is a large bird with white plumage, black flight feathers and a long red beak. It likes to build its nest on roofs and chimneys and is therefore familiar to many people. It once died out in Switzerland and returned thanks to dedicated conservationists.
wichtigste: The white stork has a red beak and red legs.
Its large flight feathers are black.
It often builds its nest on roofs and chimneys.
Storks communicate by clattering their beaks.
It likes to eat frogs, mice and insects.
Storks often reuse their old nest every year.
Around 1948, people began to reintroduce storks in Altreu in the canton of Solothurn.
Many Swiss storks spend the winter in Spain or in Africa.

abschnitte.text: The white stork is about a metre tall and has a **wingspan** of about two metres. Its plumage is white; only the large **flight feathers** on the wings are black. The beak and long legs are bright red. Males and females look almost the same.

Storks live in open landscapes with damp meadows, pastures and fields. They build their huge **nest** on church towers, roofs, chimneys, masts or trees. The stork couple often returns to the same nest every year and builds it up further. In this way a nest can become several hundred kilograms heavy over time.

The white stork stalks slowly across meadows and snaps up its prey in a flash. It eats **frogs**, mice, earthworms, grasshoppers and other insects. Sometimes it follows tractors during mowing, because then many animals are startled into the open. The young are fed by both parents.

Adult storks have almost no voice. Instead they **clatter** their beaks loudly, throwing their heads far back. The partners greet each other at the nest with this clattering. That is why in German fables the stork is also called “Meister Adebar” or simply the “Klapperstorch” (clattering stork).

The white stork is a **migratory bird**. In August and September the storks leave Switzerland and fly via France to Spain or further on to West Africa. On the way they use warm updraughts, **thermals**, and glide for hours without beating their wings. For a few decades now, many storks have stayed in Spain, where they find food on rubbish dumps.

Around 1950, no white storks bred in Switzerland any more, because wetlands had been drained. Around 1948 the conservationist **Max Bloesch** began reintroducing storks in **Altreu** in the canton of Solothurn. The birds were first kept in enclosures and later released. Today several hundred pairs of storks breed in Switzerland again, and Altreu is known as the stork village.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large nest of a stork or bird of prey; in German “Horst”.
Rising warm air on which birds glide upwards without beating their wings.
The width of a bird from one wingtip to the other.
An animal species that has disappeared is settled again in a place.

gewusst: Storks often sleep standing on one leg.
A stork's nest is sometimes used again and again over many decades.
With small transmitters on their backs, researchers follow the journey of Swiss storks as far as Africa.

teile.einleitung: Lake Vostok is a huge lake hidden deep beneath the ice of Antarctica. Above it lies a layer of ice almost 4 kilometres thick, and yet its water is liquid. It is the largest of the known lakes beneath the Antarctic ice and a fascinating puzzle for researchers.
wichtigste: Lake Vostok lies beneath about 4 kilometres of ice in Antarctica.
It is the largest lake beneath the ice of Antarctica.
Its area is about 12,500 square kilometres.
The water stays liquid because of the pressure of the ice and the Earth's heat.
In 2012 Russian researchers reached the lake water with a borehole.
The name comes from the Russian Vostok station; Vostok means east.
The lake is similar to the seas beneath the ice of Jupiter's moons.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Vostok** lies in East Antarctica, beneath the Russian **Vostok research station**. It is about 250 kilometres long and has an area of about 12,500 square kilometres. That is almost a third of the area of Switzerland. Above the lake lies an ice sheet almost 4 kilometres thick. In places the lake is several hundred metres deep.

It is icy cold in Antarctica, yet the water of the lake is liquid. This is due to the enormous **pressure** of the masses of ice, which lowers the freezing point of the water slightly. On top of this comes **geothermal heat**, which rises from the rock below. The thick ice also acts like a blanket that keeps out the cold from above. The water has a temperature of about minus 3 degrees.

Vostok station was founded by the Soviet Union in 1957. As early as the 1970s there were signs of a lake when aircraft scanned the ice with **radar**. In the 1990s, measurements by Russian and British researchers confirmed that it was a huge lake. Today hundreds of such lakes beneath the ice are known in Antarctica.

Russian researchers drilled a deep hole into the ice over many years. In February 2012 they finally reached the water of the lake. Lake water then rose up the borehole and froze. The researchers had to be careful not to pollute the lake with drilling fluid or germs from above. The ice cores also reveal a lot about the **climate** of the last several hundred thousand years.

The lake has been cut off from the outside world for a very long time, without sunlight and under high pressure. Researchers wonder whether tiny **microbes** can survive there. That is why space scientists are interested in Lake Vostok too. It is similar to the seas beneath the ice of Jupiter's moon **Europa** and Saturn's moon Enceladus, where life may perhaps also be possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The region around the South Pole with its ice-covered continent.
Lying beneath a glacier or beneath the ice.
A long column of ice from a borehole that tells us about the climate of earlier times.
A measuring method using radio waves that can detect things through ice.

gewusst: On 21 July 1983, minus 89.2 degrees was measured at Vostok station, the lowest air temperature ever recorded at a weather station on Earth.
Above the lake the ice is so thick that you could stack about eleven Eiffel Towers on top of each other.
Lake Vostok is one of the largest freshwater lakes on Earth, even though no human has ever seen it.

teile.einleitung: The alphorn is a long wooden wind instrument known above all from Switzerland. It has no finger holes and no keys, yet you can play whole tunes on it. Its warm, far-carrying sound can be heard across valleys and mountainsides.
wichtigste: The alphorn is usually made of wood, often spruce.
It is especially well known from Switzerland and is regarded as a typical Swiss instrument.
An alphorn has no finger holes and no keys.
The player makes the different notes with the lips alone.
In the past herders used the alphorn to give signals.
The end of the alphorn curves upwards and is called the bell.
Because of its loud, far-carrying sound, it can be heard a very long way.

abschnitte.text: An alphorn is usually about 3 to 4 metres long and consists of a long, conical **wooden tube**. Conical means that the tube gets wider and wider from the mouthpiece to the end. At the end it curves upwards and opens into the **bell**. In the past people looked for spruce trees that had grown on steep slopes and had become curved at the bottom by themselves. Today the parts are hollowed out and glued together by instrument makers, and often wrapped with rattan cane.

The player presses their lips against a mouthpiece and makes them **vibrate** while blowing in. This sets the column of air in the tube vibrating, and **sound waves** are produced. The longer the tube, the lower the fundamental note. In terms of physics, an alphorn is therefore similar to a trumpet, only much longer and without valves.

Because there are no finger holes, an alphorn can only play certain notes, the **natural notes**. The player chooses them by tightening or loosening the lips and giving more or less air. Higher natural notes lie close together, so tunes are usually played in the upper range. One special note lies between F and F sharp and is often called the **alphorn fa**. It sounds a little unusual to our ears and gives the music its typical character.

Herders in the Alps used to use the alphorn to give **signals**, for example to call the cows or to communicate with other alpine pastures. In the evening they also played a prayer or a tune on it to calm the animals. Over time the instrument was almost forgotten. In the 19th century it became popular again with alpine herders’ festivals, and since then it has been regarded as a **symbol of Switzerland**.

Today you hear the alphorn at yodelling festivals, at celebrations on 1 August and at tourist events in the mountains. Many alphorn players play in groups, often in threes or fours. There is also modern music, jazz and orchestral pieces for alphorn. For travelling there are alphorns that can be taken apart into three pieces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A note that a tube without holes or keys can produce by itself.
The air inside the tube, which vibrates when the instrument is played.
The wide, upturned end of the alphorn, where the sound comes out.
The small part at the start of the tube against which you put your lips.

gewusst: The composer Johannes Brahms used an alphorn tune he had heard in Switzerland in his first symphony.
In calm weather an alphorn can be heard several kilometres away in the mountains.
Many alphorns are so long that the bell rests on the ground while they are played.

teile.einleitung: In physics, work means something very specific: a force moves a body over a distance. Anyone who pushes a box or carries a rucksack up the stairs is doing work. Anyone who just holds a bag still, on the other hand, is doing no work in the physical sense, even if their arms get tired.
wichtigste: Mechanical work is force times distance, when both point in the same direction.
The unit of work is the joule.
One joule equals one newton metre.
Without movement in the direction of the force, no work is done.
Work is energy that has been transferred.
The unit joule is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule.
Work per unit of time is called power, measured in watts.

abschnitte.text: Physical **work** is done when a force moves a body along a path. The formula is W = F · s, that is **force times distance**. Force and distance must point in the same direction. If you hold a heavy bag still in the air, it does not move, and you do no work on it. Your muscles still get tired, though, because they are constantly working on the inside.

If you push a trolley with 50 N over 20 m, you do 50 · 20 = 1000 J of work. If a bike pulls a trailer with 40 N over 2 km, that is 80,000 J or 80 kJ. A crane that lifts a load of 2.5 kN by 0.4 m also does 1000 J. You can also rearrange the formula: 1500 J over 300 m means a force of 5 N. And 400 J with 8 N means that the force acted over 50 m.

The unit of work is the **joule**, abbreviated J. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton acts over one metre, that is one **newton metre**. If you lift a 100 g bar of chocolate by one metre, you do roughly one joule of work. Work is closely related to **energy**: anyone who does work transfers energy to a body. If a stone is lifted up, it stores this energy as potential energy.

When lifting, you do **lifting work**, which is weight times height. When accelerating, it is called acceleration work, and when pushing across the ground, work against friction. With a ramp or a pulley you need less force, but a longer distance. The work stays the same; this is called the **golden rule of mechanics**.

The term work in physics was introduced around 1829 by the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis. In the 1840s the English brewer and physicist **James Prescott Joule** showed that work can be turned into heat. He made a paddle wheel turn in water and measured how the water got warmer. The unit joule is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force times distance, that is the energy transferred when a body is moved.
The unit of work and energy.
The work you do when lifting a body up.
How much work is done per second, measured in watts.

gewusst: If you weigh 40 kg and climb stairs 3 m high, you do around 1200 J of lifting work.
Food packaging shows the energy content in kilojoules, the same unit as work.
One kilowatt hour of electricity corresponds to 3.6 million joules.

teile.einleitung: The cell is the smallest working building unit of a living thing. All plants, animals, fungi and humans are made of cells, and some living things of just a single one. Every cell is like a tiny factory that obtains energy, makes substances and can divide.
wichtigste: The cell is the smallest working building unit of a living thing.
Most cells are so small that you can only see them with a microscope.
A human is made of about 30 trillion cells.
The genetic material, DNA, lies in the nucleus.
Plant cells have a firm cell wall and chloroplasts.
Bacteria consist of a single cell without a nucleus.
New cells form through cell division.

abschnitte.text: A **cell** is a tiny space surrounded by a covering, in which all the processes of life take place. It takes in nutrients, obtains energy, grows and can multiply. Living things made of only one cell are called **single-celled organisms**, such as bacteria or slipper animalcules. Humans, animals and plants are multicellular organisms made of countless cells.

Every cell is surrounded by a thin **cell membrane**, which decides what gets in and out. Inside there is a gel-like liquid, the cytoplasm. The **nucleus** contains the DNA, that is, the blueprint of the living thing. The mitochondria are the power stations of the cell and obtain energy from food.

Plant cells also have a firm **cell wall** made of cellulose, which gives them support. They contain green **chloroplasts**, with which the plant makes sugar from sunlight. A large vacuole stores water and keeps the cell plump. Animal cells have no cell wall and are therefore often rounder and softer.

The human body is made of about 30 trillion cells, and there are more than 200 different cell types. Red blood cells carry oxygen, nerve cells pass on signals and muscle cells can contract. Many cells are constantly renewed, for example in the skin or the gut. The largest human cell is the egg cell, which can just about be seen as a tiny dot.

Cells multiply by dividing. Beforehand, the DNA is copied exactly so that each **daughter cell** receives a complete blueprint. In this way a whole human being grows from one single cell at the very beginning. Wounds heal too, because cells divide and close the gaps.

In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at thin slices of cork with a simple microscope. He saw small chambers and, after the cells of a monastery, called them cells. Around 1838 and 1839 the German researchers Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann realised that all plants and animals are made of cells. This is **cell theory**, one of the most important foundations of biology.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the cell in which the genetic material is kept.
The thin covering that surrounds every cell.
A part of the cell that obtains energy from food.
A green part of the plant cell in which photosynthesis takes place.
A living thing that consists of just one single cell.

gewusst: Before it develops, an ostrich egg is one single giant cell.
Some nerve cells in humans have extensions that are more than a metre long.
There are roughly as many bacterial cells living in your body as there are body cells of your own.

teile.einleitung: The root is the part of a plant that is usually hidden in the ground. It holds the plant in place, takes up water and nutrients and often stores supplies. Without roots, most plants could not live.
wichtigste: The root holds the plant firmly in the ground.
Fine root hairs take up water and nutrients.
The delicate root tip is protected by the root cap.
A thick main root that grows straight down is called a taproot.
Carrots and beetroot store food for the plant in their thick root.
Orchids often have grey aerial roots that stick out of the pot.
Many roots work together with fungi in the soil.

abschnitte.text: The root **anchors** the plant in the ground so that wind and rain do not knock it over. It takes up **water** and the minerals dissolved in it, such as nitrogen. These are carried through fine tubes inside the plant all the way to the leaves. Many plants also store nutrients in the root for hard times. Unlike leaves, the root has no chlorophyll, because it grows in the dark.

At the tip sits the **root cap**, a kind of protective cap made of cells. It protects the delicate growing zone as the root pushes through the soil. A little higher up grow countless tiny **root hairs**. They greatly increase the surface area of the root and so take up much more water. Roots always grow downwards towards gravity; this is called gravitropism.

A **taproot** grows as a thick main root straight down into the depths, as in the dandelion or the silver fir. Grasses and cereals, on the other hand, have a dense tuft of many thin fibrous roots. The spruce forms shallow roots that spread out just below the surface, which is why it is more easily blown over in a storm. Orchids have **aerial roots** that can take up moisture from the air. Ivy climbs up walls and trees with small clinging roots.

Some plants store a lot of food in a thickened root. These include the orange **carrot** (“Rüebli” in Swiss German) and the dark red **beetroot** (“Rande”). The plant builds up this store in its first year so that it has strength for flowers in the next year. But we harvest the roots before that and eat them raw, cooked or as juice. Parsnips, black salsify and horseradish are edible roots too.

Many plants live together with **fungi**, whose fine threads wrap around the roots. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The fungi help the plant to get water and minerals from the soil. In return they receive sugar from the plant, which it makes with the help of sunlight. Many well-known edible mushrooms in Swiss forests, such as the cep, live together with trees in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny hairs on the root that take up water from the soil.
A protective cap on the tip of the root.
A thick main root that grows vertically down into the depths.
A partnership between plant roots and fungi.

gewusst: Added together, the roots of a single rye plant are several hundred kilometres long.
The word “root” is also used in mathematics, for example in square root.
Underground, a tree often has a root system that is wider than its crown.

teile.einleitung: A certificate is a document that officially confirms something, for example a birth, a victory or a qualification. To be genuine and valid, it carries a signature and often a stamp or a seal. Old documents of this kind, called charters, are important sources for historians.
wichtigste: A certificate is a paper that confirms something.
A signature makes the certificate genuine and valid.
Official certificates often also carry a stamp.
A winner's certificate shows the name, the achievement and the date.
When a child is born, a birth certificate is issued.
After passing a course, you often get a diploma.
Each Nobel Prize certificate is a work of art in its own right.

abschnitte.text: A **certificate**, in German “Urkunde”, is a document that records a fact or a right in a binding way. It proves, for example, who was born, who won something or who owns a piece of land. So that it can be trusted, it is **signed** by an authorised person. Official certificates often also have a **stamp** or a seal.

At sports days and competitions there are **winner's certificates** with the name, the achievement and the date. After passing a course or completing training, you receive a **diploma** or a report. Many people hang an important certificate on the wall in a picture frame. When a child is born, the civil registry office issues a **birth certificate**, which you later need, for example, for a passport.

In the past, charters were written with ink on **parchment**, which was made from animal skin. Instead of a signature, a wax **seal** was often attached, into which the seal stamp of a king, monastery or town had been pressed. A famous example from Switzerland is the **Federal Charter** of 1291, in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help. You can see it today in the Federal Charter Museum in Schwyz.

The science that studies old charters is called **diplomatics**. Its experts examine the handwriting, language, material and seals to find out whether a charter is genuine and when it was made. In the Middle Ages, charters were also forged, for example to claim property rights. Many old charters are kept today in **archives** and are digitised for research.

The certificates for the **Nobel Prize** are something special, because each one is designed individually by artists and calligraphers and is a work of art in its own right. Certificates of honorary citizenship or founding charters are also often splendidly decorated. Today there are more and more electronic certificates with a digital signature. One thing remains important: anyone who forges a certificate is committing a crime.

begriffe.erklaerung: A writing material made from treated animal skin, which was common before paper.
The impression of a stamp in wax or lacquer that authenticates a document.
The science that studies old charters.
A place where important documents are kept safely.
The office in Switzerland that records births, marriages and deaths.

gewusst: The word diploma comes from Greek and originally meant a document folded in two.
Many medieval charters in Swiss archives are more than 800 years old.
The German word “Urkunde” is related to “kund tun”, which means to make something known.

teile.einleitung: A bird's egg is a little box of wonders: inside it a chick grows, well protected by a hard shell. All birds lay eggs, from the tiny hummingbird to the huge ostrich. The eggs differ greatly in size, shape and colour.
wichtigste: The hard shell of a bird's egg consists mainly of lime.
Most birds' eggs are oval and more pointed at one end.
Birds sit on their eggs to keep them warm.
The yolk is the food for the growing chick.
A hen sits on her eggs for about 21 days until the chick hatches.
The chick breaks open the shell with a small egg tooth on its beak.
Hummingbirds lay the smallest eggs, the ostrich the largest.

abschnitte.text: On the outside is the hard **shell**, which consists mainly of calcium carbonate. It has thousands of tiny pores, through which air gets in and moisture gets out. Under the shell there are thin membranes and, at the blunt end, a small **air cell**. Inside are the egg white and the yellow **yolk**, which provides the chick with food. Two twisted cords, the chalazae, hold the yolk in the middle.

Most birds' eggs are oval and more pointed at one end. Eggs of birds that breed on rock ledges, such as the common guillemot, are especially pointed and therefore roll in a circle instead of over the edge. Owls lay almost perfectly round eggs. The largest egg is laid by the **ostrich**; it weighs about as much as twenty to thirty hens' eggs. The smallest eggs are laid by **hummingbirds**; they are only about the size of a pea.

Many birds' eggs have spots so that they are well **camouflaged** in the nest. This is especially true of birds that breed on the ground, such as the lapwing or the little ringed plover. The eggs of the blackbird are blue-green with brown spots. Birds that breed in dark holes, such as woodpeckers, often lay pure white eggs. The cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests, and they often look amazingly like the eggs of the hosts.

For a chick to develop, the egg needs even **warmth**. That is why the parents sit on it; this is called **incubation**. For this, many birds have a featherless patch on their belly, the brood patch, through which body heat passes directly to the egg. They often turn the eggs regularly with their beak. With hens, incubation lasts about 21 days, with small songbirds only about two weeks.

Shortly before hatching, the chick first pecks into the air cell and breathes air for the first time. Then it breaks open the shell with the **egg tooth**, a small hard bump on the tip of its beak. The egg tooth falls off after a few days. Hatching is hard work and can take many hours. Chicks of hens and ducks are lively soon afterwards, whereas young songbirds are still naked and blind.

Hens' eggs are an important food and are found in cakes, pasta and sauces. In Switzerland, too, many farms keep laying hens, and free-range eggs are especially popular. The eggs of wild birds, on the other hand, are protected and must not be collected. If you find a nest with eggs, you should keep your distance so that the parents come back.

begriffe.erklaerung: The yellow part of the egg, which contains nutrients for the chick.
A small bump on the beak with which the chick breaks open the shell.
Keeping eggs warm with your own body heat until the young hatch.
A small space filled with air at the blunt end of the egg.

gewusst: An ostrich egg has such a thick shell that an adult can stand on it without it breaking.
The colour of an eggshell is formed by special pigments in the female's body before the egg is laid.
The chick already breathes inside the egg, through the tiny pores in the shell.

teile.einleitung: Zurich Zoo is one of the best-known zoos in Switzerland and lies on the Zürichberg. It shows animals in large, near-natural enclosures such as the Masoala Rainforest, the Elephant Park and the Lewa Savannah. As well as showing animals, it is also committed to protecting endangered species.
wichtigste: Zurich Zoo lies on the Zürichberg.
It was opened in 1929.
The Masoala Hall shows a rainforest from the island of Madagascar.
Asian elephants live in the Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park.
The Lewa Savannah shows African grassland, with giraffes among other animals.
A zoo protects endangered animal species and supports nature conservation projects.
Zookeepers look after the animals every day.

abschnitte.text: Zurich Zoo lies at the edge of the forest on the **Zürichberg**, high above the city of Zurich. It was opened in 1929 and has grown a great deal since then. It is easy to reach by tram and bus. As a rule, well over a million visitors come every year. This makes it one of the most popular places for a day out in Switzerland.

The **Masoala Hall** opened in 2003 and is a huge glass hall with a real rainforest. Its area is about 11,000 square metres, which is about one and a half football pitches. The plants and animals come from the Masoala National Park on the island of **Madagascar**. Lemurs, flying foxes, chameleons and colourful birds, for example, live freely among the trees. It is warm and humid there all year round, just like in the tropics.

Asian elephants live in the **Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park**, which opened in 2014. It is named after a national park in Thailand. In the **Lewa Savannah**, opened in 2020, you can see African grassland with giraffes, rhinos, zebras and other animals. Its name comes from a conservancy in Kenya. The zoo also has an Australia enclosure in which koalas live.

A modern zoo does not just show animals; it also helps with **species protection**. Zurich Zoo supports nature conservation projects in the regions its enclosures come from, for example in Madagascar, Thailand and Kenya. Many endangered animal species are bred in **conservation breeding programmes** in which zoos from all over Europe take part. In this way a healthy reserve population is kept. Visitors also learn why habitats have to be protected.

Every day, **zookeepers** take care of the animals' food, cleanliness and health. They watch closely to see whether an animal is well and keep things varied with activities. Vets examine and treat sick animals. Gardeners look after the many plants, especially in the Masoala Hall. Biologists also work at the zoo and study the animals' behaviour.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measures to stop endangered animal and plant species from dying out.
A dense forest in warm regions where it rains a great deal.
A warm grassland with scattered trees.
The planned breeding of endangered animals in zoos in order to preserve the species.

gewusst: In the Masoala Hall it rains artificially so that the rainforest plants get enough water.
The Elephant Park has a roof made of wood and plastic so that the elephants have plenty of space and light in winter too.
Many animals live freely in the Masoala Hall, so that you sometimes meet a lemur or a bird right next to the path.

teile.einleitung: Optical aberrations are faults that stop a lens or mirror from producing an image that is completely sharp or completely true to shape. Instead of a fine point a small blur appears, lines become curved or edges get coloured fringes. Opticians fight these faults with cleverly combined lenses.
wichtigste: Optical aberrations make the images of lenses and mirrors worse.
Ludwig von Seidel distinguished five monochromatic aberrations.
In spherical aberration the edge rays of a converging lens are bent more strongly than rays near the axis.
Stopping down, that is using a smaller aperture, reduces spherical aberration.
Aspherical lenses largely avoid spherical aberration.
In distortion, straight lines at the edge of the image appear curved.
Coma makes a point look like a comet with a tail when light comes in at an angle.

abschnitte.text: An ideal lens would form each point of an object again as a sharp point. Real lenses with spherically ground surfaces never quite manage this. The deviations are called **optical aberrations**. A distinction is made between faults that occur even with light of a single colour and faults caused by the different colours of light. In 1856 the mathematician **Ludwig von Seidel** described the five most important faults for single-coloured, that is monochromatic, light.

In **spherical aberration** the outer zones of a converging lens bend light more strongly than the centre. As a result the edge rays meet at a different point from the rays near the axis, and the image becomes a little blurred. A simple remedy is **stopping down**: a smaller aperture only lets through the rays near the centre. Better still are **aspherical lenses**, whose surfaces are not ground to an exact sphere. Today they are found in many cameras and mobile phone lenses.

When light enters a lens at an angle, **coma** occurs, in which a point looks like a comet with a tail. In **astigmatism**, slanting beams of light are not focused to a point but to two separate lines at different distances. In **field curvature** the sharp image does not lie on a flat plane but on a curved surface. Then the centre and edge of the image cannot both be sharp at the same time on a flat sensor. Together with spherical aberration and distortion, these are the five Seidel aberrations.

With **distortion** the image is sharp, but warped. Straight lines at the edge of the image appear curved. If they bend outwards, it is called barrel distortion; if they bend inwards, pincushion distortion. Distortion is especially strong in **fisheye lenses**, which deliberately show a very wide angle of view. Today many cameras and mobile phones correct this fault automatically with software.

Glass bends blue light more strongly than red, so simple lenses have a slightly different focal point for each colour. This **colour fault**, chromatic aberration, produces coloured fringes along bright edges. If you combine two lenses made of different types of glass, you get an **achromat**, which greatly reduces this fault. Good camera lenses therefore consist of many individual lenses that correct each other. The Hubble Space Telescope also had an optical fault after its launch in 1990, which was corrected during a repair mission in space in 1993.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for an optical fault in an image.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and gathers light rays at one point.
An adjustable opening that determines how much light passes through a camera lens.
A combination of lenses that greatly reduces colour faults.
A fault in which straight lines in the image appear curved.

gewusst: The mirror of the Hubble telescope was ground wrongly at the edge by only about two thousandths of a millimetre.
The human eye also has optical aberrations, and the brain makes up for many of them.
A modern camera lens can consist of more than ten individual lenses.

teile.einleitung: An absorption spectrum shows which colours or wavelengths of light a substance swallows. If you send white light through a gas, certain colours are missing afterwards and show up as dark lines. These lines are like a fingerprint that lets you recognise substances even on distant stars.
wichtigste: An absorption spectrum forms when light with a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas.
The gas swallows very particular wavelengths, which are then missing as dark lines.
According to Kirchhoff’s law of radiation, a gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths that it also gives out.
Every chemical element has its own pattern of lines.
Chlorophyll in plants absorbs mainly blue and red light.
Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb strongly in the infrared and so contribute to the greenhouse effect.
The ozone in the stratosphere absorbs a large part of the sun’s UV radiation.

abschnitte.text: White light contains all colours, as you can see in a rainbow or behind a prism. Such a band of colours without gaps is called a **continuous spectrum**. If this light passes through a cooler gas, the gas swallows individual colours. Dark lines then appear in the spectrum, and the result is called an **absorption spectrum**.

The electrons in an atom can only take on very particular energy levels. If light with exactly the right energy hits the atom, it lifts an electron to a higher level and is swallowed in the process. Light with a different energy simply carries on. That is why only very particular wavelengths are missing. According to **Kirchhoff’s law of radiation**, they are the same wavelengths that a hot gas of the same substance gives out as bright lines.

Around 1814 the German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer discovered hundreds of dark lines in the light of the sun. Today they are called **Fraunhofer lines**. Around 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen explained that these lines come from gases in the sun’s atmosphere. This made it possible to find out what substances the sun is made of without ever having been there. The element helium was even discovered first in the solar spectrum and only found on Earth later.

The colours of things are also linked to absorption. A pane of glass with red dye absorbs the other colours and lets mainly red through, which is why it looks red. Leaves look green because **chlorophyll** swallows blue and red light for photosynthesis and reflects green. In chemistry a **photometer** is used to measure how much light a solution swallows.

How strongly a substance swallows light is described by its **absorbance**. With an absorbance of 1, 10 per cent of the light still gets through; with an absorbance of 2, only 1 per cent. According to the **Beer-Lambert law**, absorbance equals the absorption coefficient times concentration times path length. If a solution in a 1 cm cuvette has an absorbance of 0.6 and a coefficient of 12,000 L/(mol · cm), the concentration is 0.00005 mol/L.

The Earth’s atmosphere acts like a huge filter. The **ozone** in the stratosphere absorbs a large part of the dangerous UV radiation and so protects skin and eyes. Carbon dioxide and water vapour, on the other hand, absorb heat radiation in the **infrared**. As a result heat stays in the atmosphere, which is called the greenhouse effect. Today researchers also use absorption spectra to measure how much greenhouse gas is in the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of light into its individual colours or wavelengths.
The distance between two wave crests; it determines the colour of light.
The swallowing of light by a substance.
A number that shows how strongly a sample weakens light.
A narrow bright or dark line at a particular wavelength in the spectrum.

gewusst: The element helium was first discovered in the light of the sun in 1868, before it was found on Earth.
With absorption spectra researchers can even study the air of planets around distant stars.
Without the absorption of UV light by ozone, life on land would hardly be possible.

teile.einleitung: A weather satellite is a satellite that observes the Earth's clouds, temperatures and humidity from space. You know its pictures from the weather forecast on television. Without weather satellites, today's weather forecasts would be much less accurate.
wichtigste: Weather satellites observe clouds, weather and the Earth's surface from space.
Geostationary weather satellites such as Meteosat orbit about 36,000 kilometres above the equator.
A geostationary satellite needs about 24 hours for one orbit and therefore seems to stand still.
Polar-orbiting weather satellites fly lower and provide images with finer detail.
Infrared images show the temperature of cloud tops and the Earth's surface.
The water vapour channel makes the moisture in the middle and upper troposphere visible.
The European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites, EUMETSAT, is based in Darmstadt.

abschnitte.text: A **weather satellite** is an uncrewed spacecraft that orbits the Earth and constantly radios measurements and images back to Earth. It observes clouds, storms, fog, snow and sea surfaces. The first successful weather satellite was **TIROS-1**, which the USA launched in 1960. Today there are dozens of weather satellites from different countries.

**Geostationary** satellites orbit about 36,000 kilometres high exactly above the equator. They need about 24 hours for one orbit, the same time as the Earth needs to turn once. That is why they always seem to be above the same point and can deliver a new image every few minutes. But because they are above the equator, they look at the polar regions at a very steep angle and see them only poorly.

**Polar-orbiting** satellites fly much lower, usually at about 800 kilometres, and cross both poles. As the Earth turns beneath them, they gradually cover the whole surface of the Earth. Because they are closer to the Earth, they provide images with finer detail and precise measurements for the weather models. An example is the European satellites of the MetOp series.

In **visible light** you see clouds and snow as we would see them with our eyes, but only during the day. **Infrared images** show the temperature of cloud tops and the Earth's surface, even at night. High, cold clouds appear especially bright in them. The **water vapour channel** makes the moisture in the middle and upper troposphere visible, including where there are no clouds.

The European weather satellites are called **Meteosat**; the first was launched in 1977. They are operated by **EUMETSAT**, the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites, based in Darmstadt in Germany. Switzerland is a member of EUMETSAT, and MeteoSwiss uses the data for its forecasts. Since 2022, satellites of the third Meteosat generation have been launched into space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flying object that circles the Earth on a fixed path.
An orbit on which a satellite always stays above the same point on Earth.
Heat radiation that our eyes cannot see but sensors can measure.
The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which the weather takes place.

gewusst: From its position, a Meteosat satellite can see almost half the Earth at once.
Weather satellites also help to detect forest fires, volcanic ash and sandstorms.
The first weather satellite, TIROS-1, sent pictures for only about two and a half months, but it showed how useful the view from above is.

teile.einleitung: A variable is a quantity that can change, for example a temperature, a length or the colour of a flower. In experiments, different types of variable are distinguished. There are also variables in maths, where they are letters such as x.
wichtigste: A variable is a quantity that can change.
The quantity that you measure as a result is called the dependent variable.
Quantities that you deliberately keep the same are called control variables.
A quantity that never changes is called a constant.
A confounding variable affects the result unintentionally.
Quantitative variables can be measured in numbers; qualitative ones, such as flower colour, cannot.
In maths, a letter such as x stands as a variable for a number.

abschnitte.text: The word **variable** comes from the Latin variabilis and means “changeable”. In science, a variable is any quantity that can take different values. The temperature outside, the size of a plant or the number of children in a class are variables. In contrast, a **constant** is a quantity that never changes in an experiment, for example the acceleration due to gravity at a particular place.

The quantity that you deliberately change is called the **independent variable**. The quantity that you measure because it changes as a result is called the **dependent variable**. All the quantities that you keep the same so that the test is fair are called **control variables**. For example, if you test how fertiliser affects plant growth, you change the amount of fertiliser, measure the height and keep light, water and soil the same.

Sometimes a quantity affects the result without you noticing or wanting it to. Such a quantity is called a **confounding variable**. If, for example, one plant pot is closer to the window than the others, it gets more light and may grow better because of that. Good researchers look for such confounding variables and eliminate them so that the result is correct.

Variables that can be measured in numbers are called **quantitative variables**, for example length, weight or temperature. Other variables describe a property without a measured number; they are called **qualitative variables**. Flower colour, eye colour or favourite sport are examples of these. Qualitative variables can be counted and shown, for example, in a bar chart.

In maths, a letter such as **x** stands for a number that is still unknown or can change. In the equation x plus 3 equals 7, for example, x is 4. In computing, a variable is a named storage space in which a program stores a value, such as the score in a game. The score changes during the game, but the name of the variable stays the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that does not change.
A quantity that you deliberately keep the same in an experiment.
A quantity that affects the result unintentionally.
Measurable in numbers.
Describing a property, without a measured number.

gewusst: Around 1600 the French mathematician François Viète introduced letters for numbers into algebra.
The fact that unknowns are often written as x goes back to the philosopher and mathematician René Descartes.
Computer programs often use thousands of variables at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Perception means that we take in the world around us with our senses. Eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin collect stimuli, and the brain turns them into a picture of reality. In doing so, the brain works much more actively than you might think.
wichtigste: Humans perceive the world with several senses, above all seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
In the eye, the cones are responsible for colour vision.
At dusk it is mainly the rods that work, which is why we hardly see colours then.
People with normal vision have three types of cone.
The image on the retina is upside down, and the brain turns it round.
As well as sweet, sour, salty and bitter, there is the taste umami.
In the cochlea in the inner ear, sounds are turned into nerve signals.
Optical illusions show that the brain actively interprets sensory impressions.

abschnitte.text: Perception begins with a **stimulus**, for example light, sound or a smell. Special **sensory cells** pick up the stimulus and turn it into electrical nerve signals. These signals travel along nerves to the brain. Only there does what we see, hear or feel come into being.

Light falls through the pupil and the lens onto the **retina** at the back of the eye. There are the **cones** for colours and sharp vision and the **rods** for weak light. Because the lens turns the image round, it is upside down on the retina. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no sensory cells; this is the blind spot.

Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones in the middle ear, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibration on. In the **cochlea** in the inner ear, fine hair cells turn the vibrations into nerve signals. The organ of balance is also located in the inner ear.

The tongue recognises the basic tastes sweet, sour, salty, bitter and **umami**, which is the savoury taste of, for example, stock or Parmesan. But much of what we think of as taste actually comes from the nose. That is why food tastes bland when you have a cold. The skin senses pressure, warmth, cold and pain.

With **optical illusions** you see things differently from how they really are. Two lines of the same length, for example, look different lengths if you draw arrowheads on them. This shows that the brain interprets sensory impressions and fills in gaps. Usually this helps us to understand quickly what is happening around us, but sometimes it leads us astray.

If you know how perception works, you also understand glasses, hearing aids or colour blindness better. In a common form of **colour vision deficiency**, one type of cone works differently, so that red and green are hard to tell apart. Researchers also use this knowledge to design road signs that are easy to see. Art, film and computer games also play cleverly with our perception.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that excites a sense organ, such as light, sound or a smell.
The thin layer at the back of the eye with the light-sensitive sensory cells.
Sensory cells in the eye that recognise colours.
Sensory cells in the eye that tell light from dark when there is little light.
The fifth basic taste, savoury and hearty.

gewusst: You do not notice the blind spot in everyday life, because the brain simply fills in the gap.
The ossicles in the middle ear are the smallest bones in the human body.
Many birds and insects can also see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to humans.

teile.einleitung: An engineering material is a material from which objects are made, for example wood, metal, plastic or glass. Depending on the task, you need a material that is hard, light, flexible or heat-resistant. The history of humanity is so closely linked to materials that whole ages are named after them.
wichtigste: Engineering materials are materials from which components and objects are made.
The main groups are metals, plastics, ceramics and glass, natural materials and composites.
Bronze is an alloy consisting mainly of copper and tin.
Brass is a golden-yellow alloy of copper and zinc.
Steel is made when carbon is added to iron.
Diamond has the highest value, 10, on the Mohs hardness scale.
Because of its good electrical conductivity, copper is usually used for electric cables.

abschnitte.text: An **engineering material** is a solid substance that is used to make things. Materials are usually divided into groups: **metals** such as iron or aluminium, **plastics** such as PET, **ceramics and glass**, and **natural materials** such as wood, leather or wool. There are also composites, which combine several materials. Engineers choose the right material for each task.

Human history is partly divided according to materials: the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age. **Bronze** is a mixture of copper and tin and was harder than pure copper. Later people learned to melt and forge iron. If you add a little carbon to iron, you get **steel**, which today is one of the most important materials of all.

An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with other elements. This changes its properties; the material becomes, for example, harder or rusts less. **Brass**, made of copper and zinc, is golden yellow and is used for door handles, screws and brass instruments. Stainless steel contains chromium and is used, for example, for cutlery and sinks.

**Density** says how much mass a material has per volume; aluminium, for example, is much lighter than steel. **Hardness** shows how well a material resists scratches and dents; on the Mohs scale, diamond is the hardest at 10.
