Strength, elasticity and conductivity for electricity and heat are also important. Copper conducts electricity especially well and is therefore found in almost every cable.

Many metals react with oxygen and water from their surroundings; this is called **corrosion**. With iron, reddish-brown rust forms in damp air and destroys the material over time. Protective layers such as paint, zinc or plastic prevent this. Copper, on the other hand, forms a green layer over time, which you can see on old church tower roofs.

Many materials can be **recycled** and used again. In Switzerland, for example, aluminium cans, glass bottles, PET bottles and waste paper are collected separately. Recycling aluminium needs much less energy than producing new aluminium. In this way raw materials and the environment are protected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal and other elements.
How much mass a substance has in a particular volume.
How strongly a material resists scratching or denting.
The slow destruction of a material by substances from its surroundings, for example rust.
How well a material passes on electricity or heat.

gewusst: The Mohs hardness scale was developed by the mineralogist Friedrich Mohs and begins with soft talc at 1.
Aluminium is almost three times lighter than steel.
Glass is actually not a crystal but a solidified melt.

teile.einleitung: The principle of action is the second of Newton’s three laws of mechanics. It says how strongly a body accelerates when a force acts on it. Its short formula F = m · a is one of the most famous equations in physics.
wichtigste: The basic equation of the second law is F equals m times a.
The greater the force, the greater the acceleration.
If you triple the force, the acceleration also triples.
If the same force acts on twice the mass, the acceleration halves.
The unit of force is the newton; 1 N corresponds to 1 kg · m/s².
Isaac Newton published the law in 1687 in his work “Principia”.
For acceleration it is always the resultant force that counts, that is the sum of all forces.

abschnitte.text: The **principle of action** is also called Newton’s second law or the fundamental law of mechanics. It links three quantities: the **force** F, the **mass** m and the **acceleration** a. The formula F = m · a means: a force changes the speed of a body. A heavy body needs more force than a light one for the same acceleration.

To accelerate 2 kg at 3 m/s², you need 2 · 3 = 6 N. If a force of 12 N acts on a trolley of 4 kg, it accelerates at 12 : 4 = 3 m/s². A car of 1000 kg needs a force of 2000 N for 2 m/s². If a force of 600 N accelerates a body at 4 m/s², it has a mass of 150 kg. So you can rearrange the formula for any of the three quantities.

A bike and its rider together weigh 80 kg. If, after subtracting air resistance and friction, a **resultant force** of 40 N remains, they accelerate at 0.5 m/s². A football of 0.5 kg that is accelerated at 20 m/s² when kicked experiences a force of 10 N. An empty shopping trolley is easy to push off, a full one only with effort. That is exactly what the principle of action describes.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** presented the law in 1687 in his book “Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica”. In it he described three laws: the principle of inertia, the principle of action and the principle of interaction. Newton actually formulated it in terms of **momentum**: force equals the change in momentum per unit of time. The unit newton was later named after him.

With the principle of action experts calculate how strong brakes, engines and rocket motors need to be. The orbits of planets and satellites can also be worked out with it. Weight is a special case: F = m · g with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² on Earth. Only at very high speeds close to the speed of light do you need Albert Einstein’s more precise theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can accelerate or deform a body, measured in newtons.
How much matter a body has and how sluggish it is, measured in kilograms.
How fast the speed changes, measured in m/s².
The force that is left when you add all the forces together.

gewusst: One newton is roughly the weight of a 100 g bar of chocolate.
Rockets keep getting lighter in flight because they burn fuel, and so with the same thrust they accelerate more and more strongly.
Newton wrote his “Principia” in Latin, the language of science at that time.

teile.einleitung: A camera trap is a small, weatherproof camera that automatically takes a photo or video as soon as an animal moves in front of it. It is also called a trail camera. With it you can watch shy animals without disturbing them.
wichtigste: A camera trap is triggered when an animal moves.
At night it takes pictures with infrared light, which does not dazzle the animals.
The night pictures are usually black and white.
A green-brown camouflage pattern makes it almost invisible in the woods.
It is usually fixed to a tree trunk and runs on batteries.
In Switzerland, lynx are often counted with camera traps.
When setting it up, you have to make sure that no people are filmed.

abschnitte.text: A **camera trap** is a camera in a robust, waterproof case. It usually hangs on a tree trunk and waits for days or weeks for visitors. It gets its power from **batteries**, and some also from a small solar panel. The pictures are stored on a memory card, and newer devices even send them to your mobile phone over the mobile network.

A **motion sensor** detects warmth that is moving, for example a fox or a roe deer. Then the camera is triggered in a fraction of a second. At night it lights up the scene with **infrared light**, which is invisible to most animals and to humans. That is why the animals are not dazzled, and the night pictures are usually black and white. During the day the camera takes normal colour pictures.

Many camera traps have a green-brown pattern so that they are well **camouflaged** in the woods. You fix them to a tree trunk with a strap, at about knee to hip height. Game trails, that is, paths that animals often use, are ideal. The camera should not point directly into the sun, otherwise warm air or shadows can set it off by mistake.

For research, camera traps are very valuable, because no person disturbs the animals. In Switzerland, the foundation **KORA** regularly uses them to count **lynx**. Every lynx has its own pattern of spots in its fur, which can be recognised in the pictures like a fingerprint. In this way it is known how many lynx live in an area. Wolves, golden jackals and wildcats are also detected in this way.

Anyone who sets up a camera trap must make sure that no **people** are filmed. Footpaths, neighbours' gardens or public places must not be in the picture, because that violates privacy. In Switzerland, the Data Protection Act applies to this. In the forest you also often need permission from the forest owners or the authorities.

You can also make exciting discoveries with a camera trap in your own garden. Hedgehogs, foxes, martens or badgers often walk into the camera trap. You should leave the camera in the same place for a few days and not put out food to attract animals. The best pictures are usually taken at dusk and at night.

begriffe.erklaerung: A camera that triggers itself when something moves; in German “Fotofalle” or “Wildkamera”.
Light that our eyes cannot see but that the camera records.
A sensor that notices when something warm moves.
A path that wild animals use regularly.

gewusst: The lynx had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1971.
Camera traps have even found animal species that were thought to be extinct.
A modern camera trap can stand ready for months on one set of batteries.

teile.einleitung: A composite material consists of two or more different materials that are firmly joined together. Together they have better properties than each material on its own. Such materials are found in tower blocks, skis, bikes and even aeroplanes.
wichtigste: A composite is a material made of several firmly joined materials.
Usually strong fibres are embedded in a base material called the matrix.
Reinforced concrete consists of concrete and steel, with the steel mainly taking the tensile forces.
Wood is a natural composite made of fibres and a binding substance.
In the past, straw was mixed into mud bricks so that they cracked less as they dried.
The rotor blades of wind turbines are usually made of fibre-reinforced plastic.
Composites are often light and yet very stable.

abschnitte.text: A **composite material** is created when different materials are combined so that they work together. Often there is a base material, the **matrix**, with fibres or particles embedded in it. The fibres make the material strong, while the matrix holds them together and protects them. In this way a material can be created that is light, tough and stable at the same time.

Concrete withstands a great deal of pressure but breaks easily when it is pulled. Steel, on the other hand, withstands pulling very well. That is why in **reinforced concrete** there are steel bars in the concrete, which take over the tensile forces. In 1867 a French gardener called Joseph Monier patented concrete flower tubs with iron inserts. Today bridges, tunnels and tower blocks in Switzerland are largely made of reinforced concrete.

Nature also has composites. **Wood** consists of strong cellulose fibres held together by the binding substance lignin. Bones are also a composite of hard minerals and elastic protein fibres. Thousands of years ago, people were already mixing straw into clay so that mud bricks cracked less as they dried.

In **glass-fibre-reinforced plastic** (GRP) or **carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic** (CFRP), fine fibres lie in synthetic resin. These materials are light and yet very stiff. They are found in racing bikes, skis, boat hulls, helmets and aircraft. The long rotor blades of wind turbines are also usually made of fibre-reinforced plastic.

Composites save weight, which in vehicles, for example, saves fuel or electricity. One disadvantage is that the joined materials are difficult to separate again. That is why **recycling** is often complicated. Researchers are working on making composites easier to recycle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The base material that surrounds the fibres and holds them together.
A very thin, long thread that withstands tensile forces well.
A force that pulls on a body and tries to pull it apart.
Abbreviation for plastic reinforced with carbon fibres; in German “CFK”.
A natural binding substance that makes wood firm.

gewusst: In modern airliners such as the Boeing 787, a large part of the fuselage and wings is made of carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic.
The inventor of reinforced concrete was not an engineer but a gardener who wanted sturdier plant tubs.
Even a scrap of paper with paste is, in principle, a simple composite material.

teile.einleitung: A windsock is a fabric tube that hangs from a pole and can turn, making the wind visible. At a glance it shows which direction the wind is blowing from and how strong it is. You see it at airfields, at helicopter landing pads and on motorway bridges.
wichtigste: A windsock shows the direction and strength of the wind.
It is a fabric tube that is wider at the front than at the back.
It is often striped red and white or orange and white.
If it hangs down limply, there is almost no wind.
If it sticks out completely horizontally, a strong wind is blowing.
At airfields it helps pilots take off and land.
On some motorway bridges it warns of dangerous crosswinds.

abschnitte.text: A windsock is a cone-shaped **fabric tube** that is wider at the front and narrower at the back. The large opening is attached to a metal ring that can turn freely on a pole. So that it is easy to see, it is usually striped in **signal colours**, often red and white or orange and white. At night it is often lit up at airfields.

The wind blows into the wide opening and fills the tube. As it does so, the windsock turns so that the opening faces the wind and the narrow end points away from it. This shows the **wind direction**. The harder the wind blows, the more the tube lifts.

If the windsock hangs down limply, there is almost **no wind**. If it sticks out halfway, a moderate wind is blowing. If it sticks out completely **horizontally**, the wind is strong. On airfield windsocks with five stripes, each filled stripe means about 3 knots more wind; fully stretched out, it is about 15 knots or around 28 kilometres per hour.

Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind whenever possible, because then they need a shorter distance. That is why there is at least one windsock next to every runway. Pilots can also see it well from the air. Windsocks are also found at **helicopter landing pads**, for example at hospitals or in the mountains, and at take-off sites for paragliders.

On high bridges, viaducts and in narrow valleys, strong **crosswinds** can suddenly occur. This is dangerous for lorries, caravans and motorbikes, because the wind pushes them sideways. A windsock at the roadside warns drivers. Then the rule is: slow down and hold the steering wheel firmly.

Windsocks also stand at factories that work with dangerous gases. In an accident, people can see at once which way the gas is being blown and can escape in the opposite direction. The fire brigade uses this information as well. So in an emergency a simple windsock can save lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direction the wind is coming from.
How fast and how hard the wind is blowing.
Wind that comes from the side, across the direction of travel.
A unit of speed in aviation and shipping; one knot is about 1.85 kilometres per hour.

gewusst: You can make a simple windsock yourself from an old shirt sleeve and a wire ring.
On a windsock the tip points to where the wind is blowing to; on a weathercock the head points to where it is coming from.
Windsocks work without any electricity and are therefore reliable even in a power cut.

teile.einleitung: Science journalism is the part of journalism that reports on research: on new medicines, the climate, space or animals. Science journalists explain research in an understandable way and put it into context critically. They are a bridge between the laboratory and the public.
wichtigste: The main task is to explain research clearly and put it into context critically.
Good reports check how certain a result really is.
Press releases from universities sometimes exaggerate results.
A link in a statistic does not yet mean that one thing causes the other.
Results from studies with mice cannot be transferred directly to humans.
With “false balance”, a minority opinion is given the same weight as the opinion of almost all experts.
SRF's science magazine on television is called “Einstein”.

abschnitte.text: Science journalism reports on **research** in newspapers, on the radio, on television and online. The topics range from medicine, technology and the environment to archaeology. Journalists read scientific papers, talk to researchers and explain the results in simple language. They should not simply advertise research but also ask **critical** questions. They show what a study has found out and what is still uncertain.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the news come from?
abschnitte.text: New research usually appears in **scientific journals** such as “Nature” or “Science”. Before a paper appears there, other experts check the work; this is called peer review. Many journals send new papers to journalists in advance, but with an **embargo**. Only from a certain time may anyone report on it, so that there is enough time for thorough research. Universities also send out press releases about their own research.

A common mistake is confusing **correlation and causation**. If, for example, more ice cream is eaten on hot days and more people get sunburnt, the ice cream still does not cause sunburn. Another mistake is presenting results from animal experiments with mice as if they were certain to apply to humans too. “False balance” is also dangerous: when a single outsider gets as much space as the **consensus** of the experts. And anyone who just copies the press release sometimes takes over its exaggerations.

Good science journalists read the original study and not just a summary. They ask independent experts who were not involved in the study for their opinion. The **Science Media Center**, for example, helps with this by quickly putting the media in touch with experts' assessments of current topics. Important questions are: how many people or animals were studied? Who paid for the study? Has the result already been confirmed by others?

Swiss Radio and Television SRF has its own science departments. The television magazine **“Einstein”** explains research with experiments and reports. Large newspapers also have sections for science, technology or health. During the coronavirus pandemic it became clear how important reliable science reporting is for everyone. At that time, studies were often published as early versions, called **preprints**, and discussed in the media straight away.

begriffe.erklaerung: A magazine in which researchers publish their new results for other experts.
The checking of a piece of research by other experts before it is published.
A point in time before which the media may not yet report on a piece of news.
Two things often occur together, without one necessarily causing the other.
The view that almost all experts have agreed on.

gewusst: A single study rarely proves anything; only many studies together give a reliable picture.
Science journalists sometimes have to correct a report too, if a result later turns out to be wrong.
Many science journalists studied biology, physics or medicine themselves.

teile.einleitung: A weather forecast predicts what the weather will be like in the next hours and days. It tells you whether the sun will shine, whether it will rain, how warm it will get and how strongly the wind will blow. Behind every forecast are measurements from all over the world and huge computers.
wichtigste: A weather forecast gives information about what the weather will be like.
Experts who forecast the weather are called meteorologists.
In Switzerland, the federal office MeteoSwiss is responsible for weather forecasts.
Precipitation includes rain, snow and hail.
A high probability of rain such as 90 per cent means: better take an umbrella.
Weather symbols show the weather with simple pictures.
The foehn is a warm, dry downslope wind from the Alps.

abschnitte.text: A weather forecast is a prediction of the weather for the next few days. You find it on television, on the radio, in the newspaper and in weather apps. It gives the **temperature**, the **precipitation**, the wind and the cloud cover. Some forecasts also show the pollen count or how strong the UV radiation is.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the data come from?
abschnitte.text: All over the world, **weather stations** measure temperature, air pressure, humidity and wind. Satellites photograph the clouds from space, and radar devices detect where it is raining at the moment. At Payerne in the canton of Vaud, **weather balloons** with measuring instruments go up every day. All this data goes into computers, which use weather models to calculate how the air moves.

Weather experts are called **meteorologists**. They compare the results of different computer models and use their experience, especially in the mountains. In Switzerland the federal office **MeteoSwiss** is responsible, and there are also private weather services. The forecast for the next two to three days is usually quite reliable, but for ten days it is only approximate.

Weather forecasts often contain simple **symbols**: a sun for sunny, a cloud with drops for rain. A sun with a cloud means that sun and clouds alternate. The **probability of rain** says how certain it is to rain: at 10 per cent rather not, at 90 per cent almost certainly. Then you had better take an umbrella.

Because of the Alps, the weather in Switzerland is often very different from place to place. While it is raining in the north, the sun may be shining in Ticino, or the other way round. A typical wind is the **foehn**, a warm, dry downslope wind that blows down from the Alps. The cold, dry **bise**, on the other hand, blows from the north-east across the Central Plateau.

For thunderstorms, storms, heavy rain or heat, MeteoSwiss issues **severe weather warnings**. They have five danger levels, from low to very high danger. You can find them, for example, in the MeteoSwiss app. If you are going hiking or into the mountains, you should always check the weather forecast beforehand.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the weather and of the Earth's atmosphere.
Water that falls from the sky, for example rain, snow or hail.
A computer program that calculates how the weather will develop.
A warm, dry wind that descends from the mountains into the valley.

gewusst: The foehn is so typical of the Alps that in German the hairdryer (“Föhn”) was named after it.
A weather balloon rises more than 30 kilometres high before it bursts.
Many people use traditional weather sayings, but modern weather models are much more accurate.

teile.einleitung: A weather station is a place with measuring instruments that continuously record the weather. It measures, for example, temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation and sunshine. In Switzerland, automatic stations run by MeteoSwiss deliver new measurements every 10 minutes.
wichtigste: A weather station measures temperature, humidity, air pressure, wind, precipitation and sunshine.
A classic Stevenson screen is white, because white reflects the sunlight.
Its side walls of slanted slats let air through but no sun in.
Weather stations ideally stand on short-cut grass in an open position.
The wind is normally measured at a height of 10 metres.
MeteoSwiss's automatic ground measuring network is called SwissMetNet.
The automatic stations deliver measurements every 10 minutes.
A pyranometer measures solar radiation.

abschnitte.text: In the past, every weather station had white **Stevenson screens** on legs. The white colour reflects the sunlight so that the screen does not heat up. The walls are made of slanted **slats**: air can flow through, but the sun's rays cannot. In this way the thermometer inside measures the real air temperature in the shade, at a height of about two metres.

A weather station should deliver values that are as undisturbed as possible. That is why it ideally stands on **short-cut grass** in an open position, far away from houses, trees and tarmac. The wind is normally measured on a mast at a **height of 10 metres**. Only in this way can the values of different stations be compared well.

A **thermometer** measures the temperature and a hygrometer the humidity. A barometer shows the air pressure, and an anemometer measures the wind speed. The rain gauge collects the precipitation. A **pyranometer** measures how strongly the sun is shining.

In the past, the hours of sunshine were measured with the **sunshine recorder**. A glass ball focuses the sun's rays like a magnifying glass and burns a trace into a strip of paper. The longer the burnt trace, the longer the sun shone. Today electronic sensors do this job.

MeteoSwiss runs an automatic measuring network called **SwissMetNet**. Its stations are in the lowlands, in valleys and on mountain peaks such as the Säntis or the Jungfraujoch. They measure around the clock and send their values to the headquarters every 10 minutes. The network is supplemented by many precipitation stations.

The measurements from weather stations are the basis for **weather forecasts** and severe weather warnings. Long series of measurements show how the climate changes over decades. Airports, road services and agriculture also need precise weather data. Many schools and private individuals also run their own small weather stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A white box with slats that protects measuring instruments from sun and rain; in German “Wetterhütte”.
An instrument that measures humidity.
An instrument that measures the strength of solar radiation.
An instrument with a glass ball that records the hours of sunshine on paper.
MeteoSwiss's automatic weather measuring network.

gewusst: A temperature measured in the full sun can be many degrees too high.
The glass ball of a sunshine recorder can set paper alight like a magnifying glass.
Some Swiss weather stations are at more than 3000 metres above sea level, for example on the Jungfraujoch.

teile.einleitung: The central dogma of molecular biology describes how the genetic information in a cell is used. The information flows from DNA to RNA and from there to proteins, but not back again from the proteins. This basic rule was formulated by the British researcher Francis Crick in 1958.
wichtigste: Francis Crick formulated the central dogma in 1958.
It states that information flows from nucleic acids to proteins but not back.
The transfer from DNA to RNA is called transcription.
The translation of RNA into a protein is called translation.
The enzyme reverse transcriptase rewrites RNA into DNA.
Retroviruses use this rewriting in order to multiply.
According to the RNA world hypothesis, in the early days of life RNA stored information and at the same time sped up reactions.

abschnitte.text: In every cell, the genetic information is held in **DNA**, a long molecule with a kind of alphabetic script. For the cell to make use of this information, it has to make **proteins** from it. Proteins are the workers of the cell: they build muscles, digest food or fight germs. The central dogma describes the path of the information: from DNA via RNA to protein. The British researcher **Francis Crick** set out this rule in 1958, a few years after he and James Watson had discovered the double helix of DNA.

In the first step, a section of the DNA, a gene, is copied out. This produces a molecule of **RNA**, called messenger RNA or mRNA. This process is called **transcription**, which means making a copy in writing. You can compare it to copying out a recipe from a precious cookery book. The original, the DNA, stays safely in the nucleus.

The mRNA travels to the **ribosomes**, the protein factories of the cell. There the information is read; every three letters stand for a particular building block, an **amino acid**. The amino acids are joined together like beads on a necklace, and this produces a protein. This step is called **translation**. The information is translated from the language of nucleic acids into the language of proteins.

Later it was discovered that information can also flow from RNA back to DNA. The enzyme **reverse transcriptase**, found in 1970, rewrites RNA into DNA. **Retroviruses** use it to build their genetic material into the DNA of the infected cell. Many other RNA viruses, such as the flu virus, copy their genetic material directly from RNA to RNA with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. But this does not disprove the core of the dogma: no information flows from a protein back to a nucleic acid.

The central dogma is a cornerstone of modern **biology** and medicine. It explains why a change in the DNA, a mutation, can lead to a changed protein. Modern mRNA vaccines are also based on it: they deliver building instructions from which the cell itself makes a protein. The discovery of **ribozymes**, RNA molecules that speed up reactions, led to the **RNA world hypothesis**. According to it, RNA may have been both store and tool in the early days of life.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in which the genetic information is stored.
A molecule similar to DNA that, among other things, carries information out of the nucleus.
A substance that carries out many tasks in the cell.
A tiny protein factory in the cell.
A virus that rewrites its RNA genetic material into DNA.

gewusst: By his own account, Crick chose the word “dogma” without quite knowing that it really means an unshakeable article of faith.
Howard Temin and David Baltimore received the Nobel Prize in 1975 for discovering reverse transcriptase.
The genetic code is the same in almost all living things, from bacteria to humans.

teile.einleitung: An accumulator, usually just called a rechargeable battery, is a battery that you can charge again and again. It stores electrical energy and gives it out again later. Without rechargeable batteries there would be no mobile phones, tablets or e-bikes.
wichtigste: A rechargeable battery is a store for electrical energy that can be recharged.
Almost every mobile phone has a rechargeable battery built in.
When the battery is flat, you charge it up again with a charger.
The battery symbol on a phone shows how full the battery is.
After many years of use a rechargeable battery does not last as long.
Heat, for example in a car in the sun, damages a rechargeable battery.
Old rechargeable batteries do not belong in the rubbish, but back in the shop at the collection point.

abschnitte.text: A normal battery is finished when its energy has been used up. An **accumulator**, on the other hand, can be recharged hundreds of times. The word comes from Latin and means something like collector or store. In everyday German people often just say “Akku”, and sometimes simply battery.

Inside a rechargeable battery there are two terminals, the **positive terminal** and the **negative terminal**, separated by a conducting liquid or paste. When it discharges, chemical reactions take place that make electrons flow through the connected device. When it charges, the charger pushes current in the opposite direction. This reverses the chemical reactions, and the battery is full again.

Mobile phones, tablets, laptops and wireless headphones almost always have a **lithium-ion battery**. On an e-bike, too, a rechargeable battery gives the motor its energy. Electric cars contain very large batteries with thousands of individual cells. Normal cars with a petrol engine have a **lead-acid battery** that supplies the starter motor with electricity.

In 1859 the French physicist **Gaston Planté** built the first usable lead-acid battery. Later came nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries. In 1991 the company Sony brought the first lithium-ion battery onto the market. Three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019 for developing it.

Rechargeable batteries age over time and after a few years do not last as long. Heat is especially bad for them, so you should never leave a phone in a hot car in the sun. Great cold also weakens a battery for a while. Many experts recommend not letting lithium-ion batteries run completely flat all the time. A damaged or swollen battery can become dangerous and should be handled by experts.

Rechargeable batteries contain substances that harm the environment, so they do not belong in the normal rubbish. In Switzerland you take old rechargeable and ordinary batteries back to the shop, to the **collection point**. Shops that sell batteries must also take them back. When you buy them, you pay a small **advance recycling fee**, which pays for the recycling. Valuable metals are recovered from old batteries.

begriffe.erklaerung: An energy store that can be recharged again and again.
Charging fully once and then discharging again.
The most common type of rechargeable battery today in phones, laptops and electric cars.
Processing old things so that the raw materials can be used again.

gewusst: The first lead-acid battery of 1859 works in principle in the same way as the battery in today’s petrol cars.
An electric car battery can store as much energy as hundreds of phone batteries together.
Many small devices such as toothbrushes or toys also contain a rechargeable battery that should be recycled.

teile.einleitung: The Wildkirchli consists of several caves below the summit of the Ebenalp in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden. Bones of cave bears and stone tools that probably come from Neanderthals were found here. This makes the Wildkirchli one of the oldest sites of Swiss prehistory.
wichtigste: The Wildkirchli caves lie below the Ebenalp in the Alpstein.
They are at about 1500 metres above sea level.
The researcher Emil Bächler dug here between 1904 and 1908.
Especially many bones of cave bears were found.
According to today's interpretation, the old stone tools come from Neanderthals.
The Wildkirchli is one of the oldest sites of Swiss prehistory.
In later centuries, hermits lived in the caves.
Nearby, the well-known mountain inn Aescher clings to the cliff face.

abschnitte.text: The Wildkirchli is in the **Alpstein**, the mountain range around the Säntis, in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden. The caves are in a cliff face below the summit of the **Ebenalp**, at about 1500 metres above sea level. A cable car runs from Wasserauen up to the Ebenalp. From there a footpath leads down through the caves.

Between 1904 and 1908 the St Gallen researcher **Emil Bächler** dug in the Wildkirchli. He found thousands of bones and simple **stone tools**. Bächler realised that people had already been here in the Palaeolithic. At the time this was a sensation, because nobody had expected such old traces in the Alps.

Most of the bones come from the **cave bear**, an extinct relative of the brown bear. Cave bears were bigger than today's brown bears and used caves to spend the winter. Many animals died in the cave during their winter rest. In this way large amounts of bones built up over a long time.

The stone tools in the Wildkirchli are now attributed to the **Neanderthals**. These people lived in Europe in the Palaeolithic, tens of thousands of years ago. They probably used the caves as shelter on hunting trips. That is why the Wildkirchli is so important for the **prehistory** of Switzerland.

Much later, from the 17th century, **hermits** lived in the Wildkirchli. A small **chapel** with an altar was set up in one of the caves. This is also where the name Wildkirchli comes from: it means little church in the wilderness. The last hermit left the caves in the 19th century.

Today the Wildkirchli is a popular destination for outings, with a small museum in the former hermit's hut. Right next to it, the **mountain inn Aescher** clings to the cliff face and has become world-famous through photos. On the walk you can see Lake Seealp far below in the valley. The writer Joseph Victor von Scheffel was inspired here for his novel “Ekkehard”.

begriffe.erklaerung: An extinct large bear that lived in Europe during the Ice Age.
An extinct form of human that lived in Europe in the Palaeolithic.
The period of humanity before there were written records.
A person who lives alone and secluded for religious reasons.

gewusst: Cave bears fed mainly on plants, even though they were bigger than today's brown bears.
The mountain inn Aescher can only be reached on foot and clings directly to the cliff face.
The Wildkirchli was one of the first sites to show that people were already travelling in the Alps in the Palaeolithic.

teile.einleitung: A weather balloon is a large balloon that carries a small measuring device high into the atmosphere. On the way, the device measures temperature, humidity and wind and radios the values back to Earth. In Switzerland, such balloons go up at Payerne in the canton of Vaud.
wichtigste: A weather balloon is filled with a gas that is lighter than air.
A measuring device, the radiosonde, hangs below the balloon.
The sonde measures temperature, humidity and wind.
The measurements are sent to Earth by radio.
High up, the balloon gets bigger and bigger and finally bursts.
A small parachute then slows the sonde down.
A weather balloon goes up at Payerne twice a day.
The balloons from Payerne reach a height of about 30 kilometres.

abschnitte.text: A weather balloon is made of thin, stretchy rubber, usually **latex**. It is filled with **helium** or hydrogen, two gases that are lighter than air. That is why it rises when it is let go, just like a child's balloon. A small measuring device, the **radiosonde**, hangs on a string underneath.

The radiosonde is a light box with sensors and a radio transmitter. During the ascent it constantly measures temperature, **humidity** and air pressure. Its position is determined with a satellite receiver, and from this the wind direction and wind speed are calculated. All the values are sent by **radio** to the ground station.

The higher the balloon rises, the thinner the air around it becomes. That is why the gas in the balloon keeps expanding, and the balloon becomes much bigger than at the start. At a height of about 30 kilometres the skin is stretched so much that it **bursts**. The whole ascent takes about one and a half to two hours.

After the balloon bursts, the sonde falls back to Earth. A small **parachute** slows the fall so that nobody is hurt. Because the wind can carry the balloon a long way, sondes often land many kilometres away. If you find one, you can report it to the weather service.

At **Payerne** in the canton of Vaud, MeteoSwiss runs Switzerland's aerological station. A weather balloon goes up there twice a day, at the same time as at hundreds of other stations around the world. The measurements from Payerne are among the longest series of measurements of this kind. They also help to study climate change in the upper atmosphere.

Weather balloons provide measurements from heights that are otherwise hard to reach. The data goes into the **weather models** with which computers forecast the weather. Wind and temperature at altitude are also important for aviation. Without weather balloons, weather forecasts would be less accurate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small measuring device with a radio transmitter that hangs from a weather balloon.
A gas that is lighter than air and does not burn.
The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
The science of studying the higher layers of the air.

gewusst: When it bursts, a weather balloon can be several metres across.
At a height of 30 kilometres it is often colder than minus 50 degrees Celsius.
All over the world, hundreds of weather balloons are launched at the same times every day.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach is the most important research institute for birds in Switzerland. It is located in the little town of Sempach on Lake Sempach in the canton of Lucerne and has been observing how the birds in our country are doing since 1924.
wichtigste: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach studies birds and works for their protection.
It was founded in 1924.
It is located in Sempach on Lake Sempach in the canton of Lucerne.
Researchers put small rings on birds' legs in order to recognise them again.
Ringing is used to study the journeys of migratory birds.
The barn swallow is a migratory bird that flies to Africa in autumn.
In a visitor centre, families and school classes can learn a lot about birds.
The institute is a non-profit foundation and is supported by many donors.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach, in German “Vogelwarte Sempach”, is a **foundation** devoted entirely to birds. It was founded in 1924 by bird lovers who wanted to study **bird migration** over Switzerland. Today biologists and many other experts work there. They do research, count birds, advise authorities and explain to the public how birds can be protected.

The institute is on the shore of **Lake Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne. The little town of Sempach is also known from history, because the Battle of Sempach took place there in 1386. The lake and the reeds on the shore are a good habitat for water birds. So the researchers have their subjects of study right on their doorstep.

In **ringing**, trained people carefully catch birds with fine nets. Each bird is given a light metal ring with its own number and the address of the institute on its leg. Then it is weighed, measured and released again immediately. If someone later finds the bird in another place, it is known how far it has travelled and how old it was.

Today the institute also uses tiny transmitters and **geolocators** that weigh very little. With them it was possible to show, for example, that Alpine swifts stay in the air for months without landing. With radar devices, researchers watch at night how many migratory birds fly over Switzerland. Volunteers help by counting birds and reporting their observations.

The institute publishes the **breeding bird atlas**, which shows where in Switzerland which bird species breed. It also helps to draw up the **Red List** of endangered bird species. In this way it is known which species are doing badly, for example ground-nesting birds such as the skylark. With this knowledge, protection programmes are planned.

In the visitor centre in Sempach you can learn a lot about birds through exhibitions and games. There is also a **care centre** where injured or weakened wild birds are looked after. When they are healthy again, they are released. Many school classes visit the institute on a trip.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird is given a small ring with a number on its leg so that it can be recognised later.
The yearly journey of many birds to warmer areas in autumn and back in spring.
An organisation that pursues a particular goal with money and work, here the protection of birds.
A list that shows which animal or plant species are endangered.

gewusst: A bird ring weighs so little that the bird hardly notices it.
Some ringed birds are only found again after many years and thousands of kilometres away.
Using transmitters, the institute found out that Alpine swifts can fly for more than 200 days at a stretch.

teile.einleitung: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut of our brain. We estimate how frequent or likely something is according to how easily suitable examples come to mind. This is quick and often works, but sometimes it leads to quite wrong judgements.
wichtigste: With the availability heuristic, you estimate how frequent something is by how easily examples come to mind.
It was described in 1973 by the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman.
Spectacular events such as plane crashes stick in the memory and are therefore overestimated.
Common but inconspicuous dangers such as cardiovascular diseases are often underestimated.
Individual examples from among your friends can distort your view of a statistic.
Asking for base rates and statistics can help you avoid this mistake in thinking.

abschnitte.text: A **heuristic** is a simple rule of thumb with which the brain quickly comes to a judgement. Instead of laboriously checking all the facts, it takes a shortcut. With the **availability heuristic**, the shortcut is: whatever comes to my mind quickly must be common. Often this is even true, because things we experience often are usually really common.

The psychologists **Amos Tversky** and **Daniel Kahneman** published their work on this in 1973. In one experiment they asked whether in English there are more words that begin with K or more words with K in third position. Many guessed K at the beginning, because such words come to mind more easily. In fact, though, there are more words with K in third position. Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, partly for this research.

Plane crashes are very rare, but they get a lot of attention in the **media**. That is why many people overestimate the risk of flying. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, many people in the USA avoided planes and drove by car instead. Studies show that there were more deaths on the **roads** afterwards, because driving is much more dangerous than flying per kilometre.

Someone knows two smokers who lived to be over 90 and therefore thinks smoking is harmless. That is a typical example of the availability heuristic. The two known cases are very present in their mind, but the many sick people in the **statistics** are not. The other way round, many people underestimate common causes of death such as cardiovascular diseases, because they are not spectacular and rarely make the headlines.

In 1991 the psychologist Norbert Schwarz showed something surprising. Participants were asked to name either 6 or 12 examples of their own self-confident behaviour. Those who had to name 12 examples afterwards rated themselves as less self-confident. The reason: finding twelve examples is hard work, and this feeling of **effort** counts more for the judgement than the number.

The best counter-strategy is to ask for **base rates** and statistics. You can ask yourself whether an example is just striking or really typical. It also helps to look deliberately for counter-examples. When reading the news, you should remember that the media report mainly on what is unusual.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule of thumb with which you decide quickly, but not always correctly.
A typical error that almost everyone makes when reasoning.
How often something really happens, according to statistics.
When we judge something differently from how it actually is.

gewusst: Many people fear sharks, yet only very few people in the world die from shark attacks each year.
Daniel Kahneman was a psychologist and still received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.
Even a single film about a disaster can increase our fear of it for a while.

teile.einleitung: A prejudice is an opinion about people or things that you form before you really know them. It often concerns whole groups, for example because of their origin, language, religion or appearance. Psychology studies how prejudices arise and how they can be reduced.
wichtigste: A prejudice is a judgement you make without knowing the person or thing properly.
A simplified, generalised idea about a whole group is called a stereotype.
In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport published the influential book “The Nature of Prejudice”.
People tend to favour their own group; this is called in-group favouritism.
Confirmation bias leads people to notice mainly information that confirms their own opinion.
Positive contact on an equal footing can reduce prejudices.
Shared goals can reduce hostility between groups.

abschnitte.text: The word says it already: you judge “before”, that is, before you know the facts. A **prejudice** is usually an evaluation, often a negative one, that refers to a whole group. A **stereotype** is the picture in your head, for example “everyone from this group is like that”. When people are treated worse because of a prejudice, it is called **discrimination**.

Our brain likes to sort the world into boxes so that we can decide quickly. This is often practical, but it can lead to false generalisations. We also pick up prejudices from family, friends or the media. Through **confirmation bias**, we then mainly notice examples that confirm our picture, while we overlook counter-examples.

In 1954 the American psychologist **Gordon Allport** described in his book “The Nature of Prejudice” how prejudices work. He also came up with the **contact hypothesis**. It says that prejudices can become smaller when groups meet on an equal footing and work together. Many later studies have confirmed this idea.

In 1954 the researcher **Muzafer Sherif** studied two groups of boys at a summer camp in the USA. Competitions quickly created hostility between the groups. Only shared goals that could be reached only together reduced the conflict. In 1968 the teacher **Jane Elliott** divided her class by eye colour so that the children could experience for themselves how unfair it is to be disadvantaged because of a feature.

When you get to know people personally, you quickly notice that every person is different. It helps to question your own opinion and to look for counter-examples. In Switzerland, a law, the so-called **anti-racism criminal provision**, has prohibited public incitement against people because of their origin or religion since 1995. At school, it helps not to look away when someone is excluded and to support those affected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified picture in your head about a whole group of people.
When someone is treated unfairly because of a feature.
The tendency to notice mainly what confirms your own opinion.
The tendency to think your own group is better than other groups.
The idea that positive contact between groups reduces prejudices.

gewusst: Even being divided randomly into two groups can lead people to favour their own group.
Prejudices can also sound positive, for example “everyone from this group is good at maths”, and still be unfair.
Jane Elliott later also carried out her eye-colour exercise with adults.

teile.einleitung: A weather radar is a measuring device that detects rain, snow and hail from a great distance. It sends out invisible microwaves and catches their echo again. This is how the coloured precipitation maps that you know from weather apps are made.
wichtigste: A weather radar sends out microwave pulses and measures the echo from the drops.
From the travel time of the echo, the distance of the precipitation is calculated.
If an echo returns after 0.4 milliseconds, the precipitation is 60 kilometres away.
A Doppler radar also measures how fast the particles are moving towards or away from the radar.
Radars with dual polarisation can tell rain, snow and hail apart better.
Radar reflectivity is given in dBZ.
Large drops dominate the echo, because reflectivity grows with the sixth power of the diameter.
Swiss weather radars stand on high peaks so that mountains block the beam as little as possible.

abschnitte.text: The word **radar** stands for a technique with which objects are located using radio waves. A rotating antenna sends out short **microwave pulses**, which travel at the speed of light. When they hit raindrops, snowflakes or hailstones, a small part is reflected back. From the time until the echo arrives, the distance is calculated: in 0.4 milliseconds the pulse travels 120 kilometres, that is, 60 kilometres there and 60 back.

How strong the echo is, is described by the **reflectivity**, which is given in the unit **dBZ**. High values mean heavy rain or hail, low values light precipitation. Reflectivity grows with the sixth power of the drop diameter. So a drop twice as large gives an echo 64 times stronger.

A **Doppler radar** uses the Doppler effect, similar to how the siren of a passing ambulance sounds different. In this way it measures whether precipitation is moving towards or away from the radar and how fast. This makes it possible to detect winds and swirls in thunderstorms. Radars with **dual polarisation** send out waves vibrating horizontally and vertically and can therefore estimate the shape of the particles and tell rain, snow and hail apart better.

MeteoSwiss runs five weather radars: on **La Dôle** in the Jura, on the **Albis** near Zurich, on **Monte Lema** in Ticino, on the Pointe de la Plaine Morte in Valais and on the Weissfluhgipfel in the Grisons. They stand high up, because otherwise the mountains would block the radar beam. Together they monitor the whole country and the neighbouring areas. Every few minutes a new precipitation image is produced.

Radar images are especially important for **nowcasting**, that is, forecasts for the next few minutes to a few hours. Computers calculate where an area of rain or a thunderstorm is moving. In this way warnings of hail or heavy rain can be sent out in time. Farmers, organisers of open-air festivals and the fire brigade, for example, benefit from this.

A radar does not see everything. Because the Earth is curved, at great distances the beam runs high above the ground and misses low clouds. Mountains, buildings and even flocks of birds can create **clutter**. That is why radar data is always compared with measurements from ground stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A technique that detects objects with radio waves and their echo.
A measure of how strongly precipitation reflects the radar signal.
The change in a wave when the source or the target is moving.
A weather forecast for the next few minutes to a few hours.
A radar signal that does not come from precipitation, for example from a mountain.

gewusst: A raindrop twice as large produces a radar echo 64 times stronger.
Weather radars sometimes also see large flocks of migrating birds or swarms of insects.
Radar technology was originally developed for locating aircraft and ships.

teile.einleitung: The anti-lock braking system, ABS for short, is a technology in cars and motorbikes that stops the wheels from locking during an emergency stop. This keeps the vehicle steerable, so you can still swerve round an obstacle. Today ABS is fitted in almost all new cars.
wichtigste: ABS stops the wheels from locking during an emergency stop.
Rolling wheels can still be steered; locked wheels only skid straight ahead.
Sensors constantly measure the speed of each wheel.
When the ABS is working, you often feel a juddering or pulsing in the brake pedal.
Electronic ABS first came onto the market in production cars in the 1970s.
The anti-skid system ESP uses the sensors of the ABS.
On loose gravel or fresh snow the braking distance can be longer with ABS than without.

abschnitte.text: If you brake very hard without ABS, the wheels can stop turning. They **lock** and skid over the road. A skidding wheel can no longer be steered, and the car simply carries on straight ahead. The **anti-lock braking system** prevents this by briefly reducing the braking force at the right moment.

At each wheel a **wheel speed sensor** measures how fast it is turning. A control unit compares the values many times a second. If it notices that a wheel is suddenly slowing down sharply and about to lock, it briefly lowers the brake pressure at that wheel. As soon as the wheel is rolling again, the pressure is increased again. You feel this rapid releasing and braking as a juddering or **pulsing** in the brake pedal.

**Friction** acts between the tyre and the road. As long as the wheel is rolling, static friction acts, which is stronger and makes steering possible. If the wheel skids, only the weaker **sliding friction** acts. That is why a rolling wheel usually brakes better on a dry road and can still be steered at the same time. On loose gravel or fresh snow, however, a locked wheel pushes a braking wedge of material in front of it, so there the braking distance can be longer with ABS.

The first anti-lock systems already existed earlier in aeroplanes and trains. Electronic ABS for cars went into series production in the 1970s, in 1978 in the Mercedes-Benz S-Class with technology from Bosch. In the following decades ABS became cheaper and more widespread. Today it is standard on new cars in Europe.

On a motorbike ABS is especially helpful, because a locked front wheel easily leads to a fall. Further assistance systems build on ABS. **ESP**, the electronic stability programme, uses the ABS sensors and prevents skidding in bends. To do so it brakes individual wheels in a targeted way. Even so, no system replaces a sensible speed and enough distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a wheel stops turning while braking and skids over the road.
The friction as long as two surfaces are not sliding against each other.
The weaker friction when two surfaces slide along each other.
A driver assistance system that stops a car from skidding.

gewusst: With ABS you can press the brake fully in an emergency stop and steer at the same time.
ABS adjusts the brake pressure many times a second.
Modern bikes and e-bikes are now also available with ABS.

teile.einleitung: The ten per cent myth is the widespread claim that we humans use only 10 per cent of our brain. That sounds exciting but is wrong. Brain research shows that practically all areas of the brain are used.
wichtigste: The myth claims that we use only 10 per cent of our brain.
Brain research shows that practically all areas of the brain are used.
With functional magnetic resonance imaging you can see which areas are active at the moment.
The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight but uses about 20 per cent of the energy.
Even small brain injuries can have serious consequences.
The origin of the claim is unclear; there is no study behind it.
The myth persists because it promises hidden abilities.

abschnitte.text: The myth says that 90 per cent of our **brain** lies dormant and unused. Anyone who wakes up this reserve could supposedly become much cleverer or develop special powers. The idea turns up in advertising, self-help books and films, for example in the 2014 film “Lucy”. But it is a **myth**, that is, a false idea that many people believe is true. Brain experts clearly reject it.

With **functional magnetic resonance imaging**, fMRI for short, you can make visible which areas of the brain are working at the moment. Such images show that practically all areas become active over the course of a day. Not all of them work at the same time, because different areas are responsible for seeing, speaking, moving or remembering. If all **nerve cells** fired at maximum at once, it would cause a seizure. By the way, the brain is also very active during sleep.

An adult's brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, which is only about 2 per cent of body weight. Even so, it uses about 20 per cent of the body's **energy**. From the point of view of **evolution**, it would make no sense at all to carry around such an expensive organ that is 90 per cent unused. In addition, nerve connections that are never used tend to be broken down over time. So the brain works on the principle: what you use, you keep.

Doctors observe that even small **brain injuries** can have serious consequences. A stroke in a small area can, for example, disturb speech or the movement of one side of the body. If 90 per cent of the brain were unused, most injuries would have no effect. But that is not the case. However, after an injury the brain can relearn some tasks; this is called **plasticity**.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the myth come from?
abschnitte.text: Where the ten per cent claim comes from is **unclear**; there is no scientific study behind it. Perhaps statements by researchers around 1900 were misunderstood when they said that people could make even better use of their abilities. Early brain researchers, who did not yet know the tasks of many areas of the brain, may also have contributed. The myth is popular because it promises **hidden abilities**. The only true part is this: by practising and learning, you really can train your brain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A widespread idea that is not true.
A cell in the brain and nerves that passes on signals.
A scanner that shows which parts of the brain are working at the moment.
The brain's ability to change and learn new things.

gewusst: There are about 86 billion nerve cells in the human brain.
Even while you read this sentence, many areas of your brain are working together at the same time.
In surveys, a large proportion of people still believe in the ten per cent myth.

teile.einleitung: A weather map shows at a glance how the weather is distributed over a large area. With lines, letters and symbols it shows high and low-pressure areas, fronts and winds. If you can read the symbols, you understand much better what the weather will bring in the next few days.
wichtigste: Lines of equal air pressure are called isobars.
If the isobars lie close together, a strong wind blows.
In the German-speaking world, a large T stands for a low-pressure area and an H for a high.
A cold front is drawn as a blue line with triangles.
A warm front is shown as a red line with semicircles.
When a cold front catches up with a warm front, an occlusion forms.
A narrow extension of a high is called a ridge of high pressure.
A cold front often brings showers, thunderstorms and a sudden drop in temperature.

abschnitte.text: A weather map is a map on which the weather at a particular time is drawn. There are **surface weather maps**, which show the air pressure at ground level, and upper-air maps for the higher layers of air. On television and in apps you often see simplified maps with suns, clouds and temperatures. Meteorologists work with more detailed maps full of symbols and numbers.

The curved lines on the map are called **isobars**. They connect places with the same air pressure, which is given in **hectopascals**. The closer together the isobars are, the stronger the wind blows. If they are far apart, it is rather calm.

An **H** marks a high-pressure area, in which the air sinks. Highs usually bring dry and often sunny weather. A **T** (for the German “Tief”) stands for a low-pressure area, in which the air rises and forms clouds. That is why lows often bring rain, wind and changeable weather.

A **front** is the boundary between warm and cold air. A cold front is drawn as a blue line with triangles, a **warm front** as a red line with semicircles. The symbols always point in the direction in which the front is moving. When the faster cold front catches up with the warm front, an **occlusion** forms, which is shown in purple.

Ahead of a warm front, high veil-like clouds often appear first, followed by longer-lasting rain. A cold front usually comes quickly and brings **showers**, thunderstorms, strong wind and a noticeable drop in temperature. After that it often clears up again. In Switzerland, fronts often bank up against the Alps, which can bring a lot of precipitation on the north side.

The first weather maps appeared in the 19th century, when weather data could be collected quickly thanks to the telegraph. Today weather maps are produced by computers from millions of measurements. In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** publishes up-to-date maps every day. You can also look at weather maps with rain, wind and temperature on your mobile phone at any time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line on the weather map that connects places with the same air pressure.
The unit in which air pressure is given.
The boundary where warm and cold air masses meet.
A front that forms when a cold front catches up with a warm front.
A narrow extension of a high-pressure area.

gewusst: In the English-speaking world, weather maps show an L for “low” instead of a T for “Tief”.
Without the telegraph, it would not have been possible in the past to draw up-to-date weather maps.
In the northern hemisphere, the wind turns anticlockwise around a low.

teile.einleitung: Viruses are tiny pathogens that are much smaller than bacteria. They cannot multiply by themselves but need the cells of humans, animals, plants or even bacteria to do so. Viruses cause, for example, flu, colds, measles and chickenpox.
wichtigste: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and only visible with an electron microscope.
A virus consists essentially of genetic material in a protein coat.
Viruses can only multiply in other cells and are therefore usually not counted as living things.
The Latin word “virus” means poison.
Viruses infect humans, animals, plants and even bacteria.
Antibiotics do not help against viruses, but vaccinations protect against many viral diseases.
Cold viruses often spread through droplets when people cough and sneeze.

abschnitte.text: A **virus** is a tiny particle of genetic material surrounded by a coat of protein. Some viruses also have a fatty envelope. Most viruses are between 20 and 300 nanometres in size, that is, a thousand times smaller than the thickness of a hair. That is why they cannot be seen with a normal light microscope, only with an **electron microscope**. A virus has no metabolism of its own; it does not eat and does not grow.

A virus docks onto a suitable **host cell** and smuggles its genetic material inside. Then it gets the cell to make many new viruses, as if it were a factory. The new viruses leave the cell and infect more cells. In the process, the cell is often damaged or destroyed, and you become ill. Because viruses cannot do any of this on their own, they are usually not counted as living things.

Many well-known diseases are caused by viruses, for example **flu**, colds, measles, mumps, chickenpox and Covid-19. The chickenpox virus stays in the body after the illness and can cause **shingles** years later. Plants can also become ill, for example through the tobacco mosaic virus, which causes spots on leaves. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect only bacteria. Not all viruses make you ill; many are harmless to humans.

**Antibiotics** do not work against viruses, because they only fight bacteria. So an antibiotic does not help against flu. A **vaccination**, on the other hand, gives good protection: the immune system gets to know the pathogen without you becoming really ill. For some viruses there are also special medicines that slow down their multiplication. Usually, though, your own immune system defeats the viruses by itself after a few days.

Many viruses spread through tiny **droplets** when people cough, sneeze and talk. That is why you should sneeze into the crook of your arm rather than into your hand. Washing your hands regularly with soap removes viruses from the skin. If you are ill, it is better to stay at home so that others do not catch it. Airing rooms well also helps, because fewer viruses stay in the air.

At the end of the 19th century, researchers noticed that the mosaic disease of tobacco was transmitted by a pathogen that slipped through the finest filters. In this way the first virus was discovered, the **tobacco mosaic virus**. Only with the electron microscope, which was developed in the 1930s, could viruses really be seen. As early as 1796 the doctor Edward Jenner had developed a first vaccination against smallpox. Thanks to worldwide vaccination, the World Health Organization declared **smallpox** eradicated in 1980.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny cause of disease, for example a virus or a bacterium.
A cell that a virus infects and in which it multiplies.
The body's own defence against pathogens.
A preventive measure in which the immune system learns to recognise a pathogen.
One millionth of a millimetre.

gewusst: There are also giant viruses that are bigger than some bacteria and can even be seen under a light microscope.
One litre of seawater often contains billions of viruses, which mainly infect bacteria.
Parts of our own genetic material come from viruses that infected our ancestors a very long time ago.

teile.einleitung: In the volcano experiment you make a foaming “lava” bubble out of a small mountain. All you need is bicarbonate of soda and vinegar from the kitchen. The experiment shows in a simple way a chemical reaction in which a gas is produced.
wichtigste: For the kitchen volcano you mix bicarbonate of soda and vinegar.
This produces lots of gas bubbles of carbon dioxide.
Food colouring turns the foam lava red.
A squirt of washing-up liquid makes more foam.
The foam lava is not hot; it actually becomes slightly cool.
Instead of vinegar you can also use lemon juice.
When the bicarbonate of soda is used up, the foaming stops.

abschnitte.text: The **volcano experiment** is a popular experiment for school and at home. You build a small mountain of modelling clay, papier mâché or sand around a glass or a bottle. When you mix the right ingredients, colourful foam comes bubbling out of the top. It looks like a volcanic eruption but has nothing to do with real lava.

You need **bicarbonate of soda**, vinegar, a squirt of washing-up liquid and some red food colouring. Bicarbonate of soda is sold in small packets in the supermarket, often next to the baking powder. First put two spoonfuls of bicarbonate of soda, the washing-up liquid and the colouring into the glass. Then pour in the vinegar and step back. It is best to set everything up on a tray, because the foam overflows.

The chemical name of bicarbonate of soda is **sodium hydrogen carbonate**. Vinegar contains acetic acid, and acids react with bicarbonate of soda. This produces the gas **carbon dioxide**, the same gas that fizzes in sparkling water. The washing-up liquid holds the gas bubbles in place, which turns them into thick foam. Lemon juice also works, because it contains citric acid.

The foam lava is not hot; on the contrary, it becomes slightly cool. This is because the reaction takes heat from its surroundings; it is called **endothermic**. When all the bicarbonate of soda has been used up, it stops foaming. Then you have to add more bicarbonate of soda for the volcano to erupt again.

In real volcanoes, glowing hot **magma** rises from the Earth's interior. It is more than 1000 degrees hot and also contains gases, which push upwards during an eruption. So the kitchen volcano shows well how gas can build up pressure. There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland today; the Hegau volcanoes just across the border near Schaffhausen have long been extinct.

The experiment is harmless, but vinegar should still not get into your eyes. Safety goggles are therefore a good idea. You can try out how the amount of bicarbonate of soda or vinegar changes the eruption. It is best to record the result in a small **lab report**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A white powder from the kitchen, chemically sodium hydrogen carbonate.
An invisible gas that is also found in fizzy water.
A substance such as vinegar or lemon juice that tastes sour and reacts with bicarbonate of soda.
Describing a reaction that takes heat from its surroundings.

gewusst: Baking powder also contains bicarbonate of soda, which is why a cake rises in the oven.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and can therefore put out a burning candle in a glass.
With a bottle and many more ingredients, the foam can shoot more than a metre high.

teile.einleitung: Water is a transparent liquid without which no living thing on Earth could exist. Its chemical formula is H₂O, so it consists of hydrogen and oxygen. Water exists as ice, as a liquid and as vapour.
wichtigste: The chemical formula for water is H₂O.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at sea level at 100 degrees Celsius.
About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water.
Only a small part of the water on Earth is fresh water.
The human body consists of about 60 per cent water.
Because of its many springs and lakes, Switzerland is called the water tower of Europe.

abschnitte.text: Water is a **chemical compound** of hydrogen and oxygen. A tiny particle, a **molecule**, consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, hence the formula H₂O. Pure water has no colour, no smell and no taste. In large amounts, for example in the sea, it shimmers slightly bluish.

Below 0 degrees Celsius, water becomes solid **ice**. Between 0 and 100 degrees it is liquid, and above that it becomes gaseous water vapour. The special thing is that ice is lighter than liquid water and therefore floats on top. Water is densest at 4 degrees, which is why lakes freeze from the top and fish survive at the bottom.

About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water, which is why the Earth is also called the blue planet. However, about 97 per cent of it is salty seawater. A large part of the **fresh water** is frozen in the ice of the poles and glaciers. Only a tiny part is directly available to us in rivers, lakes and groundwater.

All living things need water, because the processes in their cells take place in it. The body of an adult consists of about 60 per cent water. Water carries nutrients in the blood and cools us down through sweating. Without drinking, a person survives only a few days, which is why children should drink about one to one and a half litres a day.

Switzerland is regarded as the **water tower of Europe**, because many large rivers rise here. The Rhine flows into the North Sea, the Rhône into the Mediterranean, the Inn via the Danube into the Black Sea and the Ticino via the Po into the Adriatic. About six per cent of Europe's fresh water reserves are in Switzerland. The tap water here is so clean that you can drink it without worry almost everywhere.

abschnitte.titel: Water as a power and a helper
abschnitte.text: Water is an excellent **solvent**, in which salt, sugar and many other substances dissolve. In Switzerland, about 60 per cent of the electricity produced in the country comes from **hydropower**. Large reservoirs such as the Lac des Dix in Valais store water for this. The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen also show the power of water impressively.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle made of several atoms joined together.
Water with very little salt, as in rivers, lakes and groundwater.
A substance in which other substances dissolve.
Using flowing or falling water to generate electricity.

gewusst: Under certain conditions, hot water can freeze faster than cold water; this is called the Mpemba effect.
On average, a drop of water spends only about nine days in the air before it falls as rain again.
Because ice is lighter than water, icebergs float, with the largest part under water.

teile.einleitung: The launch angle is the angle relative to the ground at which a ball, a javelin or a shot is thrown. Together with the speed, it decides how high and how far something flies. If you know the right angle, you can throw and jump further in sport.
wichtigste: The launch angle is measured between the direction of flight at release and the horizontal ground.
Without air resistance a ball flies furthest if you throw it at 45 degrees.
Two angles that add up to 90 degrees, for example 30 and 60 degrees, give the same distance without air resistance.
Twice the launch speed gives four times the distance.
At 90 degrees the ball flies straight up and lands back where it was thrown from.
Good long jumpers take off at only about 20 degrees.
Shot putters push the shot a little flatter than 45 degrees, because it leaves the hand above the ground.

abschnitte.text: If you throw an object upwards at a slant, it follows a curved path. This path is called a **trajectory parabola**, because it has the shape of a parabola. The **launch angle** is the angle between the starting direction and the horizontal ground. At 0 degrees you throw flat, at 90 degrees straight up.

In a slanted throw the motion can be split into two parts. Horizontally the ball keeps flying steadily, while vertically **gravity** slows it down and pulls it back down. Without air resistance the distance is: v squared times sin(2α) divided by g. So at 10 m/s and 45 degrees, with g equal to 10 m/s², a ball flies 10 metres. Because the speed appears squared, throwing twice as fast gives four times the distance.

A flat throw moves forward quickly but lands early. A steep throw stays in the air for a long time but hardly moves forward. At **45 degrees** the best balance between flight time and forward speed is reached. Angles that are the same distance from 45 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same distance, but the steeper throw flies higher.

In real sport the best angle often looks different. Long jumpers take off at about **20 degrees**, because otherwise they would lose too much run-up speed. In the **shot put** the best angle is a little under 45 degrees, because the shot is released at a height of about two metres. The Swiss athlete Werner Günthör became world champion in the shot put in 1987, 1991 and 1993. In the javelin and discus, too, professionals throw much flatter than 45 degrees.

In reality the air slows down every thrown object. As a result the end of the trajectory becomes steeper and the distance shorter. With light balls such as a shuttlecock this **air resistance** is especially strong. That is why the best angle with air is usually less than 45 degrees.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved flight path of an object thrown at a slant.
How fast an object is moving at the moment it is let go.
How strongly the Earth pulls things down, about 9.81 m/s², often rounded to 10.
The braking force of the air on everything that moves.

gewusst: Back in the 17th century Galileo Galilei found out that thrown objects fly along a parabola.
On the Moon a ball thrown the same way would fly about six times as far as on Earth.
Without air, a ball thrown at 30 degrees flies as far as one thrown at 60 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Twin research studies twins in order to find out what shapes us as humans. It asks: how much of our characteristics comes from our genes and how much from our environment? Because twins grow up at the same time, they are ideal pairs for comparison.
wichtigste: Identical twins have practically the same genetic material.
Non-identical twins share on average about half of their genetic material, like other siblings.
Researchers compare both kinds of twins to tell apart the influence of genes and environment.
Francis Galton in the 19th century is regarded as the founder of twin research.
Identical twins who grew up apart are especially revealing.
The share of differences that comes from genes is called heritability.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

abschnitte.text: **Twin research** is a branch of science that compares pairs of twins with each other. For example, it measures height, health, talents or personality traits. Then it looks at how similar the two are. From this you can estimate what role **genes** and what role the **environment** play. Environment means everything a person experiences: family, school, friends, food and much more.

**Identical twins** have practically the same genetic material and therefore usually look very alike. Their blood group is practically always the same. **Non-identical twins**, on the other hand, share on average only about half of their genetic material, just like other siblings. They can also be a boy and a girl. Even so, both kinds of twins grow up at the same time in the same family.

If a characteristic is much more similar in identical twins than in non-identical ones, that points to a strong influence of genes. If both kinds are about equally similar, the environment plays a bigger role. From such comparisons researchers calculate **heritability**. It shows what share of the differences between people in a group comes from genes. Heritability, however, says nothing about how strongly an individual person is determined by their genes.

The Englishman **Francis Galton** is regarded as the founder of twin research. He was a cousin of Charles Darwin and was already studying pairs of twins in the 1870s. From 1979 the famous **Minnesota Twin Study** took place in the USA. It examined identical twins who had grown up apart in different families. They have the same genes but a different environment, and are therefore especially valuable for research.

A well-known recent study was carried out by NASA with the identical twins Scott and Mark Kelly. Both were astronauts. Scott spent almost a year on the International Space Station, while Mark stayed on Earth. Afterwards experts compared their bodies closely to see how a long stay in space changes a human being. Most of the changes went back to normal after his return.

Twin research shows that almost all characteristics are influenced both by genes and by the environment. For height or eye colour, genes play a big role. For likes, hobbies or the language you speak, the environment is decisive. That is why even identical twins are never completely the same. Every person stays unique, even if there seem to be two of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The building instructions for the body that are found in every cell.
A section of the genetic material that helps determine a particular characteristic.
