Everything a person experiences and everything that affects them from outside.
How much of the differences in a characteristic within a group comes from genes.
A scientific investigation with many participants.

gewusst: Identical twins do not have the same fingerprints, because these depend on small chance events before birth.
In the Minnesota study some twins who had grown up apart met for the first time as adults.
Francis Galton made the English pair of words “nature and nurture” well known, meaning inborn qualities and environment.

teile.einleitung: A virus is a tiny pathogen that is much smaller than a bacterium. Unlike bacteria, a virus can only multiply in other cells. Viruses cause diseases such as flu, colds, measles or Covid-19.
wichtigste: A virus is much smaller than a bacterium.
Viruses can only multiply in other cells.
They consist of genetic material and a protective protein coat.
Viruses have no metabolism of their own.
Antibiotics do not help against viruses.
Vaccinations protect against many viral diseases.
Viruses are found in humans, animals, plants and even bacteria.

abschnitte.text: The word **virus** comes from Latin and means poison or slime. Viruses are so small that they can only be seen with an **electron microscope**. Most are between 20 and 300 nanometres in size, that is, many thousands of times thinner than a hair. A bacterium is often about ten to a hundred times bigger.

A virus consists essentially of genetic material, that is, DNA or RNA, and a coat of proteins, the **capsid**. Some viruses also have a fatty envelope. Viruses have no organs of their own, no metabolism and cannot grow by themselves. That is why experts argue about whether viruses count as living things at all.

A virus docks onto a suitable cell and smuggles its genetic material inside. The infected **host cell** is reprogrammed and now builds many new viruses. These leave the cell, which often dies in the process, and infect more cells. A bacterium, on the other hand, is a cell in its own right and can multiply by itself by dividing.

Viruses cause, for example, colds, flu, measles, chickenpox and mumps. From 2020 the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 caused the worldwide Covid-19 **pandemic**. Viruses are transmitted in different ways, for example through droplets when coughing, through touch or through insect bites. Washing your hands and sneezing into your elbow help to avoid infections.

**Antibiotics** only work against bacteria; they do not help against viruses. The immune system fights viruses with defence cells and antibodies. A **vaccination** trains the body to recognise a pathogen quickly. In 1796 the Englishman Edward Jenner developed the first vaccination against smallpox, and in 1980 smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide.

At the end of the 19th century, researchers studied a disease of tobacco plants. In 1892 the Russian Dmitri Ivanovsky found that the pathogen passed even through the finest filters that held back bacteria. In 1898 the Dutchman Martinus Beijerinck called the invisible pathogen a virus. The **tobacco mosaic virus** was therefore the first virus to be discovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A foreign cell in which a virus multiplies.
The protein coat that protects the genetic material of a virus.
A protection that prepares the immune system for a pathogen.
A disease that spreads across many countries and continents.
A virus that infects bacteria.

gewusst: There are viruses that attack only bacteria; they are called bacteriophages.
Part of our own genetic material originally comes from viruses that settled in millions of years ago.
Computer viruses are called that because, like real viruses, they multiply in other programs.

teile.einleitung: A lab report is a precise account of an experiment. It says what you wanted to find out, what you did and observed and what the result means. In this way others can follow the experiment and repeat it.
wichtigste: A lab report is mainly there so that others can follow the experiment.
Right at the beginning comes the question.
All the equipment and substances belong under “Materials”.
Under “Observations” you write only what you see and measure.
In the analysis, the results are interpreted and explained.
You note measurements immediately and always with the unit.

abschnitte.text: A **lab report** records everything that happens in an experiment. With it, others can follow, repeat and check the experiment. This is a basic principle of science: results should be **verifiable**. You yourself can also read later exactly what you did.

Right at the beginning comes the **question**, for example: “Does sugar dissolve faster in warm water than in cold?” This is often followed by a **prediction**, also called a hypothesis. In it you write what result you expect. Only the experiment shows whether the prediction is right.

In the **Materials** section you list all the equipment and substances, such as a beaker, a thermometer, a spoon and sugar. Then you describe the **method** step by step. A simple sketch of the set-up often helps more than many words. The description must be so precise that someone else can do the experiment in exactly the same way.

Under **Observations** you write only what you see, hear, smell or measure, without explaining it yet. It is best to note measurements immediately during the experiment, so that you do not remember them wrongly. Many measurements are shown most clearly in a **table**. With a number like “12” the unit must not be missing, because 12 seconds is something quite different from 12 degrees.

In the **analysis**, the results are interpreted and explained. You compare them with the prediction from the beginning. A chart often helps here. Sources of error also belong here, for example inaccurate reading or fluctuating temperature.

Researchers record their experiments in a **lab notebook**. Everything is entered with the date, including experiments that did not work. Today there are often electronic lab notebooks on the computer for this. Careful records are important to show that results were obtained honestly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reasoned prediction that you test with an experiment.
The precise description of what you do step by step in the experiment.
The part in which you explain and interpret the results.
A notebook or file in which researchers record all their experiments.

gewusst: Famous researchers such as Marie Curie kept laboratory notebooks that can still be seen in archives today.
Even a failed experiment belongs in the report, because you can learn a lot from it.

teile.einleitung: Adaptive optics is a technique that lets large telescopes take sharp pictures even though the air keeps blurring the starlight. A deformable mirror makes up for these disturbances hundreds of times a second. In this way telescopes on the ground see almost as sharply as in space.
wichtigste: Adaptive optics makes up for the turbulence of the Earth’s atmosphere.
A deformable mirror constantly changes its shape to correct the light wave.
A wavefront sensor, often a Shack-Hartmann sensor, measures the distortion of the light.
The correction is adjusted hundreds to over a thousand times a second.
For an artificial guide star, a laser makes sodium atoms glow at a height of around 90 km.
Horace Babcock was the first to propose the principle, in 1953.
In eye medicine adaptive optics makes individual cells of the retina visible.

abschnitte.text: Stars twinkle because their light has to pass through the Earth’s restless air. Warm and cold layers of air are constantly mixing and bend the light slightly. For a telescope this means blurred, trembling images. Astronomers call the sharpness limited by air turbulence **seeing**. That is why even a huge telescope sees hardly more sharply than a small one without help.

First a **wavefront sensor** measures how strongly the light is distorted. A commonly used type is the **Shack-Hartmann sensor**, which works with an array of small lenses. From this a computer calculates the necessary correction at lightning speed. Then tiny actuators bend a thin, **deformable mirror** so that it exactly cancels out the distortion. This loop runs hundreds to over a thousand times a second.

To measure the distortion, you need a bright star close to the object being observed. Often there is no suitable one. That is why many observatories shoot a **laser** into the sky. It makes sodium atoms glow at a height of around 90 kilometres, creating an artificial **guide star**. At night you can see the yellowish laser beam as a fine line above the telescope.

The American astronomer **Horace Babcock** was the first to propose the principle, in 1953. At that time, however, technology was not advanced enough to manage the fast corrections. Only from the 1990s did observatories use adaptive optics regularly. Today it is used, for example, by the large telescopes of the European Southern Observatory, ESO, in Chile, of which Switzerland is also a member.

The human eye also distorts light slightly. With adaptive optics eye doctors can therefore make individual cells of the **retina** visible, for example the light-sensing cells. This helps to detect and research eye diseases early. The technique is also used in microscopes and for laser links through the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The blurring of telescope images caused by restless air.
The shape in which a light wave spreads out, ideally completely flat.
A bright star or laser spot used to measure the distortion.
A thin mirror whose surface can be bent in a controlled way.

gewusst: With adaptive optics, telescopes on the ground can sometimes take sharper pictures than the Hubble Space Telescope.
The laser for the artificial guide star shines in the same yellow colour as old sodium street lamps.
The deformable mirror of a large telescope can be moved by more than a thousand small actuators.

teile.einleitung: Aquaplaning is when a car on a wet road suddenly floats on a film of water. The tyres then no longer have proper contact with the road. Steering and braking hardly work any more, and the car starts to slide about.
wichtigste: In aquaplaning the tyre floats up on a film of water.
It happens when the tyre tread cannot push the water away quickly enough.
The danger increases at higher speed.
Tyres with worn tread increase the risk.
A particularly large amount of water collects in ruts.
A warning sign is that the steering suddenly feels very light.
If the car starts aquaplaning, you should take your foot off the accelerator and keep the steering wheel straight.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “aqua” for water and the English “planing” for gliding. In heavy rain a layer of water forms on the road. If a car is going too fast, the water pushes itself like a wedge under the tyre. The tyre lifts off and **floats** on the film of water. There is then hardly any **friction** between the tyre and the road.

The **tyre tread** consists of grooves and channels. They lead the water away to the side and backwards so that the tyre keeps contact with the road. A new tyre can push away several litres of water per second. If the tread is worn, it can no longer do this, and the danger of aquaplaning rises sharply. In Switzerland the tread must by law be at least **1.6 millimetres** deep, but experts recommend much more.

The faster a car goes, the less time the tyre has to lead the water away. That is why the danger increases with speed. Wide tyres and deep puddles increase the risk further. **Ruts**, dips in the road surface in which a lot of water collects, are especially dangerous.

Often the steering suddenly feels very light. Sometimes the engine briefly revs up because the wheels are spinning. The car hardly reacts to steering any more because the tyres have no grip. Anyone who notices this should not panic.

In aquaplaning you should immediately **take your foot off the accelerator** and press the clutch, or with an automatic simply stop accelerating. You keep the steering wheel straight and do not steer jerkily. Braking hard is dangerous, because otherwise the car can swerve. As soon as the tyres grip again, the car goes in the direction the wheels are pointing. The best way to prevent aquaplaning is a sensible speed in the rain and good tyres.

begriffe.erklaerung: The grooves in the tyre that lead water away and give grip.
A dip in the road surface caused by many heavy vehicles.
The force between the tyre and the road that gives grip.
How deep the grooves in the tyre still are.

gewusst: Aeroplanes can also aquaplane when landing on a wet runway.
A film of water just a few millimetres thick can be enough to make a fast car float up.
With a coin you can roughly check how deep the tyre tread still is.

teile.einleitung: In an adiabatic process a gas is compressed or expands without any heat being exchanged with its surroundings. In the process its temperature changes all by itself. This explains why a bicycle pump gets warm and why the foehn wind blows so warmly into the valley.
wichtigste: Adiabatic means that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
If a gas is compressed adiabatically, it warms up.
If a gas expands adiabatically, it cools down.
For an ideal gas, p·V^κ = constant.
Dry air has an adiabatic index κ of about 1.4.
Sinking dry air warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres of height.
In a p-V diagram an adiabat is steeper than an isotherm.

abschnitte.text: The word **adiabatic** comes from Greek and means roughly “not passing through”. It means that no heat passes through the walls into or out of the gas. This happens when a process runs very quickly or the gas is well insulated. The work done in compressing it then stays in the gas as **internal energy**. That is why the temperature rises.

For an **ideal gas** in adiabatic processes, p·V^κ = constant. This relationship is also called **Poisson’s equation**, after the French physicist Siméon Denis Poisson. The adiabatic index κ is about 1.4 for dry air and 5/3 for monatomic gases such as helium. If a monatomic gas at 100 kPa is compressed to half its volume, the pressure rises to around 317 kPa. In an isothermal process it would only have risen to 200 kPa, which is why the adiabat is steeper in the diagram.

If you pump up a bike tyre quickly, the bottom of the pump gets warm because the air is **compressed**. When you open a bottle of sparkling water, a fine mist often forms in the neck of the bottle. The gas expands quickly, cools down, and water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. Spray cans also get cold when you spray for a long time.

When air rises or sinks along mountains, its pressure changes and it warms or cools adiabatically. Dry air warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres as it sinks. If foehn air is 4 °C on an Alpine pass 2100 m high and sinks to 500 m in the valley, it becomes around 20 °C warm. This explains the warm **foehn**, which blows, for example, into the Reuss valley, the Hasli valley or the Rhine valley. Moist air cools more slowly as it rises, because heat is released when clouds form.

In a **diesel engine** air is compressed very quickly and strongly. If air at 300 K, that is about 27 °C, is compressed to a tenth of its volume, it reaches around 750 K, which is almost 480 °C. That is hot enough for the injected diesel fuel to ignite by itself. That is why a diesel engine does not need a spark plug. Rudolf Diesel developed this engine in the 1890s.

begriffe.erklaerung: Without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
A process in which the temperature stays the same.
Squeezing a gas into a smaller volume.
The number κ, which shows how strongly pressure and temperature react in adiabatic processes.
A warm, dry wind blowing down the side of a mountain range that faces away from the wind.

gewusst: With the foehn it can suddenly get warmer than 15 °C in the valley on a winter’s day.
With a glass fire piston you can set a piece of cotton wool alight by compressing air quickly.
Clouds often form because rising air cools adiabatically until the water vapour condenses.

teile.einleitung: The cell nucleus is the control centre of a cell. The genetic information is stored in it, that is, the blueprint for the whole living thing. Almost all cells of plants, animals and humans have a nucleus.
wichtigste: The genetic information, DNA, is stored in the nucleus.
The nucleus is surrounded by a double membrane with pores.
Between two divisions, DNA and proteins are loosely spread out as chromatin.
In the nucleolus, building blocks of the ribosomes are made.
Chromosomes consist mainly of DNA and proteins.
Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.
In 1831 the Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the nucleus and gave it its name.

abschnitte.text: The cell nucleus is usually the largest structure in a cell. It holds the **DNA**, the genetic information that determines how a living thing is built and how it works. From here, instructions are sent to the rest of the cell. That is why the nucleus is often compared to a library or a command centre. Only living things with a true nucleus are called eukaryotes.

The nucleus is surrounded by a **nuclear envelope** made of two membranes. In this envelope there are many tiny **nuclear pores**, like doors in a wall. Messenger substances pass out through them and building materials pass in. In this way the precious DNA stays protected in the nucleus, while its information can still be used. Inside there is also the dense nucleolus, in which building blocks of the ribosomes are made.

DNA is a very long, thin thread that is wound around proteins. Between two cell divisions this mixture is loosely spread out and is called **chromatin**. Before a division, the DNA winds itself up tightly and forms thick, clearly visible **chromosomes**. Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes. If you unrolled the DNA from a single nucleus, it would be about 2 metres long.

Not all cells have a nucleus. Mature **red blood cells** lose their nucleus so that there is more room for the red blood pigment that carries oxygen. Bacteria have no true nucleus at all; their DNA lies loose inside the cell. Other cells, on the other hand, have several nuclei, such as the long fibres of skeletal muscles. But the vast majority of body cells have exactly one nucleus.

In 1831 the Scottish botanist **Robert Brown** described the nucleus in the plant cells of orchids. He called it “nucleus”, the Latin word for kernel. In a school microscope, nuclei are often hard to see because they are almost transparent. With a dye such as **methylene blue** they become clearly visible, for example in cells from the lining of the mouth. Today researchers can even take pictures of individual nuclear pores with modern microscopes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long molecule that contains the blueprint of a living thing.
A tightly packed piece of DNA that can be seen before cell division.
A tiny opening in the envelope of the nucleus.
The small body in the nucleus in which parts of the ribosomes are built.
A living thing whose cells have a true nucleus.

gewusst: A nucleus usually measures only a few thousandths of a millimetre and still contains about 2 metres of DNA.
Robert Brown is also known for Brownian motion, the constant jiggling of tiny particles in liquids.
In cell division, all the DNA is first copied so that each new cell receives a complete blueprint.

teile.einleitung: The second voyage of HMS Beagle lasted from 1831 to 1836 and went all the way round the world. On board was the young naturalist Charles Darwin. What he saw and collected on the way later led him to the idea of evolution by natural selection.
wichtigste: The Beagle was a small British warship of the Royal Navy.
The captain on this voyage was Robert FitzRoy.
The main task was to survey the coasts of South America and draw sea charts.
Charles Darwin travelled as naturalist and was only 22 years old when they set off.
The voyage lasted almost five years, from December 1831 to October 1836.
On the Galápagos Islands Darwin collected birds that later turned out to be closely related species of finch.
Darwin’s travel account first appeared in 1839 under the title “Journal of Researches”.

abschnitte.text: **HMS Beagle** was a sailing ship only about 27 metres long, roughly as long as two buses one behind the other. Around 70 people lived on board in very cramped conditions. Captain **Robert FitzRoy** was himself only 26 years old. He wanted an educated companion he could talk to, and so Charles Darwin came on board.

The Beagle set off from Plymouth in England on 27 December 1831. Its main task was the **survey** of the coasts of South America, so that ships could sail more safely. In January 1832 Darwin went ashore for the first time on the Cape Verde Islands. After that came Brazil, Argentina, Tierra del Fuego, the Falkland Islands, Chile and Peru. Via the Galápagos Islands, Tahiti, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa the ship returned to England in October 1836.

Darwin spent more time on land than on the ship. In Argentina he dug up bones of extinct giant animals, for example of **giant ground sloths** such as Megatherium. On the way he read the book “Principles of Geology” by **Charles Lyell**. Lyell explained that the Earth changes through slow processes over a very long time. This idea helped Darwin to think about the slow change of living things too.

In February 1835 Darwin experienced a strong earthquake near Concepción in Chile. Afterwards he noticed that the **coast had risen**, because mussel beds were suddenly above the water. This showed him that mountain ranges such as the Andes can form bit by bit. In 1836, on the Keeling Islands in the Indian Ocean, he tested his theory on how **atolls**, ring-shaped coral islands, form.

In autumn 1835 the Beagle stayed about five weeks at the **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific. Darwin saw giant tortoises, marine iguanas and many birds. He noticed that animals differed slightly from island to island. Only after the voyage did the ornithologist **John Gould** recognise that Darwin’s birds were closely related species of finch. Today they are called Darwin’s finches.

The travel account of 1839 made Darwin famous and is often called “The Voyage of the Beagle” today. For over 20 years Darwin thought about his observations. In 1859 he published his famous book “On the Origin of Species”. In it he explained **evolution** by natural selection, one of the most important ideas in biology.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who closely observes and studies animals, plants, rocks and nature.
The remains of a living thing from very long ago that have turned to stone, for example a bone.
A ring-shaped island made of coral that surrounds a lagoon in the middle.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
The precise measuring of coasts and land in order to draw maps.

gewusst: Darwin was often seasick on the ship and was therefore glad of every trip ashore.
Originally the voyage was supposed to last only about two years; in the end it was almost five.
At first Darwin did not label his finches on the Galápagos Islands carefully by island, which he later regretted.

teile.einleitung: Anders Celsius was a Swedish astronomer who lived almost 300 years ago. The temperature scale in degrees Celsius that we use every day is named after him. The astonishing thing is that his scale was exactly the other way round at first.
wichtigste: Anders Celsius was above all an astronomer, a scientist who studies the stars.
He lived from 1701 to 1744 and was only about 42 years old when he died.
He worked in the Swedish university town of Uppsala.
In 1742 he presented his temperature scale.
Originally the scale was the other way round: water boiled at 0 and froze at 100 degrees.
He studied the northern lights and linked them to the Earth’s magnetic field.
In 1736 he took part in the Lapland expedition to measure the Earth.

abschnitte.text: Anders Celsius was born in 1701 in **Uppsala** in Sweden and died there in 1744. He came from a family of scholars; his father and grandfather had both been professors. Celsius himself became professor of **astronomy** at Uppsala University. He also travelled through Europe, for example to Germany, Italy, France and England, to get to know other scientists and observatories.

In 1742 Celsius proposed a temperature scale with two fixed points: the **freezing point** and the **boiling point** of water. He divided the gap between them into 100 equal parts. In his version, however, the boiling point was at 0 degrees and the freezing point at 100 degrees. Only after his death was the scale turned round, so that water today freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. Another important discovery of his was that the boiling point depends on the air pressure.

In 1736 Celsius travelled with a French expedition under Pierre Louis Moreau de Maupertuis to **Lapland** in the far north. There the researchers measured how long one degree is along a meridian of the Earth. The result showed that the Earth is slightly **flattened** at the poles, so not perfectly round. In this way they confirmed a prediction by Isaac Newton.

Celsius closely observed the **northern lights** in the sky over Sweden. Together with his assistant Olof Hiorter he noticed that compass needles trembled restlessly when northern lights were shining. In this way they recognised a connection between the northern lights and the Earth’s **magnetic field**. Celsius also made sure that Uppsala got a modern observatory, which was finished in 1741.

The Celsius scale is used today in almost every country in the world, including Switzerland. Only a few countries such as the USA still use degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life. In science people often calculate in **kelvin**, where a step of 1 kelvin is exactly the same size as 1 degree Celsius. A crater on the Moon and a minor planet also bear the name Celsius.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scientist who studies stars, planets and the sky.
The temperature at which water turns to ice, today 0 degrees Celsius.
The temperature at which water boils, about 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
Glowing bands of colour in the night sky, mainly in the far north and south.

gewusst: On the original Celsius scale, a hot summer’s day of 30 degrees today would have been a day of 70 degrees.
Celsius died of tuberculosis at only about 42, before his scale became world-famous.
A temperature difference of 1 degree Celsius is exactly the same size as 1 kelvin.

teile.einleitung: Every year in autumn, millions of birds leave Switzerland and fly to the warm south. In spring they return. This great journey is called bird migration and is one of the most amazing natural spectacles in the world.
wichtigste: Birds that fly away in autumn and come back in spring are called migratory birds.
Birds that stay with us all year round are called resident birds.
Many Swiss migratory birds spend the winter in Africa.
Before the journey, migratory birds eat their way to a reserve of fat.
To find their way, they use the sun, the stars and the Earth's magnetic field, among other things.
Many small migratory birds fly at night.
Geese often fly in a V formation.
The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back.

abschnitte.text: In winter many birds can hardly find any food here. Those that eat **insects**, such as swallows, would have nothing left to eat in the cold. That is why these birds fly to areas where it is warm and there is enough food. In spring they return, because then there is plenty of food and space to breed here.

**Migratory birds** such as the barn swallow, the common swift, the cuckoo and the white stork leave Switzerland in autumn. **Resident birds** such as the blackbird, the house sparrow or the great tit stay here all year round. Some birds are **partial migrants**: some of the birds leave, the others stay. Other birds from the north, such as some ducks, even come to us in winter.

Before leaving, migratory birds eat especially a lot and build up **fat reserves**. Small songbirds can almost double their weight in a short time. The fat is their fuel for the long distance. On the way, many birds take breaks at stopover sites to refuel.

Migratory birds find their way with amazing abilities. They orient themselves by the position of the **sun** and at night by the **stars**. Many can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, as if with a built-in compass. Mountains, rivers and coasts also help them find their way.

Many small songbirds fly at **night**, because the air is calmer and cooler then and fewer enemies are about. During the day they rest and look for food. Large birds such as geese and cranes often fly in a **V formation**. Each bird uses the upwash of the bird in front and so saves energy.

On its migration between the Arctic and the Antarctic, the **Arctic tern** covers tens of thousands of kilometres every year. No other animal travels so far. On the journey, birds face storms, the Sahara, panes of glass and lit-up buildings. The destruction of stopover sites also causes problems for many migratory birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that travels back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter area.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round.
A bird species in which only some of the birds leave in winter.
A place where migratory birds take a break on the way and feed.

gewusst: The common swift can stay in the air for months and even sleeps while flying.
Many millions of birds fly over Switzerland every autumn, most of them unnoticed at night.
Young cuckoos find their winter quarters in Africa even though nobody shows them the way.

teile.einleitung: Werner Arber is a Swiss biologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1978. He discovered how bacteria defend themselves against viruses with special enzymes. These so-called restriction enzymes are an important tool of genetic engineering today.
wichtigste: Werner Arber was born in 1929 in Gränichen in the canton of Aargau.
He studied how bacteria protect themselves against bacterial viruses.
Bacteria cut up foreign DNA with restriction enzymes.
They protect their own DNA through methylation.
In 1978 he shared the Nobel Prize with Daniel Nathans and Hamilton Smith.
From 1971 he did research at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel.
In 2011 he became the first Protestant president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences.
Restriction enzymes are essential in genetic engineering for cutting DNA precisely.

abschnitte.text: Werner Arber was born in 1929 in **Gränichen** in the canton of Aargau. He studied natural sciences at ETH Zurich. After that he did research at the University of Geneva and for some time in the USA. He is one of the best-known Swiss scientists of the 20th century.

In Geneva, Arber studied **bacteriophages**, which are viruses that infect bacteria. He observed that these viruses multiplied to different degrees depending on the strain of bacteria. From this he concluded that some bacteria have a defence system against foreign genetic material. He called this phenomenon **restriction**.

Arber realised that bacteria make **restriction enzymes**, which cut up foreign DNA like scissors. So that they do not destroy their own DNA, the bacteria mark it with small chemical tags. This process is called **methylation**. In this way the enzyme can tell its own DNA from foreign DNA.

In 1978 Werner Arber received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine. He shared it with the US researchers **Daniel Nathans** and **Hamilton Smith**. Smith had found an enzyme that cuts DNA at one very particular point, and Nathans used such enzymes to study genetic material. From 1971 Arber taught and did research at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel.

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at precisely defined sequences of letters. With them, researchers can cut out genes and insert them elsewhere. This is the basis of **genetic engineering**. Today, for example, insulin for people with diabetes is made with the help of bacteria in this way.

Arber also dealt with questions about evolution and the responsibility of research. In 2011 Pope Benedict XVI appointed him president of the **Pontifical Academy of Sciences**. He was the first Protestant in this office. The academy advises the Vatican on scientific questions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The genetic material in which the building plan of a living thing is stored.
A virus that infects bacteria.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a particular point, like scissors.
A chemical marking of DNA that protects it from the cell's own cutting enzyme.
Methods with which genetic material is changed in a targeted way.

gewusst: Arber once explained his research with a story for his young daughter, which became known as the “Tale of Silvia”.
Without restriction enzymes, many modern medicines made from bacterial cultures would not exist.
Arber was president of an academy of the Vatican, even though he himself is a member of the Reformed Church.

teile.einleitung: Wolfgang Pauli was one of the most important physicists of the 20th century. He was born in Vienna, taught at ETH Zurich for almost 30 years and later became a Swiss citizen. In 1945 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the exclusion principle that is named after him.
wichtigste: Wolfgang Pauli was born in Vienna on 25 April 1900 and died in Zurich in 1958.
From 1928 he was professor of theoretical physics at ETH Zurich.
His exclusion principle explains how the electrons in an atom are arranged.
In 1930 he predicted a new, almost invisible particle, the neutrino.
Albert Einstein nominated him for the Nobel Prize, which he received in 1945.
With the Pauli matrices he described the spin of electrons mathematically.
Colleagues jokingly used the term “Pauli effect” for experiments breaking down when he was near.

abschnitte.text: Wolfgang Pauli was born in **Vienna** on 25 April 1900. Even as a schoolboy he studied Albert Einstein's new theory of relativity. He studied in Munich under the physicist Arnold Sommerfeld and, at only 21, wrote a long review article on the theory of relativity that even Einstein praised. After that he worked in Göttingen, Copenhagen and Hamburg, among other places. Colleagues feared him as a strict, sometimes mocking critic who spotted mistakes immediately.

In 1925 Pauli discovered the **exclusion principle**, also called the Pauli principle. It states that two electrons in an atom can never match in all their properties. That is why all the electrons cannot gather on the innermost orbit but are spread over different shells. This explains the structure of the periodic table of the elements and with it the whole of chemistry. For this discovery Pauli received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 1945.

In radioactive **beta decay**, energy seemed to disappear, which went against a basic law of physics. In 1930 Pauli suggested that a tiny, electrically neutral particle was carrying the missing energy away unnoticed. He began his letter to a physics conference with the joking greeting “Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen”. The particle was later named the **neutrino**, which means roughly “little neutral one” in Italian. Only in 1956 were researchers really able to detect neutrinos.

In 1928 Pauli became professor of theoretical physics at **ETH Zurich**. During the Second World War he worked for some years in Princeton in the USA and then returned to Zurich. In 1949 he was granted Swiss citizenship. In Zurich he trained many young physicists and exchanged thousands of letters with colleagues all over the world. He died in Zurich on 15 December 1958.

Pauli was a brilliant theorist but supposedly a disaster for experiments. Colleagues said that equipment broke down or glass shattered as soon as he entered a laboratory. They called this joking superstition the **Pauli effect**. Pauli himself found the stories funny and also a little intriguing. Of course this is not a real law of physics but an anecdote.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of an atom.
A property of particles that can be imagined, in simplified form, as spinning around themselves.
A very light particle without charge that passes through almost everything unhindered.
The part of physics that describes and predicts the laws of nature using mathematics.

gewusst: Pauli's godfather was the famous physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach.
Every second, many billions of neutrinos from the Sun fly through your body without you noticing.
Pauli was known for his sharp remarks and once called a poor piece of work “not even wrong”.

teile.einleitung: Anger is a strong feeling that we have when something seems unfair to us, bothers us or when we do not get something. Everyone gets angry sometimes, so anger is a completely normal feeling. What matters is how you deal with it.
wichtigste: Anger is a normal feeling that all people know.
When you are angry, your eyebrows draw together and your face sometimes turns red.
Another word for anger is rage.
Someone who gets angry very quickly is called a hothead.
Small children sometimes have violent outbursts of anger, called tantrums.
Counting slowly to ten helps when you are very angry.
You can show your anger with words without hurting anyone.

abschnitte.text: **Anger** is one of the basic human feelings, like joy, sadness or fear. It often arises when we feel treated unfairly or when something does not go the way we want. Other words for it are **rage** or annoyance. Anger is not bad; it shows us that something matters to us or that a boundary has been crossed.

When you are angry, the body releases stress hormones such as **adrenaline**. The heart beats faster, the breath becomes short and the muscles tense up. Often the face turns red because more blood flows into it. The eyebrows draw together, and some people clench their fists. The body gets ready to fight, even if that is not necessary at all.

There are many sayings for great anger. In German, someone who is very angry is “auf hundertachtzig”, “at one hundred and eighty”, like a car driving very fast. People also say someone is “bursting with anger” or “seeing red”. A person who gets angry very quickly is called a **hothead**. Images like these show how hot anger can feel.

Toddlers are not yet good at controlling their feelings. At about the age of two to four, many have violent outbursts of anger, which are called **tantrums**. They throw themselves on the floor, scream or cry. This is part of normal development, because the child is realising that it has a will of its own. Over time it learns to cope with disappointment.

When you are very angry, it helps to **count slowly to ten** and breathe deeply. You can go away for a moment, move about or punch a cushion. Afterwards it is easier to say what is bothering you, for example with the sentence: “That annoys me!” In this way you show your anger without hurting anyone. It also helps to talk about it with someone you trust.

When the anger has died down, you can talk about the argument calmly. Each side says how they experienced the situation. Anyone who said something hurtful can **apologise**. Often you find a solution together, and afterwards everyone feels better.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something you sense inside, such as joy, fear or anger.
A hormone that quickly gets the body ready when it is excited.
A violent outburst of anger by a small child.
Someone who gets angry very quickly.

gewusst: Anger can even be useful, because it gives you strength to stand up for fairness.
The German saying “auf hundertachtzig” probably comes from the speed of 180 kilometres per hour.
Even babies show the first signs of annoyance when something is taken away from them.

teile.einleitung: A scientific drawing shows a plant, an animal, a stone or a machine as accurately and as realistically as possible. It is not a work of art to dream over but a research tool. Anyone who draws like this learns one thing above all: to look very closely.
wichtigste: Researchers draw plants and animals in order to look closely and discover details.
A researcher's drawing should be accurate and as realistic as possible.
Next to the drawing you write the names of the parts; this is called labelling.
You also note how big the thing is in reality.
It is best to draw with a sharp pencil.
Over 300 years ago, Maria Sibylla Merian drew how caterpillars turn into butterflies.
Leonardo da Vinci filled many notebooks with drawings of machines and birds.

abschnitte.text: A scientific drawing records what something really looks like. It should be **accurate** and must not add anything you cannot see. Unimportant things such as a shadow or a pretty background are often left out. Instead, important parts are drawn especially clearly. This way, someone else can look at the drawing and recognise the living thing later.

When you draw, you have to look for much longer than when you quickly take a photo. For example, you count the legs of a beetle or the petals of a flower. With small animals, a **bug viewer** helps: you can catch an insect in it for a short time and look at it magnified. For even smaller things, researchers use a **microscope**. Many discoveries began with someone carefully drawing something.

You draw with a sharp pencil, because it makes fine lines and mistakes can be rubbed out. The individual parts are labelled with straight lines and their names, for example stem, leaf and flower. Then you add a **size note**, such as “2 cm long in reality”, or a small scale bar. The date, the place where it was found and the name of the object also belong on the sheet. This turns a sketch into a real **research record**.

**Leonardo da Vinci** (1452 to 1519) drew birds' wings, the human body and flying machines in his notebooks. **Maria Sibylla Merian** (1647 to 1717) travelled to Suriname in South America in 1699 and painted insects and plants there. She was one of the first to show how caterpillars change into butterflies by way of the pupa. In the 16th century the Zurich scholar **Conrad Gessner** published a large book of animals with many woodcuts. Around 1900 Ernst Haeckel became famous for his artistic pictures of tiny sea creatures.

Even in the age of mobile phone cameras, people still draw. A drawing can show what is typical and leave out what is distracting, which a photo cannot do. That is why field guides for plants and birds often contain drawings instead of photos. In medicine there are also **medical illustrators**, who draw bones and organs for textbooks, for example. At school, careful drawing is practised in the subject Nature, People, Society (“Natur, Mensch, Gesellschaft”).

begriffe.erklaerung: The names of the parts, written next to the drawing and joined to it by lines.
A note showing how much something has been drawn larger or smaller.
A small pot with a magnifying glass in the lid, in which you can look at insects.
A picture that explains or adds to a text.

gewusst: Merian's book on the insects of Suriname appeared in 1705 and is now regarded as a masterpiece.
Leonardo da Vinci wrote many notes in mirror writing, that is, from right to left.
Some animal species were first described only from a drawing, before there were any photos of them.

teile.einleitung: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that can be passed between animals and humans. Many well-known diseases originally came from animals, for example rabies or the plague. That is why experts today look at the health of humans, animals and the environment together.
wichtigste: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that is passed between animals and humans.
According to frequently quoted estimates, around 60 per cent of the known infectious diseases of humans are zoonotic in origin.
In Switzerland, rabies was fought with vaccine baits for foxes.
The fox tapeworm is passed on through eggs in fox droppings and can seriously damage the liver.
In Switzerland, ticks transmit tick-borne encephalitis.
The plague was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and was passed from rats to humans by fleas.
The “One Health” approach looks at humans, animals and the environment together.

abschnitte.text: The word **zoonosis** comes from Greek and means roughly “animal disease”. It refers to diseases whose pathogens jump from animals to humans or the other way round. Pathogens can be viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites. The term was coined in the 19th century by the German doctor Rudolf Virchow. According to frequently quoted estimates, around 60 per cent of the known infectious diseases of humans originally came from animals.

Some pathogens enter the body through a **bite** or scratch, as with rabies. Others are transmitted by insects or ticks that first bite an animal and then a human. Such carriers are called **vectors**. You can also become infected through contaminated food, for example undercooked poultry containing salmonella. Still other pathogens, such as the eggs of the fox tapeworm, get into the environment through droppings.

In Switzerland the **tick** transmits tick-borne encephalitis, TBE for short, and Lyme disease. There is a vaccine against TBE that is recommended for almost all of Switzerland. The **fox tapeworm** is a parasite whose eggs are found in fox droppings and which can seriously damage the human liver. **Rabies** was fought from 1978 onwards by laying out vaccine baits for foxes, and Switzerland was a pioneer in this. Since 1999 Switzerland has been considered free of rabies in land animals.

The **plague** is one of the best-known zoonoses. It is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which fleas carried from rats to humans. In the 14th century the “Black Death” killed about a third of Europe’s population. More recent diseases such as bird flu also come from animals. **Bats** are considered an important natural reservoir for many coronaviruses and lyssaviruses.

Because humans, animals and the environment are closely connected, doctors, vets and environmental experts work together in the **One Health** approach. They monitor diseases in wild and farm animals in order to spot new dangers early. If you want to do something yourself, wash your hands thoroughly after touching animals. After trips to woods and meadows you should check yourself for ticks. Meat and eggs should be cooked thoroughly, and you should not touch dead or unusually tame wild animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A disease that can be passed between animals and humans.
A tiny living thing or virus that causes a disease.
An animal, such as a tick or mosquito, that carries a pathogen on to others.
Animals in which a pathogen lives permanently, often without making them ill.
An approach that looks at the health of humans, animals and the environment together.

gewusst: In 1978 Switzerland was the first country to test vaccine baits for foxes in the wild.
Humans can also infect animals, for example great apes with cold viruses.
Ticks lie in wait in grass and bushes and get brushed off onto you; they do not jump down from trees.

teile.einleitung: A bird's nest is the place where a bird lays its eggs, incubates them and raises its young. Birds are true builders: they weave, glue, plait or carve their nests. Depending on the species, a nest looks very different.
wichtigste: A bird builds a nest in which to lay eggs and raise its young.
Many birds use twigs, grass and moss for their nest.
The woodpecker carves its nest as a hole in a tree trunk.
The weaver bird weaves elaborate nests from blades of grass.
The mallard often breeds in a hollow on the ground.
With a nest box you can help birds to nest.
You should not touch a bird's nest, because the parents could otherwise be disturbed.

abschnitte.text: A **nest** protects the eggs and the young birds from cold, rain and enemies. The female lays the eggs in it, and usually one or both parents incubate them. After hatching, the young are fed in the nest until they fledge. After that, in many species the nest is no longer needed.

Many birds build their nest from **twigs, grass and moss**. It is often lined with feathers, animal hair or soft plant fibres. The house martin glues its nest of damp **pellets of mud** under the eaves. The blackbird forms a firm cup, which it smooths inside with earth and mud.

The most common is the **cup nest**, an open bowl in a bush or tree. The **woodpecker** carves a hole into a tree trunk with its powerful beak, and later tits or starlings often move into such holes. The **weaver bird** from Africa and Asia weaves elaborate hanging nests from blades of grass and even ties knots in the process. The mallard, on the other hand, often breeds in a simple hollow on the ground, well hidden in the grass on the bank.

Because old trees with holes have become rare, you can help birds with a **nest box**. Depending on the size of the entrance hole, a blue tit, a great tit or a starling, for example, will move in. You hang the box where it is protected from cats and from blazing sun. It is best cleaned **in autumn**, when no birds are breeding any more, so that no parasites survive.

If you find a nest, you should **not touch** it and should move on quickly. Otherwise the parents could be disturbed and abandon the nest, and enemies could follow your trail. In Switzerland, wild birds and their nests are protected by law. That is why it is best to cut hedges and trees outside the breeding season, that is, not in spring and early summer.

begriffe.erklaerung: An open, bowl-shaped nest like the one the blackbird builds.
A wooden box with an entrance hole in which birds can breed.
Keeping the eggs warm with your own body until the young hatch.
Developed far enough for a young bird to be able to fly.

gewusst: The cuckoo does not build its own nest but lays its eggs in the nests of other birds.
Some swiftlets in Asia build their nests almost entirely from their own saliva.
Stork nests are often added to over many years and can become very large and heavy.

teile.einleitung: Water fleas are tiny animals that live in ponds, pools and lakes. Despite their name, they are not fleas but small crustaceans. Because they hop jerkily through the water, they remind people of jumping fleas.
wichtigste: The water flea is not a real flea but a small crustacean.
It is only a few millimetres long.
Water fleas row with their large antennae.
They eat algae and bacteria.
A transparent shell protects their body.
Water fleas have one single large eye.
Under a magnifying glass you can see their heart beating.
Dried water fleas are sold as fish food.

abschnitte.text: Water fleas are usually only 1 to 5 millimetres long. Their body is enclosed in a **transparent shell** made of two halves. That is why under a magnifying glass or a microscope you can look inside and even see the **heart** beating. At the front of the head there is a large, dark **compound eye**.

Water fleas belong to the **crustaceans**, just like crabs, lobsters and crayfish. The best-known genus is called **Daphnia**, which is why they are also called daphnia. They are only distantly related to insects such as the real flea. The name comes solely from their hopping way of swimming.

Water fleas row with their large, branched **antennae**. With each stroke they make a small jump upwards and then slowly sink again. This creates the typical hopping movement. Many water fleas move up in the water in the evening and back down into the depths in the morning to avoid fish.

Water fleas feed on **algae**, bacteria and small floating particles. With their legs they create a current of water and filter out the food. That is why they are called **filter feeders**. Because they eat so many algae, they can make a body of water clearer.

Water fleas are an important link in the **food chain**. They are eaten by fish, dragonfly larvae and other animals. In pet shops you can buy them dried, frozen or alive as **fish food** for aquariums. In many ponds in Switzerland you can catch them with a fine net in spring and summer.

Water fleas react sensitively to poison in the water. That is why laboratories use them to test whether waste water or chemicals are harmful to water animals. Some species even grow spines or helmets when they smell enemies. For bad times they lay especially tough **resting eggs**, which survive drought and frost.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with a hard shell and jointed legs that usually lives in water.
Another name for the water flea, after the genus Daphnia.
An animal that sieves tiny food particles out of the water.
An especially robust egg that survives cold and drought.

gewusst: Under the microscope you can watch the food travelling through a water flea's gut.
Resting eggs of water fleas can survive for years in the mud and then still hatch.
Some water fleas grow a pointed helmet when enemies are nearby, so that they are harder to eat.

teile.einleitung: A cloud is a visible collection of tiny water droplets or ice crystals in the air. Clouds form when moist air rises and cools. They bring rain and snow, and you can often tell the weather from their shape.
wichtigste: Clouds consist of billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Thick white clouds that look like cotton wool are called heap clouds.
Thin, wispy clouds high up are called feather clouds.
Layer clouds cover the sky like a grey blanket.
When the droplets become too heavy, they fall down as rain.
Dark grey clouds often mean that rain is coming soon.
In winter, low stratus often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days.

abschnitte.text: Warm air can hold a lot of invisible **water vapour**. When the air rises, for example over a mountain or on a sunny day, it cools down. Cold air can hold less water vapour, so tiny droplets form on grains of dust or salt. This process is called **condensation**. Billions of these droplets make up a visible cloud.

abschnitte.titel: The most important types of cloud
abschnitte.text: Around 1803 the Englishman Luke Howard gave the clouds Latin names that are still used today. **Heap clouds** (cumulus) are thick white puffs of cotton wool that form on fine summer days. **Feather clouds** (cirrus) consist of ice crystals and float at heights of over 6 kilometres. Layer clouds (stratus) form an even grey blanket. Small clouds that look like a flock in groups are called a mackerel sky, or “Schäfchenwolken”, “little sheep clouds”, in German.

In a cloud the droplets bump into each other and become larger. When they are too heavy, they fall to the Earth as **precipitation**: rain, snow or hail. The biggest clouds are thunderclouds, which are called **cumulonimbus**. They can tower more than 10 kilometres high and look like an anvil at the top. Clouds look dark when they are so thick that hardly any sunlight gets through.

In autumn and winter, a grey blanket of low stratus often lies over the **Swiss Plateau** for days. Cold air is then trapped near the ground, with warmer air above it like a lid. This weather situation is called an **inversion**. Anyone who then climbs a mountain such as the Rigi or the Napf often rises above the clouds into brilliant sunshine. From above, the low stratus looks like a white sea.

The white trails behind aeroplanes are called **contrails**. They form because the hot exhaust gases from the engines contain water vapour. In the icy air at great height, this freezes straight away into ice crystals. If the air is moist, the trails stay visible for a long time and can spread out into feather clouds. If the air is dry, they quickly disappear again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in the form of an invisible gas in the air.
When water vapour cools and turns into liquid droplets.
Water that falls from clouds to the Earth, such as rain, snow or hail.
A weather situation in which the air higher up is warmer than the air below.

gewusst: A single large heap cloud can contain several hundred tonnes of water and still float.
Fog is nothing other than a cloud lying on the ground.
Cloud droplets are so small that about a million of them are needed to form a single raindrop.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum is a space in which there is no matter and no air, that is, an almost completely empty space. Completely perfect emptiness does not exist, but it is possible to come very close to it. Vacuums play a role in research, in space and even in your kitchen.
wichtigste: A vacuum is a space without matter or air.
The word comes from the Latin vacuus, which means empty.
There is an almost perfect vacuum in space.
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.
Otto von Guericke showed the power of air pressure with the Magdeburg hemispheres.
Vacuums are used in vacuum flasks, packaging and laboratories.

abschnitte.text: A **vacuum** is a space from which the air and all other particles have been removed. In technology, people speak of a vacuum as soon as there is much less air than normal. **Negative pressure** arises when the pressure in a container is lower than outside. No space is completely empty, because a few particles always remain.

The air around us presses from all sides with great force; this is **air pressure**. If you pump the air out of a container, the air outside presses against it all the more strongly. That is why a vacuum-packed bag can hardly be pulled apart. A suction cup also holds because the outside air pressure presses it against the wall.

In 1643 the Italian Evangelista **Torricelli** showed with a glass tube full of mercury that an empty space forms above the liquid. The mayor of Magdeburg, **Otto von Guericke**, invented an air pump. In a famous experiment he put two metal hemispheres together and pumped the air out. Even teams of horses could not pull the spheres apart.

Between the stars and planets there is an almost perfect vacuum. On average there are only very few particles per cubic centimetre. Because sound needs air or another substance, it is completely silent in **space**. That is why astronauts need spacesuits that supply air and pressure.

A **vacuum flask** has double walls with a vacuum between them, which hardly lets any heat through. Vacuum-packed food stays fresh for longer, because bacteria grow badly without oxygen. A vacuum cleaner creates negative pressure, which sucks in the dirt. Old light bulbs and television tubes also contained a vacuum.

In the **LHC** particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva, particles fly through tubes with an extremely strong vacuum. There the pressure is even lower than on the surface of the Moon. That way the particles do not collide with air molecules. A very pure vacuum is also needed to make computer chips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A space in which there are almost no particles and no air.
The force with which air presses on everything.
A pressure that is lower than the air pressure in the surroundings.
A pump that sucks air out of a container.

gewusst: In a vacuum, a feather and a hammer fall at the same speed, as an astronaut showed on the Moon in 1971.
In a vacuum, water boils even at room temperature.
The Greek philosopher Aristotle believed that an empty space could not exist at all.

teile.einleitung: The ampere is the unit of electric current. It tells you how much electric charge flows through a wire per second. It is named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère.
wichtigste: The ampere is the unit of electric current.
The unit symbol is A, and the current itself is abbreviated as I.
It is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, SI.
It is named after the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère, who lived from 1775 to 1836.
Current is measured with an ammeter.
Current times voltage gives the electrical power in watts.
Even small currents through the body can be life-threatening.

abschnitte.text: Electric current is the flow of electrically charged particles, in metal wires the flow of **electrons**. The **current** tells you how much charge flows through the conductor per second. You can compare it with water in a pipe: the current corresponds to the amount of water that flows through per second. With 1 ampere, around 6 quintillion electrons flow through the wire every second.

**André-Marie Ampère** was a French physicist and mathematician. Around 1820 he studied how electric currents produce magnetic forces. He showed that two parallel wires attract each other when current flows through them in the same direction. In doing so he laid one of the foundations of electrodynamics. In his honour the unit of current was named after him in 1881.

The ampere is one of the seven **base units** of the International System of Units, together with the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole and candela. Since 2019 it has been defined using the electric charge of a single electron. Smaller currents are given in milliamperes; a milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere. Together with the **voltage** in volts, the current gives the power in watts.

A small light-emitting diode needs only about 20 milliamperes. A 2000-watt kettle on the Swiss mains at 230 volts draws just under 9 amperes. In Swiss homes the circuits are usually protected by **fuses** of 10 to 16 amperes. If more current is drawn, the fuse switches off so that the wires do not get too hot. A lightning bolt, on the other hand, often reaches tens of thousands of amperes.

If current flows through the human body, it can throw the muscles and the heart out of rhythm. Even a few hundredths of an ampere can be life-threatening. That is why you must never fiddle with sockets or damaged cables. A **residual current device**, or RCD for short, switches off the power in a fraction of a second if something is wrong. Railway power lines are especially dangerous, and you must never get too close to them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount of electric charge that flows through a conductor per second.
A tiny, negatively charged particle that forms the current in a wire.
A basic unit of measurement from which other units are derived.
A safety switch that cuts off the current if it gets too high.

gewusst: The unit ampere was fixed in 1881 at an international congress of electricians in Paris.
An electric eel can produce electric shocks of about one ampere.
The unit symbol A is written without the accent, even though Ampère has an accent in his name.

teile.einleitung: A petrified remain is a remnant or trace of a living thing that has been preserved in rock for a very long time. It is also called a fossil. Fossils tell us what animals and plants looked like millions of years ago.
wichtigste: Petrifactions, also called fossils, are remains or traces of living things from earlier times.
Particularly many fossils form at the bottom of seas and lakes.
During fossilisation, minerals from the water slowly fill a bone, for example.
This takes a very long time, often many thousands to millions of years.
As well as animals, wood from trees can also become petrified.
Living things without hard parts, such as jellyfish, only very rarely become fossils.
In rock layers, the lower layers are usually older than the upper ones.

abschnitte.text: A **petrifaction** or **fossil** is evidence of life from prehistoric times that has been preserved in rock. This can be bones, teeth, shells, leaves or whole tree trunks. Footprints, feeding marks or imprints also count. The science that studies fossils is called **palaeontology**.

Usually an animal dies in the water and sinks to the bottom of a sea or lake. There it is quickly covered by mud and sand and so protected from scavengers and decay. Over time, water with dissolved **minerals** gets into the bones or shells and slowly fills them. Over thousands to millions of years the mud turns into stone, and the fossil is enclosed in it.

abschnitte.titel: Why not everything becomes a fossil
abschnitte.text: Only a tiny fraction of all living things ever becomes a fossil. Hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells are preserved best. Soft animals such as jellyfish or worms usually decay before they can become fossils. Wood can also become petrified when minerals such as silica replace the wood bit by bit; this creates **petrified wood**.

Rocks often form in layers on top of one another, and the lower layers are usually older. When mountains are formed, such layers are lifted and sometimes even tilted. **Erosion** by wind, water and ice later exposes the fossils again. That is why fossils of sea creatures are found today even high up in the Alps.

**Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino is famous for its fossils from the Triassic period, which are about 240 million years old. Fish and marine reptiles were found there, and since 2003 the mountain has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In Frick in the canton of Aargau, numerous skeletons of the dinosaur Plateosaurus have been dug up. In many limestones of the Jura you can also find snail-shaped **ammonites**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or a trace of a living thing from earlier times.
The science that studies fossils and prehistoric life.
An extinct sea creature with a shell coiled like a snail's.
The slow wearing away of rock by wind, water and ice.
Deposited sand, mud or lime from which rock later forms.

gewusst: Even tiny insects can be preserved as fossils if they were trapped in tree resin that turned into amber.
Fossilised sea creatures high up in the Alps show that this rock once lay on the seabed.
There are also fossil dinosaur footprints in Switzerland, for example in the Jura.

teile.einleitung: A voltmeter is a measuring instrument used to measure electrical voltage. Voltage shows how strongly the current is “driven” through a circuit. It is measured in volts, named after the Italian researcher Alessandro Volta.
wichtigste: With a voltmeter you measure electrical voltage.
The unit of voltage is the volt, abbreviated V.
A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.
There are analogue devices with a pointer and digital ones with a number display.
The voltmeter is often part of a multimeter.
A normal battery has 1.5 volts, the mains socket in Switzerland 230 volts.

abschnitte.text: You can imagine electrical **voltage** like the pressure in a water pipe. The higher the pressure, the more strongly the water is pushed through the pipes. In the same way, voltage drives the electric charges through a wire. It is measured in **volts**, and a voltmeter shows this value.

A voltmeter has two connections, usually a red and a black lead with probe tips. You hold them to the two ends of the component whose voltage you want to measure. This is called a **parallel connection**, because the voltmeter is next to the component and not in the path of the current. A good voltmeter has a very high **internal resistance**, so that hardly any current flows through it and the measurement is not distorted.

An **analogue voltmeter** has a pointer that moves over a scale. Inside, the current deflects a coil in a magnetic field. A **digital voltmeter** shows the voltage directly as a number. Today people mostly use a multimeter, which can measure current and resistance as well as voltage.

A small AA battery supplies about 1.5 volts, a car battery about 12 volts. In Switzerland, 230 volts of alternating voltage come out of the socket. The overhead lines of the SBB even carry 15,000 volts. With a voltmeter you can check whether a battery is still full or needs replacing.

The unit volt is named after the Italian physicist **Alessandro Volta**, who lived from 1745 to 1827. Around 1800 he built the **voltaic pile**, the world's first battery. It consisted of copper and zinc discs stacked on top of each other with pieces of cloth soaked in salt water between them. With it, electric current could be produced continuously for the first time.

Measurements on batteries and small circuits are harmless and exciting. Measurements at the mains socket or on power lines, on the other hand, are deadly dangerous. Only trained experts such as electricians may carry them out. Anyone using a voltmeter must first set the correct **measuring range**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that drives electric charges through a circuit.
The unit of electrical voltage.
A circuit in which components are connected side by side to the same two points.
A measuring instrument that can measure voltage, current and resistance.

gewusst: An electric eel can give off electric shocks of several hundred volts.
Current is not measured with a voltmeter but with an ammeter, which is connected in series.
Even a lemon with a piece of copper and a piece of zinc supplies almost one volt.

th7conp.t: Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology

teile.einleitung: The Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology, VAW for short, is a research institute of ETH Zurich. It studies how water flows in rivers, lakes and dams and how glaciers change. In its large test hall it builds rivers and dams on a small scale.
wichtigste: VAW stands for the Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology at ETH Zurich (in German “Versuchsanstalt für Wasserbau, Hydrologie und Glaziologie”).
In a large test hall it tests hydraulic structures in scaled-down physical models.
Models with a free water surface are usually scaled according to Froude's model law.
In a model on a scale of 1:100, the water flows ten times more slowly than in nature.
The well-known bedload formula of Meyer-Peter and Müller was developed at the VAW.
With the Universities of Fribourg and Zurich, the VAW runs the glacier monitoring network GLAMOS.
The VAW's glaciology section also studies ice avalanches from steep hanging glaciers.
The thickness of glaciers is measured with radar waves that are reflected by the rock bed.

abschnitte.text: The **VAW** is an institute of ETH Zurich and was founded in 1930. It combines three fields: **hydraulic engineering**, that is, building on and with bodies of water; **hydrology**, the study of the water cycle; and **glaciology**, the study of glaciers. Its experts also advise the Confederation, cantons and power companies. In this way the VAW helps to protect Switzerland from floods and natural hazards.

In the large test hall, the VAW builds sections of rivers, weirs and spillways of dams as scaled-down **physical models**. In this way it can be tested whether a structure will safely carry away a large flood before it is built in reality. So that the models imitate nature correctly, they are usually scaled according to **Froude's model law**. According to this, speeds are converted using the square root of the scale: if water flows at 0.5 metres per second in a model on a scale of 1:100, in nature it flows at 5 metres per second.

Rivers carry not only water but also stones, gravel and sand; this is called **bedload**. In 1948 Eugen Meyer-Peter and Robert Müller at the VAW published a formula with which you can calculate how much bedload a river carries. The **Meyer-Peter and Müller formula** is still used around the world today. It helps, for example, in planning river restorations and in protecting against debris flows.

The VAW's glaciology section studies how glaciers grow, melt and move. Together with the Universities of Fribourg and Zurich, it runs the Swiss glacier monitoring network **GLAMOS**, which records the changes in the glaciers every year. The thickness of the ice is measured with **radar**: radar waves are sent out from the surface, reflected by the rock bed and received again. From the travel time, it is calculated how thick the ice is.

On steep **hanging glaciers**, parts can break off and crash down into the valley as ice avalanches. The VAW watches such glaciers with cameras and measuring instruments in order to detect dangerous movements early. In this way the authorities can close roads or warn villages in time. Because glaciers are shrinking as a result of climate change, such studies are becoming more and more important.

begriffe.erklaerung: Planning and building structures on bodies of water, for example dams and weirs.
The science of water and its cycle on Earth.
The science of glaciers and ice.
Stones, gravel and sand that a river drags along its bed.
The ratio between the size of a model and reality.

gewusst: A physical model of a river in the test hall can be many metres long.
Since 1850 Swiss glaciers have lost a large part of their volume.
GLAMOS stands for Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A weather forecast predicts what the weather will be like in the next hours and days. For this, experts collect measurements from all over the world and have supercomputers calculate the weather of the future. In Switzerland, the federal office MeteoSwiss is mainly responsible for this.
wichtigste: A weather forecast describes the expected weather for a particular place and period.
It is based on measurements from weather stations, radars, balloons and satellites.
Computers use weather models to calculate how the atmosphere will develop.
A forecast for the next few hours is called nowcasting.
A 30 per cent probability of precipitation means that it rains in 3 out of 10 similar cases.
The term butterfly effect goes back to the meteorologist Edward Lorenz.
MeteoSwiss runs five weather radars (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: A **weather forecast** or **prediction** states what temperatures, winds, clouds and precipitation are to be expected. For the next two to three days it is usually quite reliable today. The further you look into the future, the less certain it becomes. From about ten days onwards, usually only rough trends can be given.

For a good forecast you first need precise data about the current weather. Thousands of **weather stations** around the world measure temperature, air pressure, wind and humidity. **Weather balloons** take measurements at great heights, and weather satellites such as **Meteosat** observe the clouds from space. MeteoSwiss also runs five **weather radars** that detect rain and snow, for example on the Albis, La Dôle and Monte Lema.

A **weather model** divides the atmosphere into a grid of many small cubes. A supercomputer uses physical equations to calculate how air, heat and water change in each cube. Switzerland needs an especially fine calculation grid for this, so that mountains and valleys are represented accurately. Since 2024 MeteoSwiss has used the ICON model for this, with grid cells of about one kilometre.

In the 1960s the American meteorologist **Edward Lorenz** discovered that tiny differences at the beginning can change the weather greatly later on. This gave rise to the term **butterfly effect**. That is why weather services calculate many slightly changed versions and compare them. This produces figures such as a **probability of precipitation** of 30 per cent, which means that it rains in 3 out of 10 similar cases.

For the next few hours, **nowcasting** is used, which mainly projects radar and satellite images forward. In this way it is possible to warn, for example, when a thunderstorm will reach a particular village. In severe weather, MeteoSwiss sends out **warnings** with five danger levels. There are also monthly and seasonal forecasts, but they only say whether it will be warmer or colder than usual.

Before there were computers, people watched clouds, wind and animals to estimate the weather. This gave rise to traditional **weather sayings**, for example about Seven Sleepers' Day on 27 June. This saying claims that the weather on that day determines the weather of the following weeks. Some weather sayings have a grain of truth, but many are not reliable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A prediction of what will happen in the future.
A computer program that calculates how the weather will develop.
A very short-term forecast for the next few hours.
A device that uses radio waves to detect rain, snow and hail in the air.
The idea that tiny changes can have great consequences.

gewusst: A five-day forecast today is about as reliable as a forecast for a single day was around 1980.
The weather radar on the Weissfluhgipfel near Davos is at about 2800 metres above sea level.
As early as 1922 the Briton Lewis Fry Richardson tried to calculate the weather by hand using equations.

teile.einleitung: The cytoplasm is the entire contents of a cell inside the cell membrane, except for the nucleus. It consists of a jelly-like fluid and many tiny cell parts. Many vital processes of the cell take place here.
wichtigste: The cytoplasm includes everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus.
The fluid basic substance without the organelles is called cytosol.
Organelles are small cell parts with particular tasks.
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that supports the cell from the inside.
The endoplasmic reticulum is a system of channels made of membranes that transports substances.
Glycolysis, the first step in breaking down sugar, takes place in the cytoplasm.
In the leaves of waterweed you can see cytoplasmic streaming under the microscope.

abschnitte.text: The word **cytoplasm** comes from Greek and means roughly “cell formation”. It refers to the whole contents of a cell between the cell membrane and the nucleus. It consists of the basic fluid, the **cytosol**, and the **organelles** lying in it. In bacteria, which have no nucleus, the genetic material also lies directly in the cytoplasm.

The **cytosol** consists mostly of water. Salts, sugars, amino acids and a great many proteins are dissolved in it. That is why it is not runny like water but rather thick like a gel. Countless **enzymes** work in the cytosol, speeding up chemical reactions.

Many **organelles** lie in the cytoplasm, and they can be compared with the organs of the body. The mitochondria produce energy, and the ribosomes assemble proteins. The **endoplasmic reticulum** is a system of channels made of membranes that makes and transports substances. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large vacuole.

A network of fine protein fibres, the **cytoskeleton**, runs through the cytoplasm. It supports the cell from the inside, rather like tent poles support a tent. It also serves as a network of rails on which small vesicles and organelles are transported. During cell division it helps to share out the genetic material fairly between the two daughter cells.

The cytoplasm is constantly moving. In the leaf cells of **waterweed** you can watch under a light microscope how the green chloroplasts travel in a circle; this is called **cytoplasmic streaming**. The breakdown of sugar to obtain energy, **glycolysis**, also begins in the cytoplasm. The further steps then take place in the mitochondria.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fluid basic substance of the cytoplasm without the organelles.
A small cell part with a particular task.
A network of protein fibres that supports the cell and makes transport possible.
The first step in breaking down sugar to obtain energy.
The movement of the cell contents, which can be seen under the microscope.

gewusst: A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes in its cytoplasm.
Cytoplasmic streaming in plant cells gets faster if you shine a lamp on the cells or warm them slightly.
Human red blood cells have no nucleus at all and consist almost entirely of cytoplasm full of blood pigment.

teile.einleitung: Alpine solar plants are large photovoltaic installations built high up in the mountains. There the sun often shines above the fog even in winter, and the snow reflects extra light onto the panels. Switzerland is relying on such plants to produce more electricity for the winter.
wichtigste: Alpine solar plants supply much more winter electricity than installations on the Swiss Plateau.
Snow reflects a lot of sunlight onto the panels and increases production.
