Bifacial panels use the light on both the front and the back.
Cold makes the efficiency of solar cells rise.
The panels are often mounted very steeply so that snow slides off and the low winter sun is used well.
One of the first large alpine plants was built on the dam wall of the Muttsee in the canton of Glarus.
With the Solarexpress, Parliament decided in 2022 on temporary support for large alpine plants.

abschnitte.text: An **alpine solar plant** is a photovoltaic installation in the mountains, usually at over 1500 metres. It turns sunlight directly into electricity with **solar panels**. Some stand on open mountain meadows, others on dam walls or on avalanche barriers. In Switzerland they are regarded as an important building block of the energy transition.

On the Swiss Plateau high fog often lies for weeks in winter, and solar installations then supply little electricity. In the mountains the sun often shines above the **sea of fog**. In addition, the white snow reflects a lot of light; this reflectivity is called **albedo**. That is why alpine plants supply much more winter electricity. It is precisely in winter that Switzerland needs a particularly large amount of electricity and so far has had to import some of it.

Many alpine plants use **bifacial panels**, which catch light on both the front and the back. In this way the light reflected by the snow is also used. The panels are often mounted very steeply or even vertically. Then the snow slides off, and the low winter sun hits the surface well. In addition, the **efficiency** of solar cells rises in the cold, because they work better when cool.

One of Switzerland’s first large alpine solar plants was built on the dam wall of the **Muttsee** in the canton of Glarus. It lies at a height of around 2500 metres and was completed in 2022. Around 5000 panels hang there on the wall and together have an output of about 2.2 megawatts. The project is called AlpinSolar and was built by the energy companies Axpo and IWB.

In 2022 the Federal Parliament decided on temporary support for large alpine solar plants, the **Solarexpress**. After that many projects were planned, for example in Valais and the Grisons. Some, however, were rejected by the municipalities or made smaller. Critics fear that the landscape and nature will suffer, and building in the mountains is expensive. Supporters stress that Switzerland urgently needs more winter electricity.

How much power a plant supplies depends on its area, the solar radiation and its efficiency. You multiply the panel area by the radiation and the efficiency. With an area of 1000 m², radiation of 1000 W/m² and an efficiency of 20 per cent, this gives 200 kW. How much electricity is produced over the year also depends on the weather and the position of the sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direct conversion of sunlight into electricity.
A solar panel that turns light into electricity on both sides.
How strongly a surface reflects light; snow reflects a great deal.
Electricity produced in the winter half of the year, when demand is high.
What percentage of the incoming energy is turned into electricity.

gewusst: Solar cells work better in the cold than in the heat.
The plant at the Muttsee hangs vertically on a dam wall so that no snow settles on it.
Above the sea of fog the sun often shines for hours in winter while it is grey on the Swiss Plateau.

teile.einleitung: Science is the search for knowledge about the world using precise methods that can be checked. It explains, for example, why an apple falls from a tree or why water boils at 100 degrees. This chapter is about researchers, measuring instruments, laws of nature, substances, space and life.
wichtigste: Science searches for knowledge using methods that can be checked.
An apple falls down because of gravity.
At sea level water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
The natural sciences include physics, chemistry, biology and astronomy.
Measuring instruments such as thermometers, microscopes and telescopes make the invisible visible.
Researchers test their ideas with observations and experiments.
With ETH, EPFL and CERN, Switzerland is an important place for research.

abschnitte.text: In German the word for **science** means “creating knowledge”, and doing so in a careful way that can be checked. Researchers ask questions, observe, measure and carry out experiments. What they find out is published and checked by others. In this way an ever more accurate picture of the world gradually builds up.

**Physics** studies forces, energy, light and motion. **Chemistry** investigates substances and how they change, for example water with the formula H₂O. Biology deals with living things, from the cell to the elephant. Astronomy looks out into space, and geology studies the Earth and its rocks.

Why does an apple fall down from a tree? The answer is **gravity**, with which the Earth pulls everything towards itself. In 1687 the English scientist Isaac Newton described the law of gravitation in his famous book. According to a well-known story, a falling apple is said to have given him the idea. The same force also keeps the Moon in its orbit round the Earth.

At sea level water boils at 100 degrees Celsius and freezes at 0 degrees. Anders Celsius used these two points for his **temperature scale** in 1742. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there at lower temperatures. Fixed values like these make experiments comparable, no matter where in the world they take place.

With the **microscope** we see tiny cells and bacteria, and with the telescope distant stars and galaxies. Thermometers, voltmeters and seismographs measure temperature, voltage and earthquakes. Computers help to analyse huge amounts of data. Many discoveries only became possible once a new measuring instrument had been invented.

Switzerland is one of the strongest countries in the world for research. **ETH Zurich** was founded in 1855, and many Nobel Prize winners have studied or taught there. Albert Einstein published ground-breaking papers in Bern in 1905. At **CERN** near Geneva, founded in 1954, the World Wide Web was even invented in 1989.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule according to which processes in nature always happen in the same way.
A planned test used to check an idea.
The force with which bodies attract each other, for example the Earth an apple.
A reasoned guess that can be tested.

gewusst: On the Moon gravity is about six times weaker than on Earth, so you can jump much higher there.
On the summit of Mount Everest water boils at only around 70 degrees Celsius.
At CERN near Geneva is the LHC, the largest particle accelerator in the world; its ring is 27 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: The general theory of relativity is Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity from 1915. It explains gravitation not as an ordinary force but as the curving of space and time by masses. Without it, GPS devices would show wrong positions.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein published the general theory of relativity in 1915.
Masses curve space and time, and we feel this curvature as gravity.
According to the equivalence principle, gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart locally.
Clocks run more slowly in strong gravitational fields, so a little more slowly at sea level than on a high mountain.
Large masses bend light and can act as gravitational lenses.
The Swiss mathematician Marcel Grossmann helped Einstein with differential geometry.
The theory predicts black holes and gravitational waves.

abschnitte.text: Einstein imagined standing in a lift without windows. You could not tell whether the lift was standing on Earth or accelerating steadily upwards in space. This idea is called the **equivalence principle**. From it Einstein concluded that gravity is a property of **spacetime**. A popular comparison is a heavy ball on a stretched sheet: it makes a dip, and smaller balls roll towards it.

Einstein studied at ETH Zurich and worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909. There, in 1905, he developed the special theory of relativity. For the general theory he needed difficult mathematics. His friend from his student days, **Marcel Grossmann**, professor of mathematics at ETH, showed him the differential geometry he needed. In November 1915, in Berlin, Einstein presented his finished **field equations**. On one side they have the curvature of spacetime, on the other side, as its source, the energy-momentum tensor.

The first thing the theory explained was a small deviation in the orbit of the planet **Mercury**. In 1919 British researchers observed during a solar eclipse that starlight passing close to the sun is bent, as Einstein had predicted. Today we see **gravitational lenses**: large clusters of galaxies bend the light of galaxies behind them and show them distorted as arcs. Radar signals that travel close past the sun to a planet and back take a little longer than they would without the sun.

The theory says that time passes more slowly in strong gravitational fields. A clock at sea level therefore runs a little more slowly than a clock on a high mountain. Light travelling outwards from a strong gravitational field is **redshifted**. Around 1960 the Pound-Rebka experiment measured this redshift with gamma rays in a tower at Harvard University. GPS satellites have to take these effects into account; otherwise positions would be wrong by kilometres every day.

The theory leads to **black holes**, from which not even light can escape. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first image of the shadow of a black hole. In 2015 **gravitational waves** were measured for the first time, tiny ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging. The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for this in 2017.

Einstein also applied the theory to the whole universe. In 1917 he added the **cosmological constant** so that a static universe was possible. Later it turned out that the universe is expanding. Today such a constant is used again to describe the accelerating expansion of the universe. The general theory of relativity is therefore the basis of modern cosmology.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space and time thought of together as one four-dimensional structure.
The insight that gravity and acceleration feel the same on a small scale.
A large mass that bends light like a magnifying glass.
Light is shifted to longer wavelengths, that is, made redder.
Tiny ripples in spacetime that spread out at the speed of light.

gewusst: Einstein did not receive his Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity, but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
Because gravity is weaker up there, the clocks in GPS satellites run around 45 millionths of a second fast every day, which has to be corrected.
The first gravitational waves ever measured came from more than a billion light years away.

teile.einleitung: The WSL is the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research. It studies how the Swiss forest is doing, how avalanches form and how people can be protected from natural hazards. Its headquarters is in Birmensdorf in the canton of Zurich.
wichtigste: WSL stands for the German words for forest, snow and landscape (“Wald, Schnee und Landschaft”).
The WSL's headquarters is in Birmensdorf near Zurich.
The Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos is part of the WSL.
In winter the SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin every day.
Avalanche danger is divided into 5 danger levels.
Together with the Federal Office for the Environment, the WSL carries out the National Forest Inventory.
The WSL also studies debris flows and rockfall.

abschnitte.text: The WSL is a federal research institute and belongs to the **ETH Domain**, like ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. Its headquarters is in **Birmensdorf** in the canton of Zurich. There are other sites in Davos, Lausanne, Sion and Cadenazzo in Ticino, among other places. Its roots go back to 1885, when a forestry research station was founded. Today experts from biology, geography, physics and many other fields work there.

The **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in Davos is known worldwide. It studies how snow is built up, how a snowpack changes and when it slides off. On the **Weissfluhjoch** above Davos, the SLF has a test field where snow has been measured for decades. In addition there are automatic measuring stations throughout the Swiss Alps. The researchers also develop avalanche barriers and rescue methods.

In winter the SLF publishes the **avalanche bulletin** every day, which can be found on the internet and in the app “White Risk”. It shows on a map how great the avalanche danger is in the different regions. The scale has 5 levels: low, moderate, considerable, high and very high. Even at level 3, considerable, many avalanche accidents involving ski tourers happen. Anyone going off-piste should definitely read the bulletin beforehand.

Together with the Federal Office for the Environment, the WSL carries out the **National Forest Inventory**. Trees are counted and measured at thousands of sample points all over Switzerland. This shows which tree species are growing, how much wood grows back and whether the forest is healthy. The WSL also studies pests such as the bark beetle and the effects of drought on the trees. In the mountains the forest is especially important, because as **protection forest** it shields villages from avalanches and rockfall.

Besides avalanches, the WSL studies other **natural hazards** such as debris flows, rockfall, rockslides and floods. A debris flow is a fast stream of water, mud and stones that shoots down a stream bed. In the Illgraben in Valais, the WSL runs a well-known measuring station for debris flows. With their findings, the researchers help communes to draw up hazard maps and plan protective structures. Because of climate change, permafrost is thawing, which is why this research is becoming more and more important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A daily report that warns of avalanche danger in the mountains.
A fast stream of water, mud and rock in a stream bed.
A forest that protects settlements and roads from natural hazards.
A large count and survey of the whole Swiss forest.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: Snow has been measured regularly on the Weissfluhjoch since the 1930s.
The SLF studies not only snow but also, for example, how glaciers and permafrost are changing.
A large part of the Swiss forest is protection forest and shields villages, roads and railway lines from natural hazards.

teile.einleitung: In physics, absorption means that a substance takes in light, heat radiation or sound and, so to speak, swallows it. A red apple, for example, looks red because it reflects red light and swallows the other colours. The energy taken in does not disappear, but is usually turned into heat.
wichtigste: Absorption means taking in or swallowing radiation or sound.
A red apple reflects red light and swallows the other colours.
The opposite of absorption is reflection, throwing back.
The absorbed energy is usually turned into heat.
Black objects swallow almost all light and get especially warm in the sun.
Plants absorb red and blue light and therefore look green.
Sound can also be absorbed, for example by curtains or foam.

abschnitte.text: White sunlight is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. When it hits an object, some of the colours are **absorbed** and some are **reflected**. We only see the colours that are thrown back into our eyes. A red apple swallows green and blue and reflects red. A white sheet of paper reflects all colours, while a black T-shirt swallows almost all of them.

When a substance absorbs light, it takes in its **energy**. This energy makes the particles of the substance move more strongly, and it gets warmer. That is why a black car heats up much more in the sun than a white one. In summer people therefore like to wear light-coloured clothes. **Solar collectors** on house roofs are dark so that they take in as much of the sun’s heat as possible.

Plants contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**. It mainly absorbs red and blue light and uses the energy for photosynthesis. Green light is reflected, which is why leaves look green. The **ozone layer** in the atmosphere absorbs a large part of the sun’s dangerous UV radiation. Without it, life on land would hardly be possible.

**Sound waves** can also be absorbed. Soft and porous materials such as carpets, curtains, upholstered furniture or foam swallow sound especially well. That is why special wall panels are fitted in recording studios and concert halls. In an empty room with bare walls, on the other hand, there is a strong echo. Fresh snow also swallows a lot of sound, which is why a snowy landscape seems so quiet.

**Sunglasses** absorb part of the visible light and above all UV rays, which can damage the eyes. Sun cream contains substances that swallow or reflect UV radiation. In a microwave oven the water in the food absorbs the microwaves and gets hot. Researchers use the absorption of light to measure which substances a sample contains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The taking in of light, heat radiation or sound by a substance.
The throwing back of light or sound at a surface.
A green pigment in plants that takes in light for photosynthesis.
A layer in the atmosphere that swallows harmful UV radiation.

gewusst: The blackest artificial material swallows over 99.9 per cent of light and makes objects look like flat holes.
The sky is blue because the air scatters blue light more strongly than red.
Glacier ice looks blue because thick ice absorbs red light a little more strongly than blue.

teile.einleitung: Vaporisation is when a liquid turns into a gas, for example when water turns into water vapour. This happens in a pan when cooking, but also quite silently when a puddle dries up. Vaporisation is one of the most important processes in nature.
wichtigste: Vaporisation means that a liquid turns into a gas.
When water turns into water vapour, it is called vaporisation.
If it happens at the boiling point, it is called boiling.
If it happens below the boiling point, it is called evaporation.
Vaporisation needs energy, usually in the form of heat.
The reverse process is called condensation.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be solid, liquid or gaseous; these are the **states of matter**. In vaporisation, a substance changes from liquid to gas. The tiny particles move so fast that they break away from one another and fly off. Real **water vapour** is actually invisible; the white puffs above the saucepan are already tiny water droplets again.

If you heat water to its **boiling point**, bubbles of vapour form throughout the pan; it boils. At sea level, the boiling point of water is 100 degrees Celsius. But water can also turn into vapour at lower temperatures; this is called **evaporation**. In this case only individual particles break away at the surface, for example when washing dries.

The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure. That is why water boils at lower temperatures in the mountains. On the Jungfraujoch, at about 3450 metres, water boils at just under 89 degrees. Pasta and eggs take longer to cook there, which is why a **pressure cooker** is sometimes used.

The sun makes water evaporate from seas, lakes and plants. The water vapour rises, cools high up and **condenses** into clouds. Rain or snow falls from the clouds and flows back into rivers and lakes. This never-ending cycle is called the **water cycle**.

To vaporise, a liquid needs **energy**, and it takes this from its surroundings. That is why sweat cools our skin when it evaporates. It is also why you feel cold when you come out of the swimming pool wet. Fridges use the same effect with a special liquid that vaporises in pipes.

Water vapour takes up much more space than liquid water and can therefore produce great forces. This is the basis of the **steam engine**, which James Watt decisively improved in the 18th century. Steam locomotives used to run on many Swiss lines too, and they still do today, for example on the Brienz Rothorn Railway. In power stations, steam drives large turbines that produce electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The temperature at which a liquid boils.
Slow vaporisation below the boiling point.
The change from gas to liquid, for example when a mirror steams up.

gewusst: When one litre of water vaporises, it turns into more than 1600 litres of water vapour.
Ice can also turn directly into vapour without melting first; this is called sublimation.
On a hot summer's day, a large tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water through its leaves.

teile.einleitung: In bird ringing, a bird is given a small ring with a number on its leg. If the bird is later found somewhere, the number reveals where it comes from. In this way researchers find out where birds fly to, how old they get and how they are doing.
wichtigste: A ringed bird wears a small ring with a number and an address on its leg.
Ringing shows where birds migrate to and how old they get.
Only trained experts with a permit are allowed to ring birds.
Small birds are caught with fine nets and released again immediately afterwards.
Often their weight and wing length are measured as well.
In Switzerland, the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach is the central office for ring recoveries.

abschnitte.text: A **bird ring** is a light ring, usually made of aluminium, that sits loosely on the leg. It carries a unique number and the address of an **ornithological institute**. Rings come in many sizes, from tiny rings for a goldcrest to large rings for a swan. The ring does not bother the bird when it flies or eats.

Small birds are caught with fine **mist nets**, which are stretched almost invisibly between poles. Experts carefully free the birds and put the ring on them. At the same time they often measure the weight and wing length and estimate the age and fat reserves. Straight afterwards the bird is released again. The whole thing takes only a few minutes.

When a ringed bird is found or caught again in another place, this is called a **ring recovery**. From many ring recoveries the **migration routes** of migratory birds can be worked out, for example that Swiss storks spend the winter in Spain or Africa. We also find out how old birds get and how many young birds survive. This data helps to protect endangered species.

The founder of scientific bird ringing is considered to be the Danish teacher **Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen**. In 1899 he ringed starlings with rings that carried a number and his address. Soon researchers in many countries joined in. Today millions of birds are ringed in Europe every year, and the data is analysed jointly.

In Switzerland, ringing is coordinated by the **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne. It was founded in 1924. Anyone who wants to ring birds needs training and a permit. The ringing station on the Col de Bretolet in Valais is well known; in autumn many migratory birds fly over the Alps there.

If you find a dead bird with a ring, you report the **ring number** to the ornithological institute. It is best also to note the place where it was found, the date and, if possible, the species of bird. Today this can easily be done online. As thanks, you are usually told where and when the bird was ringed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The report of a ringed bird that has turned up again somewhere.
A bird that flies to warmer areas in autumn and returns in spring.
A very fine net with which small birds are caught gently.
A research centre that observes, studies and protects birds.

gewusst: A Laysan albatross called Wisdom was ringed in 1956 and was still laying eggs at over 70 years old.
The ring is chosen so that it does not slip off but does not pinch either.

teile.einleitung: Zoology is the science that studies animals. It investigates how animals are built, how they live and behave and how they are related to each other. Experts in this science are called zoologists.
wichtigste: Zoology is the science of animals.
The name comes from the Greek “zoon” for living being or animal.
It is a branch of biology.
There are many specialist fields, such as the study of birds or the study of insects.
Carl Linnaeus ordered the animals with two-part scientific names.
In the 16th century, Conrad Gessner from Zurich wrote a great book of animals.

abschnitte.text: Alongside botany, the study of plants, **zoology** is a large part of **biology**. The word is made up of the Greek words “zoon” for living being and “logos” for study. Zoologists study all animals, from the tiniest worm to the blue whale. So far well over a million animal species have been described, and thousands of new ones are added every year.

Because there are so many animals, many specialist fields have developed. **Ornithology** studies birds, **entomology** insects and ichthyology fish. Behavioural research, or ethology, studies why animals behave as they do. Other fields deal with the body structure, distribution or development of animals.

More than 2300 years ago the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** observed many animals closely and described them. From 1551 the Zurich scholar **Conrad Gessner** published his great book of animals, “Historia animalium”, with many woodcuts. In 1758 the Swede Carl Linnaeus introduced two-part scientific names, such as Canis lupus for the wolf. In 1859 Charles Darwin explained with his theory of evolution how animal species change over long periods of time.

Many zoologists watch animals outdoors in nature, often for months. They count populations, catch animals to ring them or fit them with transmitters. In the laboratory they study body structure or **genetic material**. Natural history museums keep millions of specimens with which species can be compared.

At Swiss universities, zoology is usually studied as part of biology. **Zurich Zoo**, which opened in 1929, takes part in research and in protection programmes for endangered animal species. The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach has been studying the country's birds since 1924. The Natural History Museum in Bern shows, among other things, the famous St Bernard dog Barry.

Zoology helps us understand which animals are endangered and how they can be protected. This knowledge is important for **species protection**, for example in the return of the bearded vulture and the lynx to the Alps. Research on animals also helps medicine, for example in understanding diseases that are passed on by animals. And it shows us how varied and amazing life on Earth is.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of plants.
The science of birds.
The science of insects.
The study of animal behaviour.
A group of living things of the same kind that belong together.

gewusst: More than half of all described animal species are insects.
In his book of animals, Conrad Gessner described not only real animals but also mythical creatures such as the unicorn.
Experts estimate that a large proportion of the animal species on Earth have not yet been discovered at all.

teile.einleitung: If you bathe or swim for a long time, your fingers and toes go wrinkly. In German this wrinkled skin is called “Waschhaut” (washing skin). The surprising thing is that the wrinkling does not simply come from softening but is controlled by the body itself through the nerves.
wichtigste: After a long bath, fingers and toes go wrinkly.
In warm water, the wrinkling starts after about 5 minutes.
The wrinkling is controlled by the nerves.
The blood vessels in the fingertips become narrower.
The skin wrinkles most on fingers and toes.
Wrinkly fingers might help you to grip wet things better.
After the bath, the fingers soon become smooth again.
Monkeys such as macaques also get wrinkly fingers in water.

abschnitte.text: Wrinkly fingers are the creased, puckered skin on fingertips and toes after a long time in contact with water. It is harmless and disappears again by itself. Doctors also call this **water-induced wrinkling**. In everyday language people simply say their fingers have gone “pruney”.

For a long time people thought that the skin simply soaked up water and swelled like a sponge. Today we know that the **nervous system** controls the wrinkling. The nerves give the signal for the **blood vessels** in the fingertips to narrow. As a result, the tissue under the skin becomes smaller, and the upper layer of skin folds into wrinkles.

abschnitte.titel: Proof that the nerves are involved
abschnitte.text: Almost a hundred years ago, doctors noticed something: if a nerve in a finger was injured, that finger did not wrinkle in water. Later this was even used as a simple **test** to check whether the nerves in a hand were working properly. This showed clearly that wrinkling is not a purely passive process. It is an active reaction of the body.

Researchers suspect that wrinkly fingers help with **gripping** in the wet. The wrinkles could channel water away, similar to the **tread** of a car tyre on a wet road. In an experiment in England, people with wrinkly fingers were able to sort wet marbles more quickly. But whether this really is the reason is still being researched.

It is not only humans who get wrinkly fingers. Monkeys such as **macaques** also get wrinkly fingers when they are in water for a long time. Japanese macaques even bathe in hot springs in winter. This suggests that this ability is already old in evolutionary history.

In warm water the first wrinkles appear after about **5 minutes**. In cold water it usually takes longer. After drying off, the fingers become smooth again within a short time. The skin on the palms and soles of the feet is thicker and has especially many nerve connections, which is why it wrinkles most clearly there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Creased skin on fingers and toes after a long time in contact with water; in German “Waschhaut”.
A tube in the body through which blood flows, for example a vein.
The network of nerves and the brain that passes on signals in the body.
The grooves in a tyre or the sole of a shoe that provide grip.

gewusst: A finger with a severed nerve stays smooth in water.
The wrinkles often form patterns similar to river channels that drain water away.
Japanese macaques bathe in hot springs in winter and also get wrinkly fingers.

teile.einleitung: William Harvey was an English doctor who discovered the circulation of the blood in the 17th century. He showed that the heart drives the blood through the body in a closed circuit like a pump. His discovery changed medicine fundamentally.
wichtigste: William Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood.
In 1628 he published his work on the movement of the heart and blood.
He disproved the old idea that blood is constantly made anew in the liver.
His most important argument: the heart pumps more blood than food could supply.
The valves in the veins only let the blood flow towards the heart.
Harvey could not yet see the finest blood vessels, the capillaries.
He studied medicine in Padua and was physician at the English royal court.

abschnitte.text: William Harvey lived from 1578 to 1657 and came from Folkestone in the south of England. After studying in Cambridge, he went to the famous University of **Padua** in Italy to study medicine. After that he worked as a doctor in London. Later he became **royal physician** to the English kings James I and Charles I.

For more than 1400 years, doctors followed the teachings of the Roman doctor **Galen**. According to these, the **liver** constantly made new blood from food. The blood was then supposed to be used up in the body, like water that seeps into the ground. A circulation was unknown.

Harvey examined carefully how much blood the heart pumps out with each beat. He calculated that in one hour the heart pumps more blood than a person weighs. So much blood cannot possibly be made constantly from food. That is why he concluded that the blood must flow round and round in a **circuit**.

Harvey described the **heart** as a muscle that works like a pump. He studied the **valves in the veins**, which his teacher in Padua had already described. With simple experiments on the arm, he showed that these valves only let blood flow towards the heart. In the **arteries**, on the other hand, the blood flows away from the heart.

In 1628 Harvey published his findings in a book in Latin. Its short title is “De motu cordis”, which means “On the Motion of the Heart”. Many doctors rejected his ideas at first, because they contradicted the old teaching. Over time, however, Harvey's discovery was accepted.

Harvey could not explain how the blood gets from the arteries into the veins. The tiny **capillaries** that connect the two could not be seen with the naked eye. Only a few years after his death did the Italian Marcello Malpighi discover them with the microscope. This fully proved Harvey's circulation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The route by which blood flows from the heart through the body and back again.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart.
A hair-thin blood vessel that connects arteries and veins.
The personal doctor of a king or an important person.

gewusst: For his research, Harvey examined the hearts of many different animals, even of fish and snails.
His famous book was not published in England but in Frankfurt am Main.
Only the microscope made visible the capillaries that Harvey could only suspect.

teile.einleitung: Comparing means putting two or more things side by side and looking for similarities and differences. In science, comparison is one of the most important methods of all. If you compare carefully, you measure rather than estimate and record your results neatly.
wichtigste: When comparing, you look for what is the same and what is different.
Measuring is more accurate than estimating, so you measure when comparing.
You compare weights with scales and lengths with a ruler.
In a fair test you change only one single thing.
A table helps you compare many measurements clearly.
Language also has forms of comparison such as big, bigger, biggest.

abschnitte.text: When **comparing**, you look closely at two or more things. You ask: what is the same, and what is different? An apple and a pear, for example, are both fruits but have a different shape. Comparisons help us to sort things and understand them.

Our eyes often deceive us, so when comparing we **measure**. With a **ruler** you compare the length of two leaves, and with **scales** the weight of two stones. With a stopwatch you can compare times. If one snail crawls 10 cm and another 15 cm, then the second crawled 5 cm further.

In research, two groups that differ in only one respect are often compared. An example: two pots of cress stand at the same window; one is watered, the other is not. In this way you compare growth with and without water. The group in which you change nothing is called the **control group**. If you also changed the position at the same time, you would no longer know what caused the difference.

If you have many measurements, a **table** helps. In it the values stand clearly side by side. It becomes even clearer with a **chart**, such as a bar chart. An ice cube that melts in 10 minutes in the sun and in 25 minutes in the shade can be shown well in this way.

We also compare all the time in language. For this there are the **degrees of comparison** of adjectives: high, higher, highest. A tree 21 m tall is higher than one 12 m tall. Vivid comparisons with “as” or “like” bring texts to life, for example “as fast as the wind”.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group in an experiment in which nothing is changed, so that you can compare.
A number with a unit that you get when you measure, for example 15 cm.
A measuring instrument with marks for reading off lengths accurately.
The one thing that you deliberately change in an experiment.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece, scholars compared animals and plants in order to sort them into groups.
In medicine, scientists often compare a real medicine with a tablet that has no effect, a placebo.

teile.einleitung: The adiabatic lapse rate describes how strongly a rising or sinking parcel of air cools down or warms up. Dry air cools by about 1 degree per 100 metres as it rises, while moist, saturated air cools more slowly. With this knowledge you can explain clouds, thunderstorms and the foehn in the Alps.
wichtigste: “Adiabatic” means that a parcel of air exchanges no heat with its surroundings.
When air rises, it expands because of the falling air pressure and cools down in the process.
Dry air cools by about 1 °C per 100 metres; this is the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
Saturated air cools more slowly, because heat is released when water vapour condenses.
At the height of the condensation level the air becomes saturated and clouds form.
The dry adiabatic lapse rate comes from the acceleration due to gravity and the specific heat capacity of air.
A layer of air in which the temperature rises with height is called an inversion.

abschnitte.text: Meteorologists often imagine an **air parcel**, a kind of invisible balloon of air that rises or sinks. **Adiabatic** means that this parcel exchanges no heat with its surroundings as it moves. Even so, its temperature changes, because the pressure changes. If it rises, it expands and cools; if it sinks, it is squeezed together and warms up, rather like a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump.

For dry air the cooling is around 1 °C per 100 metres; this is the **dry adiabatic lapse rate**. It comes from the acceleration due to gravity divided by the specific heat capacity of air. If a dry air parcel rises, for example, from 500 to 2500 metres, it cools from 20 °C to 0 °C. Saturated air, on the other hand, only cools by about 0.4 to 0.7 °C per 100 metres; this is the **moist adiabatic lapse rate**.

As it rises, the air keeps cooling until it cannot hold any more water vapour. This height is called the **condensation level**, and the first cloud droplets form there. You can see this height directly in the sky at the flat bottom of heap clouds. When water vapour condenses, heat is released, so the air then cools more slowly and can rise further, sometimes into a tall thundercloud.

Whether air rises depends on how quickly the temperature of the surroundings falls with height. If it falls more slowly than the moist adiabatic rate, a rising air parcel soon becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back; the layering is **absolutely stable**. If it falls faster, the air keeps on rising; the layering is unstable and thunderstorms can form. In an **inversion** it even gets warmer with height, as with the high fog over the Swiss Plateau in winter.

A well-known example is the **foehn** in the Alps. With a south foehn, moist air rises on the southern side of the Alps, cools first at the dry and then at the moist adiabatic rate, and loses its moisture as rain over Ticino. On the northern side the now dry air sinks and warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres. That is why it arrives in valleys such as the Reuss valley near Altdorf or the Rhine valley much warmer than it was at the same height in the south.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imagined amount of air whose path and temperature are followed.
Without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
The height at which rising air is saturated and clouds form.
A layer of air in which the temperature rises with height instead of falling.
A warm, dry wind blowing down the sheltered side of a mountain range.

gewusst: The flat bottoms of fair-weather clouds, all at the same height, show exactly where the condensation level is.
With a strong foehn, the northern edge of the Alps can suddenly feel as warm as spring in winter.
On average the temperature in the atmosphere falls by about 0.65 °C per 100 metres, which is less than the dry adiabatic rate.

teile.einleitung: A weathercock is a wind vane in the shape of a cockerel that turns in the wind on church towers and roofs. It shows which direction the wind is blowing from. Because the weather often changes with the wind, it also gives a clue about the weather to come.
wichtigste: A weathercock is a wind vane in the shape of a cockerel.
It often sits on a church tower.
The wind pushes it round until it points in the direction of the wind.
Its head points to where the wind is coming from.
Under the cockerel there are often the letters N, O, S and W for the points of the compass.
The O stands for “Osten”, the German word for east.
Wind vanes have existed since ancient times.

abschnitte.text: A weathercock is a special **wind vane**. It is usually made of metal such as copper or iron and sits on a rod so that it can turn. It is found above all on **church towers**, but also on town halls, farmhouses and barns. It is often gilded and gleams in the sun.

The cockerel is built so that its tail has a larger surface than its head. The wind presses harder against the large surface and pushes the tail away from it. As a result, the cockerel turns until its head points straight into the wind. In this way you can read off which **wind direction** the wind is blowing from.

Under many weathercocks there is a fixed cross with letters. They stand for the four **points of the compass**: N for north, O for “Osten” (east), S for south and W for west. If the cockerel's head points to W, a **west wind** is blowing. In Switzerland, a west wind often brings damp air and rain, while the bise from the north-east usually brings dry, cool weather.

The cockerel crows in the morning and wakes people up, which is why it is regarded as a sign of **watchfulness**. In the Bible, a cockerel crows after the apostle Peter has denied Jesus, so the cockerel reminds Christians of repentance and turning back to God. That is why, since the Middle Ages, people have liked to put cockerels on church towers. In Switzerland you often see the cockerel on Reformed churches, and more often a cross on Catholic ones.

Wind vanes already existed in **ancient times**. On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, which was built more than 2000 years ago, a figure of the sea god Triton turned in the wind. Since the Middle Ages, weathercocks have been widespread in Europe. Today weather stations measure the wind more precisely, but the old weathercocks have remained popular decorations.

Someone who keeps changing their opinion depending on what is popular at the moment is sometimes called a **weathervane**, in German “Wetterfahne”. The comparison fits, because the cockerel also turns with every wind. Similarly, in German people say that someone hangs their little flag according to the wind. These expressions are not meant kindly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that turns and shows the wind direction.
The direction the wind is coming from.
North, east, south or west.
A cold, dry wind from the north-east in Switzerland.

gewusst: A west wind comes from the west and blows towards the east, so the name always says where the wind comes from.
Some weathercocks on church towers are several hundred years old and have been repaired again and again.
On English wind vanes, instead of the German O for “Osten”, there is an E for east.

teile.einleitung: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895. With these invisible rays you can look inside the body and make bones visible, for example. For his discovery he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
wichtigste: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
He lived from 1845 to 1923.
He studied in Zurich at today's ETH.
He made the discovery in Würzburg in Germany.
He himself called them X-rays.
In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
He did not patent his discovery, so that everyone could use it.

abschnitte.text: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was born on 27 March 1845 in Lennep, which today is part of the town of Remscheid in Germany. He grew up partly in the Netherlands. He died in Munich on 10 February 1923. Röntgen was a careful, modest researcher who preferred working in the **laboratory** to being in the limelight.

Because he lacked a school-leaving certificate in the Netherlands, Röntgen went to Zurich. From 1865 he studied mechanical engineering there at the **Federal Polytechnic**, today's ETH Zurich. In 1869 he received his doctorate from the University of Zurich. In Zurich he also met his future wife, Anna Bertha Ludwig, and all his life he liked to spend his holidays in the Engadine, especially in Pontresina.

On 8 November 1895, in Würzburg, Röntgen was experimenting with a **cathode ray tube** that he had covered with black cardboard. Suddenly a screen lying far away in the room began to glow. He realised that invisible rays were passing through the cardboard. Because he did not know what they were, he called them **X-rays**.

Shortly before Christmas 1895, Röntgen took a picture of his wife's hand. On it you could clearly see her **bones** and her wedding ring. Soon afterwards he published his discovery, and it spread around the world at tremendous speed. Only a few weeks later, doctors were using the rays to examine broken bones.

In 1901 the **Nobel Prize** was awarded for the first time, and Röntgen received the prize for physics. He donated the prize money to his university for research. He did without a patent, because the discovery was meant to serve all people. In many countries the rays are nevertheless named after him, as “Röntgenstrahlen” in German, for example, but in English they are still called X-rays today.

**X-rays** are among the most important tools in medicine, for example at the dentist's or for broken bones. Computed tomography is also based on them. At the airport, luggage is scanned with them, and researchers use them to study crystals and works of art. Because the rays are harmful in large amounts, people protect themselves with lead aprons during X-rays.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible, high-energy rays that pass through soft materials and make bones visible.
One of the most famous awards in the world, for science, literature and peace.
A right that protects an invention for a certain time.
A glass tube without air in which electrons fly through when current flows.

gewusst: Chemical element number 111 is called roentgenium in Röntgen's honour.
In his will, Röntgen wrote that many of his notes were to be burnt after his death.
Shortly after the discovery, some shoe shops offered to X-ray people's feet in their shoes.

teile.einleitung: Weather observation means looking at the weather closely, measuring it and writing it down. Any child can do this with simple means, for example with a thermometer and a weather log. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss observe the weather with many measuring instruments around the clock.
wichtigste: A list in which you write down the weather every day is called a weather log.
A thermometer for the air temperature is hung in the shade.
It is best to measure at the same time every day, so that you can compare the days.
An anemometer shows how strongly the wind is blowing.
You can see whether it is cloudy by looking at the sky.
With a rain gauge you measure how much precipitation has fallen.
From many observations you can recognise patterns and differences.

abschnitte.text: In weather observation, you pay attention to **temperature**, clouds, wind and precipitation. You can observe with your own senses or determine exact values with measuring instruments. It is important to write everything down carefully. Only when you compare many days do you notice changes.

In a **weather log** you note the date, time, temperature, cloud cover, wind and precipitation every day. You can also draw symbols for the weather, for example a sun or a rain cloud. An example: if in one week there was rain on 2 days, then it stayed dry on 5 days. From the numbers you can later draw charts and find the warmest or wettest day.

A **thermometer** for the air temperature is hung in the shade, because otherwise the sun heats it up as well. It should hang at about eye level and not directly on a warm house wall. You measure at the **same time** every day, for example at midday, so that the values can be compared. If it is 10 degrees on Monday, 14 degrees on Tuesday and 12 degrees on Wednesday, Tuesday was the warmest.

For cloud cover, you look at the **sky** and estimate how much of it is covered with clouds. Experts divide the sky into eight parts for this, called oktas. A **wind gauge**, also called an anemometer, shows how strongly the wind is blowing, and a wind vane shows the direction. A **rain gauge** collects the precipitation, which is given in millimetres.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** is responsible for weather observation. It runs a dense network of automatic weather stations, weather radars and a balloon launch site at Payerne. On the **Säntis**, weather data has been collected since the 19th century. Many volunteers also measure, for example, the precipitation every day.

Precise observations are the basis of every **weather forecast**. If you know what the weather is like now, you can calculate better what it will be like tomorrow. Long series of measurements over many decades also show how the climate is changing. For farmers, mountain guides and pilots, weather data is especially important in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A list in which you regularly write down the weather.
An instrument that measures temperature.
A wind gauge that measures wind speed.
Water that falls from the sky, for example rain, snow or hail.

gewusst: A glass with straight sides and a ruler are enough to build a simple rain gauge.
Many weather sayings arose from centuries of weather observation.
One millimetre of rain means that one litre of water has fallen on every square metre.

teile.einleitung: A hydrometer is a measuring instrument used to find the density of a liquid. It looks like a glass thermometer with a thick, weighted bulb and floats upright in the liquid. Depending on how deep it sinks, you can read off the density on a scale.
wichtigste: A hydrometer measures the density of liquids.
In German it is also known as a “sinking spindle”.
In a liquid with a higher density it sinks less deeply.
That is why the larger density values are at the bottom of the scale.
A weighted bulb at the bottom, for example with lead shot, makes it float upright.
Winemakers use it to measure the must weight in degrees Oechsle.
An alcoholmeter is a hydrometer that shows the alcohol content.

abschnitte.text: The **hydrometer** is a floating measuring instrument made of glass. At the top it has a thin neck with a scale, and at the bottom a thick body with a weight. In German it is also called a **sinking spindle**. The weight, often lead shot, makes it float upright and steadily in the liquid.

The hydrometer uses **buoyancy**, which Archimedes already described in ancient times. A floating body sinks until it pushes aside as much liquid as it weighs itself. In a liquid with a high **density** it does not need to sink as deep to do this. That is why the hydrometer sticks out further in dense liquids. The larger density values are therefore at the bottom of the stem, and the smaller ones at the top.

At the grape harvest, winemakers measure how much sugar there is in the grape juice. The more sugar, the higher the density of the must. In Switzerland the **must weight** is given in **degrees Oechsle**. A must of 80 degrees Oechsle, for example, has a density of 1.080 g/cm³. The unit is named after the German inventor Ferdinand Oechsle from Pforzheim.

An **alcoholmeter** is a hydrometer that shows the alcohol content of a mixture of water and alcohol. This works because alcohol has a lower density than water. In the past hydrometers were also used to check how well charged the lead-acid batteries in cars were. The fuller the battery, the denser the acid inside it. The density of milk, sea water or antifreeze can also be measured in this way.

The idea is very old. As early as around the year 400, the Greek scholar Synesius of Cyrene described such an instrument in a letter to the mathematician **Hypatia**. Later it was improved again and again and given various scales. Today there are also electronic density meters, but the simple hydrometer is cheap and needs no electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example in grams per cubic centimetre.
The force with which a liquid pushes an object in it upwards.
A unit for the must weight of grape juice.
Another name for the hydrometer in German.

gewusst: In salty sea water a hydrometer floats higher than in fresh water.
The number in degrees Oechsle corresponds to the decimal places of the density: 80 degrees means 1.080 g/cm³.
Home brewers also use a hydrometer to measure how much of the sugar in their beer has already fermented.

teile.einleitung: Absolute zero is the lowest temperature that can exist at all. It is 0 kelvin, which is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. It cannot get colder, and it can never be reached exactly either.
wichtigste: Absolute zero is 0 kelvin or minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
In Fahrenheit it corresponds to minus 459.67 degrees.
As a substance approaches absolute zero, the movement of its particles becomes almost zero.
In the laboratory you can only get very close to absolute zero, but never reach it exactly.
A temperature of minus 300 degrees Celsius is physically impossible.
The background radiation in space is only about 2.7 kelvin warm.
At normal pressure helium stays liquid even close to absolute zero.

abschnitte.text: **Temperature** is a measure of how strongly the smallest particles of a substance are moving. The colder a substance is, the more slowly its atoms and molecules jiggle. At **absolute zero** this movement would be as small as the laws of nature allow at all. That is why nothing can be colder. A temperature of minus 300 degrees Celsius is therefore impossible.

Scientists measure low temperatures in **kelvin**, abbreviated K. The scale starts at absolute zero, so there are no negative kelvin values. One kelvin step is the same size as one degree Celsius. That is why 0 K corresponds exactly to minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, and water freezes at about 273 K. The unit is named after the British physicist William Thomson, who was later called **Lord Kelvin** and proposed an absolute temperature scale in 1848.

Back in the 18th and 19th centuries researchers observed that a **gas** gets smaller and smaller as it cools at constant pressure. For each degree of cooling it shrinks by about one 273rd of its volume at 0 degrees Celsius. If you carry on calculating, the volume would become zero at about minus 273 degrees. This led to the idea of a lowest possible temperature. Real gases, however, turn liquid or solid before that.

A law of nature, the **third law of thermodynamics**, says that absolute zero can never be reached completely. With laser cooling and other tricks, however, researchers have got within tiny fractions of a kelvin. In 1995 they used this to create the first **Bose-Einstein condensate**, a special state of matter in which many atoms behave like a single giant atom. At normal pressure helium even stays liquid close to absolute zero and below about 2.2 kelvin it can flow without any friction. This state is called superfluidity.

Even space is not quite that cold: the **background radiation** from the early days of the universe is about 2.7 kelvin. Some substances conduct electricity with no resistance at all at very low temperatures; this is called **superconductivity**. At CERN near Geneva the magnets of the large particle accelerator LHC are cooled to about 1.9 kelvin so that they become superconducting. MRI scanners in hospitals also use superconducting magnets cooled with liquid helium. Quantum computers also work at temperatures just above absolute zero.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero.
When a substance conducts electricity with no resistance at all in great cold.
A state of matter in which ultra-cold atoms behave like a single particle.
Weak radiation from the early days of the universe that fills the whole of space.

gewusst: The magnets of the LHC at CERN are colder than empty space.
The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded in 2001 for making the first Bose-Einstein condensate.
At normal pressure helium does not become solid even at absolute zero; that also needs high pressure.

teile.einleitung: The International Prototype of the Kilogram is a small metal cylinder that for 130 years defined exactly how heavy a kilogram is. Ultimately, all the scales in the world were based on it. Since 2019 it has no longer been needed for this, because the kilogram is now defined by a constant of nature.
wichtigste: The International Prototype of the Kilogram is a cylinder made of platinum and iridium.
It is kept by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris.
Its nickname is “Grand K”.
It lies protected under three glass bell jars.
Originally a kilogram was meant to weigh as much as a litre of water.
Because its mass changed slightly, it was replaced by a new definition.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined using the Planck constant.

abschnitte.text: The **International Prototype of the Kilogram**, in German “Urkilogramm”, is a shiny **cylinder** about 39 millimetres high and just as wide. It consists of 90 per cent platinum and 10 per cent iridium, a very hard and durable mixture. From 1889 to 2019 its mass was, by definition, exactly one kilogram. Because of its English name, it was given the nickname **Grand K**.

At the time of the French Revolution, people wanted to create units of measurement based on nature. A kilogram was meant to weigh as much as **one litre of water**. Because the density of water varies slightly with temperature and was difficult to measure precisely, a kilogram was made of platinum as early as 1799. In 1889 today's prototype was then declared the worldwide standard.

The prototype lies in a safe at the **International Bureau of Weights and Measures** in Sèvres near Paris. It stands under **three glass bell jars**, which protect it from dust and air. It was only rarely taken out to compare it with copies. Many countries received their own copies, by which they calibrated their weights; in Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, is responsible for this.

During the comparisons, it was found that the prototype and its copies had changed relative to one another by up to about 50 micrograms. That is roughly as much as a small grain of sand, but too much for science. Whether the prototype had become lighter or the copies heavier could not be said, because the prototype was by definition always exactly one kilogram. That is why a definition was sought that can never change.

Since 20 May 2019 the kilogram has been defined by the **Planck constant**, an unchanging **constant of nature** from quantum physics. With very precise instruments such as the **Kibble balance**, a kilogram can be determined from it anywhere in the world. At the same time, other base units such as the ampere and the kelvin were also redefined using constants. Since then the prototype has been a historical museum piece, but it is still carefully kept.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first, authoritative example of something.
A number in physics that never changes.
An important constant of nature from quantum physics, named after Max Planck.
A very hard, rare metal that does not rust.
The science of precise measurement.

gewusst: The prototype was the last base unit that still depended on an object and not on a constant of nature.
The prototype was never allowed to be touched with bare hands; special tongs were used.
The prototype is smaller than a drinks can, because platinum is very heavy.

teile.einleitung: Birdsong is the melodies and calls with which birds communicate. Especially in spring, the forest is full of song early in the morning. Every species of bird has its own song, and young birds first have to learn it.
wichtigste: In most bird species, it is mainly the males that sing.
Young songbirds learn their song by listening to older birds.
Most birds sing most in spring.
When many birds sing at the same time early in the morning, it is called the dawn chorus.
The nightingale is known for its beautiful song at night.
The tiny brown wren sings amazingly loudly.
Bird researchers recognise a species by its song, even if they cannot see it.
Researchers record bird calls with a microphone.

abschnitte.text: Birds make two kinds of sounds: **calls** and **song**. Calls are short and simple, for example alarm calls about a cat or contact calls with which a flock stays together. Song is longer and more melodious and serves mainly to mark a **territory** and attract a partner. In most bird species, it is mainly the males that sing.

Birds do not have vocal cords in a larynx as we do, but a voice organ of their own called the **syrinx**. It lies deep down, where the windpipe divides into the two bronchi. Some birds can use both sides of the syrinx separately and so sing two notes at the same time. Songbirds are the largest group of birds and have especially finely controlled muscles on the syrinx.

Young songbirds are not born with a finished song. They **listen to the older birds** and first practise a quiet, incomplete twittering. Over time this turns into the proper song of their species. Because they learn from their neighbours, some species even develop regional **dialects**, similar to humans.

The **nightingale** is known for its varied song, which it also performs at night. The **wren** is a tiny brown bird weighing only about 10 grams, but it sings amazingly loudly. In spring the blackbird often sings in the evening from television aerials and treetops. In spring many birds start singing even before sunrise, creating a many-voiced **dawn chorus**.

Experienced bird researchers recognise many species **by their song**, even if they cannot see the bird in the thick foliage. They record bird calls with a **microphone** and make them visible in a sonogram, a picture that shows pitch and time. Today there are also apps that recognise bird calls automatically. In Switzerland, volunteers count birds partly by their song, in order to know how the populations are doing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The voice organ of birds at the lower end of the windpipe.
An area that an animal defends against others of its kind.
The song of many birds at the same time early in the morning.
A picture that shows a song by pitch and time.

gewusst: The Australian lyrebird can imitate sounds such as camera clicks or chainsaws so well that you can hardly tell the difference.
Starlings also like to imitate other birds and even mobile phone ringtones.
In cities, some birds sing louder or higher so that they can be heard over the noise of traffic.

teile.einleitung: Zebras are black-and-white striped wild horses that live in Africa. Their striking pattern of stripes is unique to each animal, like a fingerprint. There are three species: the plains zebra, the mountain zebra and Grévy's zebra.
wichtigste: Zebras live in the wild only in Africa.
There are three species of zebra; the largest is Grévy's zebra.
According to current research, the stripes most probably protect against biting flies.
Zebras usually sleep standing up.
When fleeing they run at about 60 km/h.
Zebras often travel through the savannah together with wildebeest.
The quagga was a zebra that is now extinct.

abschnitte.text: Zebras belong to the **horse** family and are related to donkeys and domestic horses. They have a short, upright mane and a tail with a tuft. No zebra has exactly the same **pattern of stripes** as another. Under the coat their skin is dark. **Grévy's zebra** is the largest species and has particularly narrow, dense stripes.

Zebras live in the wild only in **Africa**. The common **plains zebra** lives on the grassy savannahs in the east and south of the continent. The mountain zebra lives in dry, mountainous areas in south-west Africa. Grévy's zebra is now found only in Kenya and Ethiopia and is highly endangered. All zebras need watering holes nearby, because they have to drink regularly.

Zebras mainly eat **grass**, sometimes also leaves and bark. Plains zebras live in family groups made up of one stallion, several mares and their young, the foals. Often many groups join together into large herds. Together with **wildebeest**, they travel long distances in East Africa in search of fresh grass. Plains zebras communicate with a barking call.

The main enemies of zebras are **lions** and hyenas, and at rivers also crocodiles. In the herd, many eyes and ears keep watch, and zebras usually sleep standing up so that they can flee quickly. When fleeing they reach about 60 km/h and dodge from side to side. A powerful kick from a zebra can injure even a lion. A foal can stand shortly after birth and run along with its mother.

For a long time researchers puzzled over what the stripes are good for. According to current knowledge, they most probably protect against **biting flies** such as horseflies and tsetse flies. In experiments, flies landed much less often on striped blankets than on plain ones. The stripes apparently confuse the insects' eyes as they come in to land. This is important, because such flies can transmit dangerous diseases in Africa.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most common species of zebra, which lives on the African savannahs.
A wide, warm grassland with scattered trees.
A young horse or zebra.
An extinct form of zebra from South Africa with stripes only on the front of its body.

gewusst: The last quagga died in a zoo in Amsterdam in 1883.
A zebra crossing on the road is called that because it looks like a zebra's coat.
Zebras have almost never been tamed, because they are very shy and can bite and kick hard.

teile.einleitung: When feeding birds, people put out food for wild birds, usually in winter in the garden or on the balcony. In this way you can watch tits, blackbirds and robins from close up. So that this helps the birds and does not harm them, you should follow a few rules.
wichtigste: At the bird table, tits especially like sunflower seeds.
You should not give birds bread, because it swells up in the stomach.
A bird feeder must be kept clean so that the birds do not become ill.
A bird feeder is best placed high up and with a good view.
In a seed feeder, the birds cannot step in the food.
The great tit has a yellow belly and a black head.
The robin has an orange-red breast, and the male blackbird is all black with a yellow beak.

abschnitte.text: In winter, many people hang up a **bird feeder**, a seed feeder or fat balls. Especially in snow and frost, birds find fewer insects, berries and seeds. Feeding helps mainly common garden birds and brings people closer to nature. To protect rare species, though, a natural garden with hedges, wild flowers and native shrubs is more important.

Almost all seed-eaters like **sunflower seeds**, especially tits and finches. Soft-food eaters such as blackbirds and robins prefer oat flakes, raisins or apples, which you put on the ground. Fat balls made of fat and seeds should be hung up without a plastic net, so that no birds get caught in it. **Bread** is unsuitable because it swells up in the stomach, and salted or seasoned leftovers also harm birds.

A bird feeder must be cleaned regularly, because droppings can contain pathogens. A **seed feeder** is better than an open bird table, because there the birds cannot step in the food and dirty it. You place the bird feeder **high up** and with a good view, so that no cat can creep up unnoticed. It should also not stand directly in front of a large pane of glass, because birds could otherwise fly into it.

You can recognise the **great tit** by its yellow belly and its black head with white cheeks. The blue tit is smaller and has a blue cap. The **robin** has an orange-red breast, and the male **blackbird** is all black with a yellow beak. Chaffinches, greenfinches, sparrows and sometimes a great spotted woodpecker also come to feeding places.

As well as food, birds also need water for drinking and bathing, but a **bird bath** must be filled with fresh water every day. Whether you should feed all year round is judged differently by experts. In Switzerland, the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach recommends feeding mainly in winter when there is snow and cold. If you watch birds, you can count them and report them to bird conservation organisations' public surveys.

begriffe.erklaerung: A food dispenser from which seeds slide down little by little.
Birds that eat mainly seeds and grains, for example finches.
Birds that prefer to eat fruit, insects and soft food, such as blackbirds.
A ball of fat and seeds for hanging up.

gewusst: A great tit weighs only about 20 grams, roughly as much as four sugar cubes.
On a cold winter night, small birds lose a noticeable part of their body weight and have to eat a lot during the day.
Robins are loners even in winter and defend their territory against other robins.

teile.einleitung: Hibernation is an energy-saving state that some mammals use to survive the cold season, when there is little food. Their body runs on a low flame: the temperature drops sharply, the heart beats slowly and breathing becomes shallow. In the Swiss Alps, the marmot is the best-known hibernator.
wichtigste: During hibernation, an animal's body temperature drops sharply.
During this time the animal lives on its fat reserves.
The marmot sleeps for about half a year.
Hedgehogs, edible dormice and bats also hibernate.
Squirrels, badgers and brown bears only have a winter rest.
Frogs, lizards and insects fall into winter torpor.
You should not wake animals during hibernation, because waking up costs a lot of energy.

abschnitte.text: In winter many animals can hardly find any food, and keeping warm costs a lot of energy. Some **mammals** solve the problem by almost switching their body off. In true **hibernation**, the body temperature drops to a few degrees above zero. The heart beats only a few times a minute, and the animal breathes very rarely. In this way it needs only a small part of the energy it would otherwise need.

Before winter, the animals eat until they have a thick **layer of fat**. They live on it for the whole of their hibernation. A marmot is clearly heavier in autumn than after it wakes up in spring. Many hibernators line their nest or burrow with hay, leaves or moss.

The **Alpine marmot** sleeps for about half a year, from about October to April. The whole family lies close together in a burrow deep underground, where it does not freeze. They block the entrance with earth, stones and hay. Every few weeks the animals wake up briefly and warm up before going back to sleep.

The **hedgehog** also hibernates, usually in a pile of leaves or under a hedge. In German the **edible dormouse** is called “Siebenschläfer”, “seven sleeper”, because it sleeps for about seven months. Bats hang in caves, tunnels and cellars all winter. The little hazel dormouse is a hibernator too.

Not all animals sleep so deeply. Squirrels, badgers and brown bears only have a **winter rest**: they sleep a lot, but their body temperature hardly drops, and they wake up more often. Squirrels then fetch nuts from their hiding places. Cold-blooded animals such as frogs, lizards, snakes and insects fall into **winter torpor**, because their body becomes as cold as their surroundings.

If an animal is woken from hibernation, it has to warm up its body with great effort. This uses up a lot of its fat reserves, which may then run out before spring. That is why you should never disturb bats in caves or hedgehogs in a pile of leaves. In Switzerland, many bat roosts are therefore protected or closed off in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Stored body fat that an animal can live on without food.
A light form of winter sleep in which the body temperature stays almost normal.
A rigid state that cold-blooded animals fall into when it is cold.
Describes animals whose body temperature depends on their surroundings.

gewusst: A hibernating hedgehog sometimes breathes only a few times a minute.
Marmots lose a large part of their body weight during hibernation.
Some bats hang upside down from the ceiling of a cave all winter.

teile.einleitung: A forest is a large area thickly covered with trees. It is a habitat for countless animals, plants and fungi and provides us with wood, clean air and drinking water. In Switzerland, forest covers about a third of the country's area.
wichtigste: A forest is a fairly large area on which mainly trees grow.
About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.
The most common tree in Swiss forests is the spruce.
During photosynthesis, trees release oxygen into the air.
A forest with broadleaved trees and conifers is called a mixed forest.
A protection forest protects villages and roads from avalanches, rockfall and debris flows.
Foresters look after the care of the forest.

abschnitte.text: A **forest** is more than a collection of trees; it is a whole **ecosystem**. A distinction is made between broadleaved forest, coniferous forest and **mixed forest**, in which both types of tree grow. A forest is divided into storeys: at the very bottom grow mosses, above them herbs and shrubs, and at the very top the treetops form the roof. Around the world there are, for example, tropical rainforests, broadleaved forests and the huge coniferous forests of the north.

In Switzerland, forest covers about a third of the area, that is, about 1.3 million hectares. The most common tree is the **spruce**, followed by the **beech** as the most common broadleaved tree. Other important species are the silver fir, larch, Scots pine, maple and ash. There is especially a lot of forest in the Jura, in the Prealps and on the south side of the Alps.

Almost half of Switzerland's forest protects people from natural hazards. Such a **protection forest** slows down avalanches, stops stones and prevents the ground from slipping away in heavy rain. Because many forests were cut down in the 19th century, there were severe floods. That is why in 1876 the Confederation passed a first forest law, and to this day the area of forest in Switzerland may not, in principle, be reduced.

Roe deer, foxes, badgers, woodpeckers, owls and countless insects live in the forest. On the ground, fungi, worms and tiny creatures break down the leaves into fertile soil. **Deadwood**, that is, dead trees, is especially valuable for many beetles and birds. Mosses, ferns and woodland flowers such as the wood anemone also need the shady forest floor.

During **photosynthesis**, trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. The forest filters rainwater and provides clean drinking water. Wood is an important raw material for houses, furniture, paper and heating. For many people the forest is also a place for walking, playing and relaxing, and in Switzerland anyone may enter it freely.

Hot, dry summers are hard on many trees, especially the spruce at low altitudes. Weakened trees are more easily attacked by **bark beetles**. That is why foresters are increasingly planting tree species that cope better with drought, for example oaks. A varied mixed forest is regarded as more resilient than a forest with only one tree species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A community of plants, animals and fungi together with its surroundings.
A forest with broadleaved trees and conifers.
A forest that protects people from avalanches, rockfall or landslides.
Dead trees and branches that provide a habitat for many animals.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar and release oxygen.

gewusst: Switzerland's forest has been growing for decades, especially in the Alps, where Alpine pastures are no longer used.
Beneath a forest floor there is a huge hidden network of fungal threads that is connected to the tree roots.
A single large beech can take up many thousands of litres of water a year from the ground.

teile.einleitung: Science scepticism means that people distrust science and its results. A certain amount of critical questioning is healthy and is even part of science itself. It becomes a problem when well-supported results are rejected for no reason; this is called science denial.
wichtigste: Healthy scepticism checks the evidence; science denial ignores it.
According to Robert Merton, organised scepticism is a basic norm of science.
The Science Barometer Switzerland studies how the population feels about science.
Typical denial techniques are fake experts, cherry-picking and impossible expectations.
The book “Merchants of Doubt” describes how doubt about research was deliberately spread.
When talking to sceptical people, it helps to listen and to respond to their values.

abschnitte.text: In science, every claim is critically checked before it is accepted. In 1942 the sociologist **Robert Merton** called this **organised scepticism** and counted it among the basic norms of science. Healthy scepticism asks for evidence and changes its mind when good evidence is available. Science denial, on the other hand, ignores evidence or looks only for reasons to reject it.

The **Science Barometer Switzerland** is a regular survey carried out by researchers at the University of Zurich. It studies how the population feels about science. The results show that most people in Switzerland trust science fairly or very much. A smaller group, however, is clearly critical.

The researcher John Cook summed up common techniques under the abbreviation FLICC. They include **fake experts**, that is, so-called experts without real expertise. With **cherry-picking**, only the data that fits your own opinion is chosen. An impossible expectation is demanding absolute certainty before acting. On top of that come logical fallacies and conspiracy stories that declare a broad research consensus to be a secret plot.

In 2010 the historian Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway published the book “**Merchants of Doubt**”. In it they show how some companies and people deliberately spread doubt about research results. This concerned, for example, the harm caused by smoking and later climate change. The aim was not to find the truth but to delay laws and rules.

People are rarely convinced by a flood of facts. It is considered more helpful to **listen** and to respond to people's values and worries. You can explain how science works, and that knowledge is allowed to change with new evidence. It also helps to know typical deception techniques in advance; this is described as a kind of **vaccination** against misinformation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Questioning and checking critically before you believe something.
Rejecting well-supported research results without good reasons.
The shared view of the vast majority of experts.
Choosing only the data that fits your own opinion.

gewusst: Scientific findings are always provisional until better evidence turns up, and that is a strength.
The word scepticism comes from Greek and originally meant “looking at” or “examining”.
On social media, misinformation often spreads faster than its correction.

teile.einleitung: The vacuole is a space filled with liquid inside a cell, surrounded by a thin skin. In plant cells it is often so large that it fills almost the whole cell. Without it, lettuce leaves would look limp and flowers wilted.
