wichtigste: The vacuole is a part of the cell enclosed by its own membrane.
In plant cells, the large vacuole stores water and dissolved substances.
The liquid in the vacuole is called cell sap.
The filled vacuole presses from inside against the cell wall; this pressure is called turgor.
If the vacuole loses water, the internal pressure falls and the plant wilts.
Many red and blue flower pigments are found in the cell sap of the vacuole.
Freshwater single-celled organisms such as the slipper animalcule pump out surplus water with the contractile vacuole.

abschnitte.text: The word **vacuole** comes from the Latin “vacuus” and means “empty”, because under the microscope it looks like an empty space. In reality it is filled with liquid. It is surrounded by its own membrane, which in plants is called the **tonoplast**. In a fully grown plant cell it can take up most of the space in the cell.

The liquid in the vacuole is called **cell sap**. It consists mainly of water, in which sugars, salts, acids and other substances are dissolved. The vacuole serves as a storeroom, but also as a place where the cell puts its waste. Some plants store bitter substances in it so that animals do not eat them.

A well-filled vacuole presses the rest of the cell's contents firmly against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called **turgor**. It works in a similar way to the air in a bicycle inner tube, which becomes plump and firm because of it. If there is a lack of water, the vacuoles shrink, the turgor falls and the plant lets its leaves droop. If you water it in time, it stands up again.

Many red, purple and blue pigments of flowers and fruits are dissolved in the cell sap. These include the **anthocyanins**, which colour, for example, red cabbage, cherries and blueberries. The colour of these substances can change depending on the acidity of the cell sap. That is why red cabbage juice turns reddish with vinegar and rather blue or green with bicarbonate of soda.

If you put plant cells into a salty solution, the vacuoles lose water. The cell contents shrink and come away from the cell wall; this is called **plasmolysis**. You can see this well with the red skin of an onion under the microscope. If you then add pure water again, the vacuoles fill up once more.

Single-celled organisms in fresh water, such as the **slipper animalcule**, constantly take in water, because their insides are saltier than their surroundings. So that they do not burst, they have a **contractile vacuole**. It collects the surplus water and pumps it out at regular intervals. Under the microscope you can see it fill up and contract again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The liquid in the vacuole, with water and dissolved substances.
The pressure with which the filled vacuole presses against the cell wall.
The cell contents coming away from the cell wall when the cell loses water.
The thin skin that surrounds the vacuole in plant cells.
A small part of a cell with a particular task.

gewusst: The name vacuole actually means “the emptiness”, even though it is full of liquid.
Animal cells also have vacuoles, but they are usually much smaller than in plants.
In the kitchen you can use red cabbage juice to test whether something is acidic or alkaline.

teile.einleitung: In cell division, one cell becomes two new cells, the daughter cells. This is the only way living things can grow and replace worn-out or damaged cells. Every second, millions of cells divide in our body.
wichtigste: In cell division, one mother cell becomes two daughter cells.
Before division, the DNA is copied.
The division of the nucleus in body cells is called mitosis.
After mitosis, each human body cell again has 46 chromosomes.
The spindle apparatus pulls the chromosomes apart.
Cell division is used for growth and for replacing cells.
If cells divide uncontrollably, cancer can develop.

abschnitte.text: All living things are made of **cells**, the smallest building blocks of life. New cells always form by the division of cells that already exist. The doctor Rudolf Virchow realised this around 1855 and summed it up in the sentence “Every cell comes from a cell”. In multicellular organisms such as humans, **cell division** is used for growth and for replacing old cells. Bacteria multiply by simply splitting in two.

Between two divisions comes **interphase**. During this time the cell grows and does its normal work. Above all, though, all the genetic information, the **DNA**, is copied exactly. This means that later each daughter cell can receive a complete copy. Interphase is usually the longest stage in the life of a cell.

The division of the nucleus in body cells is called **mitosis**. In prophase, the DNA condenses into visible **chromosomes**. In metaphase, all the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell. In anaphase, the **spindle apparatus**, a framework of fine fibres, pulls the halves of each chromosome towards the two poles. In telophase, two new nuclei form.

After the nucleus has divided, the rest of the cell divides too; this is called **cytokinesis**. In animal cells, the cell pinches in at the middle like a balloon with a string pulled tight around it. In plant cells this is not possible because of the firm cell wall. There, a **cell plate** forms between the daughter cells and becomes a new cell wall. In the end there are two cells with the same genetic information, in humans with 46 chromosomes each.

Without cell division, no wound would heal. The skin constantly renews itself, and old flakes of skin fall off. Every second, millions of new **blood cells** are made in the bone marrow. Hair and fingernails also grow because cells divide at their roots.

Normally, cell division in the body is strictly controlled. If this control fails, cells divide uncontrollably and **cancer** can develop. Cancer cells form tumours that push aside healthy tissue. Many cancer medicines work by slowing down cell division. That is why cell division is studied intensively in medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A package of coiled-up DNA that carries the genetic information.
The division of the nucleus into two identical daughter nuclei.
The molecule in which the blueprint of a living thing is stored.
A framework of fibres that pulls the chromosomes apart.
The time between two cell divisions.

gewusst: Under good conditions, a gut bacterium can divide about every 20 minutes.
The term mitosis was coined in 1882 by the German researcher Walther Flemming.
Nerve cells in the brain hardly ever divide in adults and can last a whole lifetime.

teile.einleitung: The toothbrush is a small tool with a handle and bristles that we use to keep our teeth clean. It removes bits of food and plaque, which could otherwise cause tooth decay. There are manual toothbrushes and electric toothbrushes.
wichtigste: With a toothbrush you remove bits of food and plaque from your teeth.
The many fine hairs of a toothbrush are called bristles.
You put toothpaste on the toothbrush, ideally with fluoride.
You should brush your teeth for about 2 to 3 minutes.
You should change your toothbrush after about 3 months.
In China there were toothbrushes with bristles more than 1000 years ago.
An electric toothbrush moves the brush head by itself.

abschnitte.text: A **toothbrush** consists of a handle, a neck and a brush head. On the head are many **bristles**, arranged in tufts. Today the bristles are usually made of plastic such as nylon. For children there are smaller heads and soft bristles so that the gums are not hurt.

Thousands of years ago, people chewed on fibrous twigs to clean their teeth, and in some countries people still do this today. In **China** there were toothbrushes with bristles more than 1000 years ago, attached to a handle made of bone or bamboo. The bristles often came from pigs. Only in the 1930s did toothbrushes with nylon bristles come onto the market.

In an **electric toothbrush**, a small motor moves the brush head back and forth by itself or makes it rotate. One of the first electric toothbrushes was developed in Switzerland in the 1950s. Electric toothbrushes can clean especially thoroughly if you guide them correctly. But your teeth also get clean with a manual toothbrush if you brush carefully.

You should brush at least twice a day, ideally after breakfast and before going to sleep, for about 2 to 3 minutes. In many Swiss schools, children learn the **KAI method** for this, from the German words for chewing, outer and inner surfaces: first the chewing surfaces, then the outer surfaces, then the inner surfaces. A pea-sized amount of **toothpaste** with fluoride is enough and strengthens the tooth enamel. Dental floss or a small interdental brush helps between the teeth.

abschnitte.titel: Why brushing your teeth is so important
abschnitte.text: Bacteria live in the mouth that feed on sugar and produce acids as they do so. These acids attack the tooth enamel and can cause **tooth decay**. The sticky **plaque** forms anew every day and so has to be brushed away regularly. Healthy teeth are important for chewing, for speaking clearly and for a nice smile.

After about three months the bristles are worn out and point in all directions. Then the brush no longer cleans well and should be replaced. After brushing, you rinse the toothbrush with water and let it dry upright. Everyone should have their own toothbrush and not share it with others.

begriffe.erklaerung: The many fine hairs on the head of the toothbrush.
A sticky film of bacteria that forms on the teeth.
Holes in the teeth caused by acids from bacteria.
A substance in toothpaste that makes the tooth enamel harder.

gewusst: The first toothbrushes in Europe often had bristles from pigs or horses.
You can tell a worn-out toothbrush by its bristles sticking out sideways.
Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the human body.

teile.einleitung: Repulsion is a force that pushes two things away from each other. You can feel it when you try to press two magnets together with the same poles facing. Electrically charged objects can also repel each other.
wichtigste: Like magnetic poles repel each other: north pole and north pole, or south pole and south pole.
Unlike poles attract each other, which is the opposite of repulsion.
Repulsion works even before two magnets touch.
If you turn one of the magnets round, they attract instead of repelling each other.
An iron nail is never repelled by a magnet, only attracted.
Only another magnet can repel a magnet, which is how you can be sure something is a magnet.
Like electric charges also repel each other.

abschnitte.text: In **repulsion** two objects push each other away without anyone touching them. With magnets this happens when **like poles** face each other. The closer the magnets get, the stronger the force becomes. You feel a soft, invisible resistance like a cushion of air.

Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**. If a pole repels the north pole of another magnet, it is itself a north pole. Two magnets that repel each other attract as soon as you turn one round. Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted, but never repelled. That is why repulsion is the reliable test of whether an object is itself a magnet.

If you put several **ring magnets** on a rod with like poles facing each other, some of them float in the air. Repulsion holds them up against gravity. If you press the top magnet down and let go, it springs back up like a spring. The more magnets there are on top, the closer together the lower ones move.

Electric charges can also repel each other. If you rub a balloon on your hair, the hairs all get the same charge. Because **like charges** repel each other, the hairs then stick out in all directions. Positive and negative charges, on the other hand, attract each other. In atomic nuclei the positively charged protons also repel each other.

Some **maglev trains** use magnetic forces so that the train floats above the track without wheels. In Japan such a train floats several centimetres above the guideway thanks to very strong magnets. Magnetic bearings in machines also use magnetic forces so that parts turn almost without friction. In everyday life you find repulsion in magnetic toys and in experiments at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two places on a magnet where the force is strongest.
The pole of a magnet that points to geographic north when the magnet can turn freely.
The opposite of repulsion: things move towards each other.
A property of particles that can be positive or negative.

gewusst: The repulsion of two magnets also works through paper, wood and water.
If you break a magnet into two pieces, each piece again has a north and a south pole.
Without the electric repulsion of electrons you could fall through a chair onto the floor.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest and simplest chemical element and has the atomic number 1 in the periodic table. It is a colourless, odourless gas and the most common element in the whole universe. The stars are made of hydrogen, and it is found in every drop of water.
wichtigste: Hydrogen has the atomic number 1 in the periodic table.
Its chemical symbol is H.
It is the lightest and most common element in the universe.
Hydrogen is a colourless, odourless and flammable gas.
Together with oxygen it forms water.
In the Sun, hydrogen fuses into helium and so provides energy.
Hydrogen can be used as a fuel for vehicles.

abschnitte.text: Hydrogen is in first place at the very top left of the **periodic table**. Its **atomic number** is 1, because a hydrogen atom has only one single proton in its nucleus. Exactly one electron circles around the nucleus. Its chemical symbol H comes from the Latin name hydrogenium.

About three quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe is made of hydrogen. Stars like our Sun are huge balls of hydrogen and helium. Inside them, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is **nuclear fusion**. On Earth, on the other hand, hydrogen is found almost only in compounds, above all in water.

Hydrogen is a gas that you can neither see nor smell. It is about fourteen times lighter than air. Mixed with oxygen it forms explosive **oxyhydrogen**, which reacts violently with a spark. In this reaction the only product is water.

In 1766 the English researcher **Henry Cavendish** described a flammable gas that forms water when it burns. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier later gave it the name “hydrogène”, which means water-maker. The German word “Wasserstoff” (water substance) came from this. In the past, airships were filled with hydrogen, until in 1937 the Hindenburg went up in flames in the USA.

In a **fuel cell**, hydrogen reacts with oxygen, producing electricity and water. Vehicles with fuel cells therefore give off only water vapour. In Switzerland, lorries powered by hydrogen have been on the roads since 2020, and there are a few hydrogen filling stations. If the hydrogen is produced with electricity from sun, wind or hydropower, it is called **green hydrogen**.

Industry needs large amounts of hydrogen, for example to make ammonia for fertiliser. Rockets such as Ariane use liquid hydrogen as fuel. For this it has to be cooled to minus 253 degrees. There are also heavier forms of hydrogen, the **isotopes** deuterium and tritium.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the place in the periodic table.
A device that produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.
A kind of atom of an element with a different number of neutrons in the nucleus.

gewusst: Hydrogen is so light that it slowly escapes from the Earth's atmosphere into space.
Talking in a high voice after breathing in helium is harmless fun, but with hydrogen it would be very dangerous, because hydrogen burns.
Every second, the Sun turns hundreds of millions of tonnes of hydrogen into helium.

teile.einleitung: The cell is the smallest building block of life. All living things are made of cells: a bacterium of a single one, a human of many trillions. Most cells are so small that you can only see them under a microscope.
wichtigste: All living things are made of cells.
A human is made of many trillions of cells.
The nucleus controls the cell.
Every cell is wrapped in a thin cell membrane.
Plant cells have a firm cell wall; animal cells do not.
Small chlorophyll grains make many plant cells green.
A bacterium consists of just one single cell.

abschnitte.text: A cell is the smallest unit that can live on its own. It takes in food, gets **energy** from it, grows and can divide. Most cells are only about a hundredth of a millimetre in size. So you need a **microscope** to see them. But there are exceptions, such as nerve cells, whose extensions can be up to a metre long.

Every cell is wrapped in a thin **cell membrane**. It decides which substances get in and out. Inside there is a jelly-like liquid, the cytoplasm. The **nucleus** contains the genetic information and controls the cell like a command centre. The mitochondria are the power stations of the cell, because energy is obtained from food in them.

In addition to the cell membrane, plant cells have a firm **cell wall** made of cellulose. It gives the plant stability, which is why a tree can stand upright without bones. Many plant cells contain small green **chlorophyll grains**, the chloroplasts. In them the plant makes sugar using sunlight. Animal cells and human cells have neither a cell wall nor chloroplasts.

Some living things consist of just one single cell; they are called **single-celled organisms**. They include bacteria, but also slipper animalcules and yeasts. Bacteria have no true nucleus; their genetic information lies loose in the cell. Plants, animals and humans are **multicellular organisms**, in which many cells work together. A human is made of many trillions of cells, including skin cells, muscle cells, nerve cells and blood cells.

In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at a thin piece of cork under his home-made microscope. He saw lots of small hollow spaces that reminded him of the tiny rooms in a monastery. So he called them “cells”, after the Latin word “cellula” for a small room. A little later the Dutchman Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was the first to discover living single-celled organisms in a drop of water. Since the 19th century we have known that all living things are made up of cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin skin that wraps around every cell.
A firm covering around plant cells that gives them support.
A green chlorophyll grain in which plants make sugar using light.
A tiny power station in the cell that supplies energy.
A living thing that consists of just one single cell.

gewusst: Every second, millions of cells in the human body die and are replaced by new ones.
Red blood cells are the most common cells in the human body.
You can see the cells of onion skin clearly even with a simple school microscope.

teile.einleitung: In a census, a state collects data about its whole population. In this way it finds out how many people live in a country, how old they are and how they live. These figures help, for example, in planning schools, roads and hospitals.
wichtigste: A census is a collection of data about the whole population.
In German it is called “Volkszählung” or “Zensus”.
The first federal census took place in 1850.
Until 2000, censuses in Switzerland usually took place every ten years.
In 2000 there was the last traditional census with questionnaires for all households.
Since 2010 the census has been carried out every year, mainly with data from registers.
The annual structural survey adds a questionnaire to the register data.

abschnitte.text: A **census** is a large survey in which data is collected about all the inhabitants of a country. Not only people are counted, but also details such as age, place of residence, language, occupation or size of home. The word **census** comes from Latin. Even in ancient Rome, citizens were counted regularly in order to plan taxes and soldiers.

Shortly after the founding of the federal state, the first **federal census** took place in 1850. After that the population was usually counted every ten years. For a long time all households filled in paper questionnaires for it, and later also on the computer. The last such full census took place in 2000.

Since 2010 the census has been carried out every year. Most of the information comes from **registers**, that is, from lists kept by the municipalities, cantons and Confederation, for example the residents' registers. In addition there is the **structural survey**, in which a sample of about 200,000 people is asked every year. Because not everyone has to fill in a questionnaire any more, the method is cheaper and less of a burden on the population.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Statistical Office** (FSO), based in Neuchâtel, is responsible. It analyses the data and publishes the results. Personal details are protected and are only shown in summarised form. In this way we learn, for example, that in 2024 Switzerland had more than 9 million inhabitants for the first time.

abschnitte.titel: What the figures are used for
abschnitte.text: The results help with many decisions. Municipalities see whether they need more school buildings or old people's homes. The distribution of seats in the National Council among the cantons is based on the population figures. Researchers and companies use the data to understand how the country is changing, for example in languages or types of family.

begriffe.erklaerung: A count of the whole population; in German “Volkszählung” or “Zensus”.
An official list in which, for example, all the inhabitants of a municipality are entered.
A selected smaller group that is asked on behalf of everyone.
Collecting, sorting and analysing numbers and data.

gewusst: At the first federal census in 1850, only about 2.4 million people lived in Switzerland.
Today the great majority of people in Switzerland no longer have to fill in a census questionnaire at all.
From the data we know which languages are spoken at home in Switzerland.
